items.title: 1. Why vascular patients are different: disease biology, organ reserve and risk
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## BEFORE YOU START — What a vascular operation is actually trying to do

A vascular surgeon is primarily restoring flow, removing a source of emboli, or preventing rupture. The anaesthetist must keep the heart and brain perfused while the surgeon may temporarily obstruct an artery, cause deliberate ischaemia, manipulate fragile plaque or introduce a graft. That tension explains most of vascular anaesthesia.

- **Three operations to picture:** (1) **Endarterectomy** = open an artery and remove plaque from within its wall; (2) **bypass** = sew a new conduit around a diseased segment, often using the patient’s vein; (3) **endovascular repair** = pass wires, balloons and stents through arterial access, guided by X-ray, without opening the full diseased segment.

- **Three different vessel diseases:** **stenosis** means narrowed lumen, producing reduced flow or an embolic source; **aneurysm** means a pathologically dilated segment at risk of rupture; **dissection** means blood travelling within a split vessel wall, potentially obstructing branches or rupturing.

- **What is unusual about the patient?** Vascular disease is usually systemic. A person with a blocked femoral artery frequently also has coronary artery disease, hypertension, chronic kidney disease or cerebrovascular disease. Poor walking distance due to claudication may hide limited cardiac exercise tolerance.

- **What is unusual about the operation?** Arterial heparinisation may make regional techniques unsafe; arterial clamps create abrupt pressure and flow changes; reperfusion releases acid, potassium and inflammatory mediators; postoperative neurological, visceral and limb examination matters as much as an uncomplicated emergence.

## A small vocabulary you should know before the specialist chapters

- **AAA** = abdominal aortic aneurysm; **rAAA** = ruptured AAA; **EVAR** = endovascular aneurysm repair; **TEVAR** = thoracic EVAR; **F/BEVAR** = fenestrated or branched EVAR, in which side branches preserve renal/visceral arterial flow.

- **CEA** = carotid endarterectomy; **CAS** = carotid artery stenting; **PAD** = peripheral arterial disease; **CLTI** = chronic limb-threatening ischaemia; **ALI** = acute limb ischaemia.

- **ACT** = activated clotting time, a rapid bedside measure used to guide large-dose unfractionated heparin; **UFH** = unfractionated heparin; **P2Y12 inhibitor** = platelet drug such as clopidogrel; **DAPT** = dual antiplatelet therapy.

- **SCPP** = spinal cord perfusion pressure, approximated by MAP minus the greater of CSF or relevant venous pressure; **CSF drain** = lumbar catheter that can lower CSF pressure in selected high-risk thoracic repairs; **MHP** = major haemorrhage protocol.

Practical starting question for every case: **Which vessel is being treated, by what operation, and what organs temporarily lose blood supply?** Then ask whether haemorrhage, ischaemia, reperfusion, embolisation or anticoagulation is the dominant immediate risk.

## 1.1 The vascular patient has a systemic disease, not merely a surgical lesion

Atherosclerosis is a chronic, inflammatory, lipid-driven disease of the arterial intima. Endothelial dysfunction permits lipoprotein retention, macrophage recruitment and development of a fibrous or lipid-rich plaque. Progressive stenosis reduces flow reserve: resting blood flow may remain sufficient, but exercise, hypotension, anaemia and increased tissue demand expose the limitation. Plaque rupture or erosion causes platelet activation, thrombosis and acute occlusion. Calcification makes vessels difficult to clamp, cannulate and reconstruct; diffuse atheroma increases embolic and access-related risk.

The coronary, carotid, renal, mesenteric and leg circulations share these mechanisms. A patient presenting for an infrainguinal bypass may therefore have silent coronary disease, impaired LV relaxation, carotid plaque and CKD. Vascular surgery adds major physiological stresses—rapid afterload changes, ischaemia–reperfusion, blood loss, anticoagulation and inflammatory activation—to pre-existing limited reserve. Preventing myocardial infarction or kidney injury is not a matter of choosing an anaesthetic drug in isolation: it is about preventing excessive demand or inadequate supply while treating the underlying disease.

Aneurysmal disease is related but distinct. An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a full-thickness dilatation involving structural degradation of elastin/collagen and altered wall mechanics. Atherosclerosis commonly coexists, but aneurysm expansion is not simply an atherosclerotic stenosis. Dissection begins when blood separates aortic wall layers through an intimal tear or intramural haemorrhage. A type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and threatens the coronary arteries, aortic valve and pericardium; type B originates distal to the left subclavian artery and threatens the distal organs through true-lumen compression, branch-vessel obstruction or rupture. These mechanisms determine whether the appropriate immediate response is anti-impulse therapy, operative repair or haemorrhage control.

## 1.2 Distinguish the major clinical syndromes before planning anaesthesia

| **Syndrome**                              | **What has failed?**                                      | **Typical clues**                                                                           | **What changes management?**                                                                                                |
|-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Intermittent claudication                 | Exercise-related skeletal-muscle perfusion reserve        | Reproducible calf/thigh/buttock pain relieved by rest                                       | Walking programme, smoking cessation, vascular risk treatment; revascularisation for persistent lifestyle-limiting symptoms |
| Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) | Resting tissue perfusion, usually with multilevel disease | Ischaemic rest pain, ulcer or gangrene for >2 weeks; diabetes may mask pain                | Limb viability, infection, angiographic anatomy, patient risk, conduit availability                                         |
| Acute limb ischaemia (ALI)                | Abrupt arterial inflow loss                               | Sudden pain, pallor, coldness, pulselessness, sensory and motor deficit                     | Rutherford class and urgency of revascularisation; immediate UFH unless contraindicated                                     |
| Symptomatic carotid stenosis              | Artery-to-artery embolism or flow failure                 | Ipsilateral retinal or hemispheric TIA/minor stroke                                         | Recent symptoms and degree of stenosis, infarct size, timing and treatment risk                                             |
| AAA                                       | Loss of aortic structural integrity                       | Usually asymptomatic; occasionally abdominal/back pain or rupture                           | Size/growth, symptoms, anatomy, fitness, suitability for EVAR versus open repair                                            |
| Acute aortic syndrome                     | Aortic wall disruption                                    | Abrupt severe chest/back/abdominal pain, pulse deficits, neurological or organ malperfusion | Type A versus B; complicated versus uncomplicated; CTA anatomy                                                              |

**Clinical distinction:** claudication is not synonymous with limb-threatening ischaemia, and a cool pulseless limb is not automatically irreversible. Loss of motor function is particularly ominous in acute ischaemia. Conversely, a patient with diabetes and sensory neuropathy may have advanced tissue loss while reporting little pain.

## 1.3 Quantifying peripheral disease and whole-patient risk

A focused vascular history asks about walking distance, rest pain, tissue loss, prior grafts, amputations, carotid symptoms, coronary symptoms, functional capacity, smoking, diabetes, renal impairment, dialysis timing, frailty, infection and previous complications of anaesthesia. Examine heart and lungs, volume status, peripheral pulses, skin temperature, wounds, bilateral pressures, neurological function and dialysis access. Document **baseline** limb power, sensation and pulses because postoperative change is a critical finding.

The ankle–brachial index (ABI) is ankle systolic pressure divided by the higher brachial systolic pressure. An ABI ≤0.90 supports PAD; values <0.40 indicate severe perfusion impairment, but values alone do not define CLTI. Noncompressible calcified arteries, common in diabetes and CKD, may yield spuriously high ABI (>1.40); toe pressures, toe–brachial index, pulse volume recordings and duplex are then more informative. Toe pressure <30 mmHg or ankle systolic pressure <50 mmHg suggests severe ischaemia in an appropriate clinical context. Duplex identifies lesion location and graft patency; CT or MR angiography provides a procedural map but introduces contrast or MRI-device considerations.

A vascular operation is frequently an elevated-risk noncardiac procedure. Estimate cardiac risk with a validated method (e.g. RCRI, NSQIP/MICA), recognise the limitations of these scores in complex aortic operations, and assess functional capacity using history or the Duke Activity Status Index when feasible. Poor functional capacity, frailty and cardiovascular disease predict harm, but routine stress tests for every vascular patient are inappropriate. Obtain a test only if it is clinically indicated and would change management, e.g. prompt investigation of active cardiac symptoms or a genuinely beneficial revascularisation. The September 2026 reaffirmation of the AHA/ACC perioperative cardiovascular guideline confirms the substance of the 2024 recommendations without changing them [1].

**Find unstable disease first.** An acute coronary syndrome, decompensated heart failure, unstable tachy- or bradyarrhythmia, severe symptomatic valve disease or uncontrolled infection may require treatment before elective repair. Urgent threatened-limb or ruptured-aneurysm surgery cannot usually wait for exhaustive optimisation; that is why readiness for physiological deterioration is central to vascular anaesthesia.

### Focused investigations and how they alter a plan

- **ECG** for rhythm, conduction, previous infarction, LV hypertrophy and active ischaemic change. An ECG is not a test of coronary perfusion reserve.
- **Hb, platelet count, coagulation studies and group-and-crossmatch** proportional to anticipated blood loss and anticoagulant exposure; assess iron deficiency and correct anaemia when there is sufficient lead time.
- **Creatinine/eGFR, potassium, glucose/HbA1c** for contrast planning, dialysis timing and drug adjustments; a normal creatinine in a frail patient does not exclude impaired GFR.
- **TTE** when symptoms, examination or prior findings suggest significant ventricular or valvular pathology; focus on EF and filling/diastolic function, RV performance, significant stenosis, and pulmonary pressure rather than simply “normal echo”.
- **Risk-directed troponin and natriuretic peptides** may assist assessment and postoperative surveillance in high-risk patients. Interpret troponin trends and clinical context; elevations are not automatically type 1 MI.
- **CTA** for aortic anatomy: proximal neck and iliac access for EVAR, branch-vessel involvement in dissection, landing zones for TEVAR, atheroma burden and possibility of left subclavian coverage. A complex operation cannot be adequately planned without knowing its anatomical extent.

## 1.4 Optimisation is treatment of risk, not a quest for perfect numbers

Smoking cessation improves cardiovascular and pulmonary health and reduces wound complications. Even a short opportunity should trigger cessation support and nicotine replacement as appropriate; longer abstinence generally brings greater benefit. Continue statins and appropriate antiplatelet secondary prevention. Optimise heart failure without precipitating hypovolaemia. Treat significant anaemia and diabetes; ensure appropriate nutrition, mobility and prehabilitation where surgery can wait. Control infection and protect tissues with ischaemic ulcers. Obtain a shared plan for antithrombotics and neuraxial techniques—stopping an antiplatelet drug may endanger a carotid or peripheral stent, while continuing it may constrain regional approaches.

**Medication decisions follow the indication and procedure:**

| **Medication**    | **Usual perioperative principle**                                                                                                                                        | **Why it matters / important caveat**                                                                                                        |
|-------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Chronic β-blocker | Continue if tolerated; do not newly start high-dose treatment on surgery day                                                                                             | Avoids rebound tachycardia and ischaemia; aggressive initiation can cause hypotension, bradycardia and stroke (POISE)                        |
| Statin            | Continue and initiate for usual secondary-prevention indications                                                                                                         | Reduces ongoing atherosclerotic risk; discontinuation removes long-term protection                                                           |
| ACE inhibitor/ARB | For treated hypertension, withholding approximately 24 h before major surgery can reduce induction hypotension; when indicated for HFrEF, continuation may be reasonable | Individualise; hypotension may be dangerous during cross-clamping and carotid surgery; balance against heart failure needs                   |
| SGLT2 inhibitor   | Hold ≥3 days before elective surgery (ertugliflozin ≥4 days); check blood ketones if unwell or urgent                                                                    | Euglycaemic ketoacidosis can occur during fasting, infection and major vascular stress; normal glucose is not reassuring [1]               |
| Antiplatelet(s)   | Decide jointly for CEA, CAS, EVAR and limb interventions                                                                                                                 | Aspirin frequently continues; carotid stenting typically requires dual antiplatelet therapy; a recent coronary stent creates additional risk |
| Anticoagulants    | Assess thrombotic indication, renal function, bleeding risk and regional technique                                                                                       | Avoid indiscriminate bridging; use drug-specific and neuraxial timing recommendations                                                        |
| Insulin           | Continue essential basal insulin with adjusted dosing; monitor glucose/ketones                                                                                           | Prevents insulin-deficient ketosis and reduces infection and wound risk; major cases may require IV insulin                                  |
| Diuretics         | Adjust for volume and potassium                                                                                                                                          | Excessive preoperative diuresis can predispose to induction collapse and AKI; withholding may worsen pulmonary congestion                    |

Patients on dialysis often benefit from haemodialysis close to surgery, commonly the preceding day, to achieve suitable fluid status and electrolytes. Protect an AV fistula arm from BP cuffs, arterial puncture and avoidable cannulation. If dialysis occurs shortly before surgery, ask about intradialytic hypotension and residual heparin. Do not label renal impairment an automatic indication for large fluid loads: overload may be worse than modest transient renal hypoperfusion.

## 1.5 Why vascular disease amplifies postoperative complications

Poor skin microcirculation, diabetes, uraemia, malnutrition, tissue oedema and graft implantation increase wound infection and dehiscence risk. Impaired peripheral sensation makes positioning neuropathies and pressure injuries harder to detect; carefully protect heels, peroneal nerves, sacrum and the contralateral ischaemic limb. Systemic inflammation, hypercoagulability, embolism and haemodynamic lability promote perioperative MI, stroke and AKI. Anaesthetic management should protect tissue oxygen delivery while avoiding oedema: adequate Hb, controlled temperature, prompt treatment of hypotension, anticoagulant review, wound care and early recognition of graft compromise are intertwined. A technically successful bypass is not a success if the new graft thromboses in recovery or the patient develops an unrecognised compartment syndrome.

## 1.6 An exam-ready perioperative plan for each major comorbidity

**Use this seven-condition framework for SS_VS 1.2.** Chapters elsewhere teach the full underlying diseases; these notes must still explain how each condition changes the operation, induction, vascular control and recovery. The decision sequence is: identify severity/stability → optimise what can safely be changed → plan perfusion and drug management → monitor for the characteristic postoperative complication.

### Ischaemic heart disease (IHD)

Before elective surgery, ask about angina frequency, recent ACS/PCI, functional reserve and coronary medications; poor walking distance from claudication is not a direct measure of cardiac limitation. Obtain ECG and risk-directed biomarkers; investigate new unstable symptoms, but do not revascularise stable coronary disease solely to lower the risk of a planned vascular operation. Continue established β-blockers and statins where tolerated; coordinate aspirin/P2Y12 timing with the coronary and vascular indications. During clamping, balance afterload, coronary perfusion pressure, heart rate and haemoglobin; during bleeding or unclamping, avoid sustained hypotension and tachycardia. Postoperatively, monitor for silent myocardial injury (serial ECG/troponin where indicated), heart failure and arrhythmia rather than waiting for chest pain [1].

### Cardiac failure and ventricular dysfunction

Define whether the patient has reduced EF, diastolic dysfunction/LVH, RV failure or important valve disease; ask about orthopnoea, oedema, congestion, recent admissions and exercise tolerance. Decompensated HF warrants treatment before elective repair, whereas rupture or threatened-limb surgery requires a rescue-ready plan. A stiff LV is preload-sensitive yet vulnerable to fluid overload; a failing systolic LV may deteriorate with the sudden afterload of a high clamp. Use arterial monitoring and targeted echo/flow assessment for higher-risk surgery; titrate fluid, vasopressor and inotrope to the mechanism rather than a CVP target. Preserve rhythm and coronary perfusion. After operation watch for pulmonary oedema, low output, renal injury and myocardial injury [1].

### Arrhythmia and cardiac devices

Establish the rhythm, haemodynamic consequences, burden of AF, ventricular rate, thromboembolic risk, anticoagulant indication and any pacemaker/ICD dependence. Correct significant potassium/magnesium abnormalities and assess recent syncope or unexplained tachycardia. Plan anticoagulant interruption/restart around surgical bleeding, procedural heparinisation and regional catheters; routine bridging is inappropriate for most patients. Agree device interrogation, electrosurgery and external pacing/defibrillation arrangements where relevant. Treat unstable perioperative tachyarrhythmia with immediate resuscitation/cardioversion as appropriate, not prolonged rate-control attempts; evaluate reversible bleeding, ischaemia, hypoxia and electrolyte triggers [1].

### Chronic hypertension

Assess usual home/clinic pressure, end-organ disease, medications, LVH and any secondary causes. A single elevated preoperative measurement is not itself proof of an unstable patient; assess persistence, symptoms, urgency and institutional guidance. Continue chronic β-blockade, and individualise ACEI/ARB withholding or continuation by indication, HF status and procedure. Avoid profound induction hypotension in a chronically hypertensive patient with impaired autoregulation and do not force the BP to a normal population value during carotid clamping or aortic reperfusion. Equally, severe postoperative hypertension after CEA risks hyperperfusion and neck bleeding and should be treated promptly against the agreed patient-specific target.

### Diabetes mellitus

Identify insulin dependence, recent control, hypoglycaemia, autonomic neuropathy, CKD, infection, vascular ulcers and any SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1/GIP treatment. Tailor the fasting, basal-insulin and IV-insulin plan; never omit essential basal insulin in type 1 diabetes. Stop SGLT2 inhibitors sufficiently before elective surgery and check ketones in an unwell urgent patient even with normal glucose. Monitor glucose throughout long, changing-perfusion operations; a commonly referenced perioperative goal is roughly 5.6–10 mmol/L when safe, adapted to local ADS–ANZCA policy and hypoglycaemia risk [1,29]. Good glycaemic control supports wound healing; diabetic neuropathy also increases positioning injury and may conceal compartment syndrome. Resume medication safely after intake, renal function and ketone risk are reassessed.

### COPD and limited respiratory reserve

Identify exacerbation, recent lower-respiratory infection, baseline dyspnoea, sputum, bronchodilator and steroid use, hypoxaemia/CO₂ retention, sleep-disordered breathing and pulmonary hypertension. Optimise inhalers, treat reversible infection/exacerbation, support smoking cessation and arrange postoperative respiratory care. Assess whether open transperitoneal repair, a thoracotomy/one-lung ventilation or prolonged supine IR sedation is tolerable; anatomically suitable EVAR may avoid an open incision but is not automatically safe. During GA permit adequate expiratory time and avoid dynamic hyperinflation; balance protective ventilation against venous return, especially during clamping or rupture. Plan dynamic analgesia, cough, physiotherapy and an appropriate extubation/HDU strategy.

### Renal failure, CKD and dialysis

Determine AKI versus chronic CKD, current potassium/bicarbonate, volume balance, residual urine, dialysis modality/time, anaemia, uraemic platelet dysfunction and vascular access. Avoid cannulating or compressing an AV fistula arm; check residual dialysis anticoagulation when planning neuraxial/deep blocks. Prevent sustained renal hypoperfusion while avoiding pulmonary oedema from routine prophylactic fluid boluses. For suprarenal clamping discuss clamp duration and renal/visceral perfusion; after EVAR distinguish renal-branch occlusion from contrast-associated injury. Dose-adjust renally cleared agents and avoid unproven “renal-dose dopamine”, prophylactic forced diuresis or dialysis solely to remove contrast. Postoperatively monitor potassium, acid–base, urine output and indications for nephrology/RRT support.

**High-yield distinction:** urgency governs how much optimisation is possible. A stable, symptomatic CAD patient scheduled for elective open AAA repair deserves assessment and risk reduction; a patient with rAAA or Rutherford IIb limb ischaemia needs treatment and physiological preparedness in parallel with immediate repair, not a prolonged cardiac work-up.

## Apply the current risk and medication guidance

For the 2021.1 day-of-surgery question, repeat the BP with an appropriate cuff after rest and review previous values, treatment and symptoms. A persistent systolic reading of 180 mmHg reaches the 2026 Association of Anaesthetists/BIHS secondary-care threshold in a patient without recent documentation of normotension, even though the diastolic reading is 110. Look for acute end-organ injury and justify proceeding or postponing by the urgency of the procedure, organ risk, repeat measurement and local policy. Avoid rapid IV normalisation simply to meet an elective threshold.

For high-risk vascular patients consider whether a preoperative biomarker or postoperative troponin surveillance will alter management. Myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery may be silent. A new troponin rise requires assessment for ischaemia and alternative causes. With GLP-1 or dual GLP-1/GIP agents, current ANZCA advice generally continues therapy and uses a 24-hour clear-fluid diet followed by the specified fasting sequence, with preparation and aspiration mitigation reviewed before anaesthesia. For this at-risk group ANZCA specifies water only in the six hours before induction, with nothing by mouth in the final two hours. Review the distinct SGLT2 inhibitor pathway for ketosis risk and the urgency of limb surgery.

[Reaffirmed AHA/ACC perioperative guideline 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [Association of Anaesthetists and BIHS 2026](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082) · [ANZCA GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP preparation pathway](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/clinical-practice-recommendations-regarding-patients-taking-glp-1)

items.title: 2. The physiology that governs all aortic surgery: clamping, unclamping and reperfusion
items.body:
### First picture the clamp: it creates two different circulations

Imagine the surgeon placing a strong clamp across a garden hose. Above the clamp, the pump must work against a higher resistance; below it, flow stops or falls. In the patient, the “pump” is the left ventricle and the “hose” is the aorta. **Proximal arterial pressure can rise while cardiac output falls** because the left ventricle struggles against a new afterload. A normal-looking radial pressure does not prove that the lower body is receiving blood.

![Aortic clamping schematic: the clamp level determines which organs become ischaemic. The picture is deliberately simplified and not to scale.](set14-ch2-1.png)

A clamp below the renal arteries (infrarenal) leaves direct renal arterial inflow intact, whereas a clamp above the renal arteries (suprarenal) interrupts kidney perfusion. A clamp above the coeliac axis also interrupts major liver and gut inflow. Longer and more proximal clamps increase the burden of ischaemia and reperfusion.

Clamping may raise LV preload transiently as venous blood is displaced centrally, but there is no guarantee: simultaneous surgical bleeding and reduced venous return can make the circulation underfilled. **Think in components:** heart rate, stroke volume, arterial pressure, filling, actual blood loss and clamp height.

When the clamp comes off, blood re-enters a large dilated circulation and venous blood may pool in the legs and splanchnic veins. Resistance and central filling can both fall. Meanwhile, previously ischaemic tissue returns lactate, hydrogen ions and potassium to the circulation; this can depress the myocardium and trigger arrhythmias. **This is not just a “needs fluids” event.** The treatment depends on whether the problem is bleeding, vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, electrolyte toxicity or several together.

- **Memory rule:** **Clamp ON → afterload/oxygen demand up; distal perfusion down. Clamp OFF → afterload and venous return may fall; acid and potassium return.** In an exam, always tell the surgeon you need warning before release.

## 2.1 Understanding proximal and distal circulations

Aortic cross-clamping creates **two different circulatory environments**. Proximal to the clamp, pressure and effective arterial impedance rise; distal to it, arterial inflow falls. The size of the haemodynamic change depends on clamp level, aortic collateral flow, preload, LV function, vascular resistance and duration. A patient with severe LVH and diastolic dysfunction may develop ischaemia or pulmonary oedema from a relatively modest increase in afterload despite apparently “adequate” blood pressure. A patient with a failing LV may instead show falling stroke volume and cardiac output despite rising proximal arterial pressure.

A simplified relationship helps: **MAP ≈ CO × SVR + CVP**, and **CO = HR × stroke volume**. An increase in MAP during clamping does not prove adequate CO or microcirculatory oxygen delivery. Moreover, the LV faces a sudden change in arterial impedance and wave reflections, not a perfectly steady resistance. This is why monitoring the direction of cardiac output, filling and ischaemic signs is more useful than memorising a fixed percentage change in systolic BP.

### Clamp level determines what is ischaemic

| **Clamp level**     | **Main physiological issues**                                                                 | **Why the risks differ**                                                                                                            |
|---------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Infrarenal          | Increased LV afterload; reduced lower-limb/pelvic flow, renal neurohumoral vasoconstriction   | Renal arteries remain perfused directly but renal blood flow may fall despite normal proximal pressure; limb/gut ischaemia possible |
| Suprarenal          | Above plus interrupted renal perfusion until unclamping                                       | Duration of renal ischaemia becomes a major AKI determinant; renal protection depends on clamp time and collateral flow             |
| Supracoeliac        | Renal and splanchnic ischaemia; larger proximal haemodynamic stress                           | Impaired hepatic/mesenteric perfusion, lactate and inflammatory mediator generation; severe reperfusion burden                      |
| Descending thoracic | Large distal territory including spinal, mesenteric and renal perfusion depending on position | High SCI and multiorgan risk; may require distal perfusion, CSF drainage and neuromonitoring                                        |

A high clamp can transiently redistribute venous blood centrally and increase LV preload while raising afterload. At a later stage of surgery blood loss, venous pooling and reduced distal venous return can reduce central filling. There is no universal claim that clamping always raises or lowers cardiac output. Assess the patient and clamp position rather than reciting an invariant rule.

## 2.2 Pre-clamp strategy: create reserve without causing fluid overload

Before clamping, establish reliable, continuously displayed arterial pressure—usually radial arterial cannulation **before** induction in high-risk open aortic cases. The patient generally requires two large-bore peripheral cannulae (often 14–16 G), a rapid-infuser and blood availability, appropriate temperature monitoring, urinary catheter and frequent arterial blood-gas/electrolyte testing. Central access is useful when peripheral access is inadequate or vasoactive infusions require it; it is not automatically a reliable measure of fluid responsiveness. In major thoraco-abdominal repair, the level of repair may justify cardiac output monitoring, TEE and spinal perfusion adjuncts. Discuss the precise clamp site, estimated clamp duration, heparin timing, anticipated blood loss and unclamp plan with the surgeon before induction.

Assess haemoglobin, calcium, base deficit/lactate, temperature, pulmonary oedema and current vasopressor requirements. Replace **demonstrable deficits** with balanced crystalloid or blood products, not a fixed prophylactic bolus. A useful fluid challenge is a small 200–250 mL aliquot with reassessment of stroke volume, arterial trace, capillary refill and signs of pulmonary congestion. If bleeding is present, red cells and haemostatic components restore oxygen carriage and coagulation more effectively than large volumes of crystalloid. Establish noradrenaline availability and a strategy for hypertension (for example titrated glyceryl trinitrate or an alternative vasodilator according to LV function).

When the team is ready to clamp, reconfirm volume status, depth of anaesthesia, heart rate and ECG ST trend, temperature and distal organ protection plan. Ask the surgeon for a verbal announcement before application. **Why:** an abrupt increase in LV wall stress increases myocardial oxygen demand just as coronary flow may be compromised by tachycardia or low diastolic perfusion pressure.

## 2.3 Clamp application and maintained clamping

Initially, MAP and proximal systolic pressure usually rise and LV wall stress increases. Treat clinically important hypertension if accompanied by ischaemia, ventricular strain or dangerous pressure, but do not automatically reduce pressure to “normal” if a high clamp requires proximal perfusion of the heart and brain. First check anaesthetic depth, analgesia, hypercarbia and other causes of sympathetic stimulation. If left ventricular function is adequate, vasodilators can attenuate the afterload increase; use short, titratable agents and reassess CO. When a weak LV fails under new impedance, an inotrope or altered vascular strategy may be preferable to indiscriminate vasodilation.

Continuously look for **myocardial ischaemia** (new ECG change, regional wall-motion abnormality, falling output, pulmonary congestion), distal perfusion failure, temperature loss, coagulopathy and increasing lactate. If a high clamp compromises renal or visceral perfusion, the decisive variable is often **ischaemic duration**—not a renal-protective diuretic. Communicate any unexpected deterioration immediately; consider clamp repositioning or use of distal perfusion when surgically feasible. The longer the clamp, the more likely distal tissue accumulates lactate, potassium, CO₂ and inflammatory mediators.

**Heparin:** systemic UFH (often 70–100 units/kg for large arterial clamping, with some teams using different doses or ACT-guided regimens) may be requested before clamping; follow the surgeon's agreed protocol and measure ACT when appropriate. Where bleeding risk is exceptional, balance thrombosis against bleeding. Protamine reversal is guided by total heparin administered, timing, ACT/clinical bleeding and the risk of hypotension or anaphylactoid reactions. A milligram of protamine neutralises approximately 100 units of recent unfractionated heparin; accumulated metabolism and local protocols mean a full calculated dose may be excessive.

## 2.4 Unclamping: why dramatic hypotension can occur

Unclamping reverses the proximal afterload increase, exposes a large dilated distal vascular bed, permits venous pooling and suddenly returns acidic, hyperkalaemic blood to the central circulation. The acute **fall in preload** and SVR can reduce MAP and myocardial perfusion; myocardial depression, acidaemia, hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia may add to the fall. Some organs have reactive hyperaemia, whereas microvascular no-reflow and endothelial injury can sustain distal malperfusion despite macrovascular restoration. The resulting shock is not simply “hypovolaemia,” so the response must be diagnostic as well as therapeutic.

Prepare several minutes before release. Communicate the anticipated time and ask for staged clamp release where possible. Reassess fluid responsiveness and haemorrhage losses. Give a small volume or blood-product bolus only if needed; avoid filling an already congested LV. Reduce an unnecessary vasodilator, prepare a titratable noradrenaline infusion or boluses and confirm adequate ionised calcium. Consider a blood gas immediately before and after release. After release monitor the ECG and rhythm, ETCO₂, lactate, pH, K⁺, ionised Ca²⁺, haemoglobin and peripheral pulses. A transient fall in ETCO₂ from reduced pulmonary blood flow can accompany hypotension, while later rising ETCO₂ may reflect washout of stored CO₂. Persistent low ETCO₂ requires assessment of CO, ventilation and embolic events.

### Practical response to severe hypotension after unclamping

- **1.** Ask the surgeon whether bleeding, clamp release or proximal obstruction is responsible; check the field and measured blood loss. Ensure oxygen delivery and a useful arterial trace.
- **2.** Treat immediately threatening hypotension with a vasopressor while rapidly differentiating low preload, vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, arrhythmia and haemorrhage. Noradrenaline is commonly appropriate for vasodilatory shock; if there is marked cardiac failure, address inotropy.
- **3.** If haemorrhage or fluid responsiveness is present, give warmed blood/crystalloid in assessed aliquots and re-evaluate; in heavy bleeding activate MHP rather than giving litres of saline.
- **4.** If widening QRS, peaked T waves, bradyarrhythmia or VF accompanies high K⁺, give IV calcium promptly, followed by potassium-shifting therapy and definitive control of ongoing K⁺ release. Acidosis is treated by restoring perfusion; sodium bicarbonate is not a substitute for correcting shock.
- **5.** Consider temporary surgical reclamping or staged reperfusion in refractory deterioration **only through immediate surgical discussion**. Repeat sampling and closely observe limb, renal and bowel perfusion.

### A worked physiological example

A 72-year-old undergoing infrarenal AAA repair has MAP 76 mmHg and CO 4.2 L/min before clamping. After clamping, MAP rises to 102 but CO falls to 3.3. A superficial interpretation would celebrate the “improved” pressure. In reality, the LV is failing to sustain flow at the increased afterload, raising myocardial oxygen demand while reducing forward oxygen delivery. Priorities are ECG/echo evaluation, avoiding tachycardia, titrating afterload and maintaining coronary perfusion—not administering fluid until a CVP target is reached. Upon release, MAP suddenly falls to 52 with CO 3.0 and a new lactate rise. Assess blood loss and volume responsiveness, support vascular tone and examine contractility before assuming the entire fall is due to a saline deficit.

## 2.5 Reperfusion is an organ-specific problem

**Limb:** oedema increases compartment pressure and reduces capillary flow; reperfusion can cause hyperkalaemia, myoglobinuria, AKI and arrhythmias. **Bowel:** mucosal injury promotes bacterial translocation, inflammatory shock and later colonic ischaemia. **Kidney:** ischaemia/reperfusion, atheroembolism and inflammatory injury act on a background of CKD. **Spinal cord:** interruption of radicular/segmental arteries, low perfusion pressure and disrupted collaterals may cause immediate or delayed paralysis. The correct response after a technically successful repair is therefore structured surveillance, not merely extubation and transfer.

## 2.6 Prolonged limb versus gut ischaemia: distinctive physiology and rescue

**Skeletal muscle ischaemia.** Arterial interruption depletes ATP, impairs Na⁺/K⁺ pumps and produces intracellular calcium accumulation, anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis. Reperfusion introduces oxygen free radicals, endothelial activation and capillary leakage into confined fascial compartments. Potassium, acid, phosphate and myoglobin entering the circulation can cause brady/ventricular arrhythmias, vasoplegia and pigment-associated AKI. Prior collateralisation changes tissue tolerance: a chronically ischaemic limb may react differently from a suddenly embolised normal limb. Duration, baseline neurological deficit and degree of muscle damage matter more than a reassuring global MAP or return of a distal pulse.

**Mesenteric and colonic ischaemia.** Supracoeliac clamping directly interrupts major splanchnic inflow; even infrarenal repair can threaten colonic collateral supply through inferior mesenteric, internal iliac or marginal-artery pathways. Low cardiac output, prolonged hypotension, haemorrhage, vasoconstriction and atheroembolism can cause non-occlusive or arterial mesenteric ischaemia. Hypoxic mucosal barrier failure followed by reperfusion promotes oedema, bacterial/endotoxin translocation, local thrombosis and systemic inflammation. Ischaemic colitis may appear after an apparently technically successful graft repair. Lactate may be normal initially and is not sensitive enough to exclude an evolving bowel catastrophe.

**Recognition and response:** record exact clamp/occlusion duration and compromised territories. During operation discuss distal perfusion, temporary shunting, clamp relocation or expediting anastomosis when feasible; maintain perfusing pressure and cardiac output while preventing excess fluid-related bowel oedema. Before and after reperfusion trend ECG, K⁺, blood gases, Ca²⁺, lactate, urine output and limb compartment findings. After aortic repair, new disproportionate abdominal pain, ileus, bloody diarrhoea, distension, increasing lactate or unexplained shock requires immediate vascular/general surgical review and appropriate CTA, endoscopy or operation; do not merely treat the acidosis. After limb revascularisation assess for compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis as in Chapter 9. These are different tissue emergencies, despite a shared ischaemia–reperfusion mechanism.

items.body:
### First visualise an open AAA repair: a surgical walk-through

An aneurysm is a weak dilated segment of aorta. In an elective **open infrarenal AAA repair**, the surgeon usually reaches the aorta through a long abdominal incision (or a retroperitoneal approach). The aim is not to tighten the native aorta; it is to replace the weak segment with a durable prosthetic tube or Y-shaped graft. “Infrarenal” refers to the graft/clamp position below the renal arteries, not a guarantee that the kidneys cannot be injured.

- **Expose and obtain control.** The aorta and iliac arteries are exposed. The surgeon identifies where clamps can safely go. At this stage a fragile aneurysm, prior surgery or adhesions can cause major bleeding; large-bore access and blood should already be available.

- **Heparinise and clamp.** Systemic heparin is often given and an aortic clamp is applied above the aneurysm, with distal iliac control. Blood pressure proximal to the clamp may rise; distal tissues become ischaemic.

- **Open the sac and construct the graft.** The aneurysm sac is opened, thrombus removed and bleeding from lumbar branches controlled. The surgeon sews the prosthetic graft to healthy vessel above and below. The anaesthetist follows blood loss, coagulation and clamp/ischaemia time.

- **Flush, de-air and release.** The surgeon flushes the graft, excludes air/debris and releases clamps in a controlled manner. Reperfusion can cause hypotension, acidosis and hyperkalaemia. This phase deserves a specific plan, not a vague order to “give some fluid”.

- **Check distal perfusion and close.** The team confirms leg pulses and haemostasis; the sac is often closed over the graft. ICU/HDU monitoring focuses on heart, lungs, kidney, gut and legs.

Why the operation is demanding: a long abdominal incision impairs coughing; major blood loss and hypothermia are possible; the clamp alters LV afterload; even with an infrarenal clamp the kidneys and bowel can be injured; regional analgesia must be coordinated with systemic heparinisation. These are separate hazards occurring at different phases.

## 3.1 What operation is actually being performed?

Open repair of an infrarenal AAA usually proceeds through a midline transperitoneal or retroperitoneal approach. The surgeon gains proximal and distal control, administers systemic heparin as planned, cross-clamps the aorta and iliac arteries, opens the sac, evacuates thrombus, ligates bleeding lumbar branches and sews a tube or bifurcated synthetic graft to suitable aortic/iliac segments. The clamp is released after de-airing/flushing and inspection of anastomoses. The sac and retroperitoneum are closed over the graft. Bifurcated grafts or aorto-bifemoral bypass for occlusive disease require more extensive distal dissection and may add time, blood loss and limb-ischaemia risk. Aortic surgery becomes physiologically different if the clamp must be moved above the renal or visceral arteries, or if thoracotomy, one-lung ventilation, left-heart bypass or cardiopulmonary support are required.

The operation's main physiological phases are: **induction**, **dissection and haemorrhage**, **heparinisation**, **clamp application**, **distal ischaemia**, **graft anastomosis**, **staged release**, **reperfusion**, and **haemostasis/closure**. Understanding their sequence anticipates when blood loss, hypertension, renal injury and hypotension occur. In open aorto-iliac occlusive surgery, the dominant issue may be prolonged ischaemia and severe background CAD rather than aneurysm rupture.

### Preoperative decision: open versus EVAR

For an asymptomatic degenerative AAA, repair decisions incorporate symptoms, rate of expansion, sex, size, life expectancy, surgical risk and feasibility of standard endograft sealing. A 5.5 cm diameter is a commonly used threshold in otherwise appropriate men; threshold decisions in women are individualised and may favour consideration at smaller sizes because rupture can occur at smaller diameters. Do not turn an isolated ultrasound diameter into an automatic instruction to operate: anatomical suitability, competing mortality and patient preferences matter. Symptomatic or rapidly enlarging aneurysms demand more urgent discussion. The ESVS 2024 AAA guideline remains the reference for this decision [2].

Open repair avoids endoleaks and the same intensity of lifelong device surveillance but entails greater early physiological stress, ventilation requirements, blood loss and recovery time. Endovascular repair reduces early procedural burden in suitable anatomy, but requires adequate landing zones, usable access and indefinite surveillance for sac enlargement, migration, endoleak and late rupture. EVAR-1 illustrates an early survival advantage without assured late advantage [16]. The correct technique is a shared anatomical and risk decision, not a declaration that EVAR is universally preferable in older or frail patients.

## 3.2 Preoperative evaluation specific to open aortic surgery

In addition to the cardiovascular assessment in Chapter 1, review the CTA with the surgeon: neck, thrombus/calcification, clamp level, renal artery anatomy, accessory renals, inferior mesenteric and internal iliac supply, previous abdominal surgery and planned distal anastomoses. Ask about chronic mesenteric ischaemia, prior bowel resections and previous aortic interventions. These predict ischaemic bowel and collateral dependence after clamping. Check creatinine/eGFR and baseline urine output, haemoglobin, coagulation/antithrombotic status, group-and-crossmatch and lung physiology. Severe COPD can make abdominal closure and prolonged ventilation challenging. Establish the likely ICU destination and the patient’s wishes concerning a prolonged postoperative course.

An epidural may improve early dynamic analgesia, coughing and respiratory mechanics after open abdominal surgery but complicates systemic heparinisation, bleeding management and hypotension. If used, insert well before heparinisation according to the applicable neuraxial–antithrombotic policy, document an atraumatic placement, and have a planned approach to traumatic/bloody tap, postoperative anticoagulation and catheter removal. A bloody tap should prompt **reassessment of the timing and safety of systemic heparin, not an automatic attempt to continue at the original schedule**; consider postponement, alternative analgesia and specialist consultation. Routine full-dose systemic anticoagulation in a patient with a traumatic neuraxial placement can create an epidural haematoma with permanent neurological injury. Some centres favour non-neuraxial options for high-bleeding-risk aortic cases.

### What I would actually set up before an elective open AAA

- **Before the patient enters theatre:** read CTA for clamp level and difficult iliac anatomy; check renal function, Hb, anticoagulants, cardiovascular reserve and planned postoperative destination. Agree heparin timing, expected clamp time, cell salvage, blood product availability, epidural policy and who will announce clamp application/release.

- **Monitoring and access:** five-lead ECG with ST trend, invasive arterial line (often before induction), two reliable large peripheral cannulae, rapid infuser/warming, urinary catheter, temperature and serial blood gases with Hb, K+, ionised Ca2+ and lactate. Advanced echo/cardiac-output monitoring is selected for high clamps or poor ventricular reserve; a central line is not a substitute for good peripheral blood access.

- **Induction:** avoid sudden hypotension in a patient with severe CAD or LVH. Titrate hypnotic/opioid rather than giving a routine full dose; be ready with noradrenaline/phenylephrine according to physiology. Avoid prolonged tachycardia, which increases myocardial oxygen demand just when coronary supply is limited.

- **Before clamp:** announce readiness, verify adequate anaesthesia, reassess filling, bleeding and vasopressor requirement, and ensure a strategy for a rapid afterload rise. **Before unclamping:** again coordinate, review blood loss, acid–base and electrolytes, consider an assessed small fluid/blood aliquot if appropriate and have vasopressors prepared.

- **Recovery:** decide on extubation based on haemostasis, pulmonary mechanics, temperature, acid–base and cardiovascular stability rather than finishing the surgery alone. Analgesia needs to permit coughing but an epidural must be safe with heparin and postoperative thromboprophylaxis.

A useful question to ask the surgeon is “Are the renal arteries above or below your clamp and how long do you expect it to stay on?” The answer changes kidney-risk counselling, fluid goals, electrolyte monitoring and the degree of ICU surveillance.

## 3.3 Anaesthetic technique, access and monitoring

A standard high-risk open repair commonly warrants a preinduction radial arterial line, continuous five-lead ECG with ST monitoring, two dependable large peripheral IVs, blood products and a rapid infuser, urinary catheter, core temperature, regular blood gases and postoperative monitored or ICU care. Central access, TEE or other CO monitoring should be based on ventricular impairment, clamp height, access difficulty and anticipated instability rather than routine convention. Consider cerebral or spinal monitoring for high thoracic work and plan lower-limb/visceral perfusion assessment if prolonged ischaemia is likely.

Induction must preserve coronary and cerebral perfusion without excessive tachycardia. For a patient with significant LVH and diastolic dysfunction, avoid abrupt vasodilation and underfilling; choose titrated induction doses and a vasopressor ready before loss of consciousness. Balanced volatile or propofol-based anaesthesia may be used—there is no reliable evidence that a particular hypnotic overcomes haemorrhage, clamp physiology or untreated CAD. Opioid or remifentanil titration reduces sympathetic peaks; maintain appropriate oxygenation and normocapnia unless a specific surgical/neurological reason changes the target. Protect renal perfusion by preventing sustained hypotension, not by routine “renal-dose dopamine”, mannitol or furosemide.

### Blood conservation and coagulation

Major arterial anastomoses and raw surfaces can bleed rapidly. **Cell salvage** is often valuable in elective open aortic surgery provided contamination and local contraindications are considered. A typical sequence is suction with anticoagulation → reservoir and filtration → centrifugation/washing → reinfusion of washed red cells; it does not replace platelets or coagulation factors. Optimise Hb preoperatively, correct hypothermia and acidosis, use careful surgical haemostasis, and obtain fibrinogen, platelets and viscoelastic testing during heavy bleeding. Follow a major haemorrhage protocol with guided component replacement, not a single arbitrary haemoglobin trigger. Recheck ionised calcium repeatedly during citrate-rich transfusion. Do not presume TXA should be given routinely to every vascular case; weigh likely blood-saving benefit, graft thrombosis/embolism risk, renal function and local evidence. Heparin/ACT testing and selective protamine reversal are coordinated with the surgeon.

### Distinguish the vascular checklist from an uncritical protocol

The sequence most likely to cause harm is: large-bore warmed access and immediate blood availability BEFORE induction; careful arterial/ECG monitoring and a team-announced clamp; serial gases (Hb, K⁺, ionised Ca²⁺, pH/lactate); and a pre-agreed controlled release. The procedure-dependent emphasis is blood loss/ischemia and acute LV afterload rather than any particular hypnotic. A fixed CVP rise before unclamping, routine epidural, blanket CPET, fixed blood-product triggers and routine postoperative intubation should not be adopted as universal requirements. Prefer the individualised volume/flow and antithrombotic principles in §§1, 2 and 13, with assessment and critical-care destination based on the actual patient and operation.

## 3.4 At clamp application and during clamping: make a physiological plan

The principles from Chapter 2 apply here. For **infrarenal repair**, the renal arteries are nominally perfused but there can still be neurohumorally mediated renal vasoconstriction and reduced renal flow. For **suprarenal or supracoeliac clamps**, interrupted renal or splanchnic inflow adds time-sensitive ischaemia. Record clamp start and finish times. Target adequate perfusion at the required territories: proximal pressure alone does not guarantee distal viability. Maintain an anaesthetic depth that prevents sympathetic surges without creating hypotension; titrate vasodilators or vasopressors based on myocardial performance. The use of a TEE to observe LV filling and function can distinguish rising afterload from fluid overload. During a prolonged high clamp, discuss perfusion adjuncts or clamp relocation as needed.

As the anastomosis approaches completion, communicate preparation for release: reassess volume, blood loss, K⁺, pH, ionised calcium, lactate and vasoactive requirements; anticipate the return of acidic blood and large lower-body vasodilation. **An examiner expects a strategy**—for example, small assessed fluid/blood aliquots, a titrated noradrenaline infusion, staged release and repeat ABGs—not the phrase “ensure euvolaemia.” [12]

## 3.5 Postoperative implications and complications

Aortic graft repair often needs HDU/ICU surveillance for bleeding, myocardial injury, AKI, respiratory dysfunction, bowel ischaemia and leg perfusion failure. Serial abdominal examination, lactate trends, urine output and Hb are useful but not specific. An elevated lactate after unclamping can represent washout; persistent or worsening metabolic acidosis with abdominal pain/distension, GI bleeding, ileus, pressor requirement or haemodynamic deterioration should raise concern for **mesenteric/colonic ischaemia**. An internal iliac or inferior mesenteric collateral problem can make this more likely. Early surgical/vascular assessment and CT/endoscopy when appropriate matter more than reassuring oneself that arterial pressure has normalised.

Other complications: myocardial ischaemia or arrhythmia, graft thrombosis or distal embolism (new pulseless/cold limb), compartment syndrome, pneumonia/atelectasis, abdominal compartment syndrome, AKI, ureteric injury, graft infection, aortoenteric fistula (usually delayed, including GI haemorrhage) and incisional failure. Monitor for epidural haematoma in a neuraxial patient, especially if anticoagulation resumes. Early extubation is appropriate when awake, warm, stable and haemostatically controlled, but may be unsafe after major blood loss, acidosis, pulmonary oedema, severe COPD exacerbation or extensive high aortic surgery.

### Analgesia after open aortic repair

A thoracic epidural (often a local anaesthetic plus opioid infusion) can provide strong movement-related analgesia, but monitor sympathetic hypotension and adjust if spinal perfusion or graft flow are concerns. If an epidural is contraindicated, options include IV opioid PCA, acetaminophen, selective low-dose ketamine, wound infiltration or abdominal wall catheters/block (e.g. rectus sheath/TAP) depending on incision. NSAIDs may be inappropriate in AKI, bleeding, renal artery clamping or heart failure; gabapentinoids increase sedation in frail or renal-impaired patients. Treat pain sufficiently for mobilisation and cough while protecting respiratory and haemodynamic reserve.
