items.body:
### First visualise EVAR and TEVAR: the graft is delivered inside the artery

**Open repair** replaces the aneurysmal segment through a large incision. In **EVAR**, the surgeon accesses one or both femoral arteries, passes wires and large sheaths to the aorta and deploys a fabric-covered metal stent-graft. Blood then flows through the stent lumen rather than pressurising the aneurysm sac. The sac remains in the patient; the aim is to exclude it from blood pressure. This is why a leak around the graft is important.

![Endovascular AAA repair: a stent-graft forms a new inner channel while the aneurysm sac remains outside it.](set14-ch4-1.png)

- **Access:** femoral punctures or cut-down; large introducer sheaths. Even without an abdominal incision, an iliac or femoral artery can rupture, causing occult retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

- **Positioning:** the operator advances guidewires and a compressed stent under fluoroscopy; contrast angiography identifies the renal arteries and appropriate sealing zones.

- **Deployment:** accurate release depends on a motionless patient and steady control of BP. Complex thoracic devices sometimes require deliberate transient changes in pressure or pacing; these must be agreed in advance.

- **Completion angiography:** the surgeon checks proximal and distal seal, branch-vessel flow and patency of both iliac limbs. External groin punctures are closed but the patient still needs haemorrhage, limb and organ surveillance.

**TEVAR** places an endograft in the thoracic aorta. The device may cover intercostal vessels feeding the spinal cord or the left subclavian artery, creating risks that differ from a simple infrarenal EVAR. **Fenestrated/branched EVAR** has carefully designed openings and branch stents to keep renal and gut arteries perfused: it often takes longer, involves more instrumentation and brings higher branch-occlusion risk.

- **Endoleak intuition:** **Type I** = inadequate seal at one end; **Type II** = blood flows backward into the sac from branch vessels; **Type III** = a hole/separation in graft components. Types I and III transmit substantial systemic pressure to the sac and generally require correction; many isolated type II leaks with stable sac size can be monitored. Late imaging matters because the native sac is still present.

- **Anaesthetic choice:** simple EVAR may be done with local infiltration and light sedation if the patient cooperates. Complex EVAR or TEVAR often favours GA for precise immobility and airway control. The right choice is not automatically “less anaesthesia is safer”: if the head is inaccessible under X-ray equipment and drapes, deep sedation may be riskier than controlled GA.

## 4.1 The principal advantage is avoiding a large incision and open cross-clamp

Standard EVAR introduces a stent-graft through femoral/iliac access, positions it below the renal arteries and extends its limbs into the iliac circulation. Completion angiography checks graft seal, branch flow, leg perfusion and endoleaks. Aorto-uni-iliac configurations may require contralateral iliac occlusion and a femoro-femoral crossover bypass. Fenestrated or branched EVAR (F/BEVAR) incorporates visceral or renal artery branches using fenestrations and bridging stents; more complex procedures require longer contrast exposure, substantial access, renal/mesenteric ischaemia precautions and sometimes spinal perfusion measures.

TEVAR similarly deploys a stent-graft in the descending thoracic aorta. It may require coverage of the left subclavian artery, proximal landing near the arch, rapid pacing or transient controlled hypotension for accurate deployment, and lower-body/spinal perfusion planning. Endovascular repair avoids an open thoracic aortic cross-clamp but **can still cause spinal cord ischaemia, embolic stroke and visceral ischaemia** from branch exclusion, aortic manipulation and altered collateral perfusion. Do not infer “minimally invasive” means “low consequence.”

## 4.2 Preoperative assessment of suitability and risk

The CTA is a procedural roadmap. For EVAR, identify proximal neck length/angulation, thrombus, calcification, iliac vessel diameter and tortuosity, common/internal iliac patency and whether branch-vessel perfusion is threatened. Consider prior abdominal aortic repair, renal transplant, dialysis, aortoiliac occlusion and previous access complications. In TEVAR, assess arch anatomy, left subclavian/vertebral circulation, extent of coverage, prior abdominal aortic repair, hypogastric flow and whether CSF drainage or a staged approach is being considered. For F/BEVAR, clarify renal and visceral stent procedures and risk of prolonged sheath occlusion.

This is an opportunity to match the expected physiology to the patient: an 82-year-old with frailty, severe COPD, stable CAD and a short-neck AAA may still be unfit for prolonged open repair but anatomically unsuitable for simple EVAR; an elaborate fenestrated plan is not automatically benign. Ask whether a conservative pathway, alternative repair or transfer to a higher-volume centre is more appropriate. The 2026.1 ANZCA Final SAQ specifically required meaningful cardiac risk assessment and optimisation—not a vague “ECG, echo and cardiology review.” [13]

### Contrast and kidney protection

Contrast-associated AKI risk increases with pre-existing CKD, intravascular depletion, shock, repeated contrast, atheroembolism and nephrotoxic exposures. Pre-procedure creatinine/eGFR and haemodynamic optimisation help; use the smallest diagnostic contrast load that still produces safe technical imaging. Avoid routine high-volume crystalloid if the patient has decompensated HF; individualise isotonic hydration for patients with high renal risk who can tolerate it. Prophylactic N-acetylcysteine, routine diuretics and dialysis solely to remove contrast are not established protective treatments. A newly rising creatinine after EVAR requires distinction among contrast-associated injury, renal artery occlusion, atheroembolism, hypoperfusion and obstruction. In a patient with a renal stent or branch graft, sudden oliguria may be a **vascular emergency**, not simply “contrast nephropathy.”

## 4.3 Anaesthesia options and working in the hybrid/interventional suite

Uncomplicated infrarenal EVAR in a cooperative, haemodynamically stable patient can often be performed with local infiltration plus carefully titrated sedation, neuraxial anaesthesia when safe, or general anaesthesia. The decision depends on patient cooperation, access complexity, duration, pain, respiratory disease, antiplatelet/anticoagulant status and need for immediate immobility. Local/sedation preserves spontaneous ventilation and may avoid sympathectomy/circulatory collapse, but movement during deployment can displace the graft; a sedated supine patient with large drapes may have an inaccessible airway. GA provides immobility and airway control but introduces haemodynamic changes and may delay early neurological assessment. Complex TEVAR/FBEVAR often needs GA with intubation, controlled ventilation and haemodynamic precision; specific staged procedures may use awake monitoring.

**Set up the room as an anaesthetic location—not a radiology room with an anaesthetist added late.** Confirm oxygen, suction, anaesthesia machine, capnography, defibrillator, blood access, heater, airway cart, infusion pumps, emergency drugs and call-for-help plan. Assess difficult patient access from the head after the C-arm moves; arrange extension tubing and pump location outside the radiation field. Wear lead apron, thyroid shield and eye protection as required, use lead screens and minimise fluoroscopy exposure. The principles are time, distance and shielding: staff exposure falls with distance and appropriate shielding; keep hands out of the primary beam. Check radiation dose reporting and escalation thresholds with the procedural team. Beware cables/surgical drapes interfering with monitoring or airway access, and limited support after hours. ANZCA professional standards for anaesthesia outside operating theatres apply [7].

### Typical monitoring

Standard anaesthesia monitors and temperature remain mandatory. An arterial line is strongly favoured for major TEVAR/FBEVAR, ruptured EVAR and haemodynamically fragile cases. Bilateral pressures may help when brachiocephalic vessels are manipulated and when left subclavian coverage changes left-arm readings. Have large-bore peripheral access and ready blood for access-vessel or aortic rupture. A central line and CO/TEE monitoring depend on cardiac function and procedure; do not cannulate solely by habit. ACT monitoring is used for heparinised stent deployment where appropriate. For prolonged spinal-risk procedures add continuous or repeated neurological assessment, and CSF drainage/MEP/SSEP according to the planned protection protocol.

## 4.4 Deployment and endograft-specific hazards

The patient must remain motionless during the critical release. Anticipate transient hypotension or rapid ventricular pacing if requested for a precise landing; clarify how long it will last and how to immediately restore perfusion. Distinguish the brief intentional reduction in arterial pulsatility for deployment from prolonged low perfusion of the spinal cord or kidneys. Other hazards include access rupture, retroperitoneal haemorrhage, aortic injury, stent malposition, embolisation, arrhythmia and sudden loss of leg flow. Following deployment confirm systemic pressure, distal pulses, renal/visceral flow and aortic seal, and observe for neurologic deficits immediately when feasible.

### Endoleaks: why the type determines the response

| **Type**        | **Mechanism**                                                                    | **Clinical meaning**                                                                |
|-----------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| I               | Inadequate proximal (Ia) or distal (Ib) seal                                     | Direct systemic-pressure flow into sac; generally demands prompt correction         |
| II              | Retrograde filling from side branches (e.g. lumbar/inferior mesenteric arteries) | Often observed if sac stable; persistent leak with sac growth may require treatment |
| III             | Component separation or fabric tear                                              | Direct flow into sac; usually urgent repair                                         |
| IV              | Graft-fabric porosity                                                            | Typically early, now uncommon; distinguish from serious types                       |
| V (endotension) | Sac expansion without visible leak                                               | Requires investigation for occult leak, device failure and risk of rupture          |

A completion angiogram without an obvious endoleak is not a substitute for long-term surveillance. Sac enlargement or late haemorrhage may reflect missed device failure. **Delayed rupture after EVAR remains a core limitation of the technique**, underpinning the long-term EVAR-1 findings [16].

## 4.5 TEVAR versus open thoracic or thoraco-abdominal repair

Open descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic repair involves thoracotomy or thoracoabdominal exposure, cross-clamping, and possibly partial left-heart bypass/distal perfusion, selective visceral/renal perfusion, intercostal reimplantation and CSF drainage. The associated severe physiological stresses include one-lung ventilation, blood loss, high afterload, extensive distal ischaemia and large reperfusion load. TEVAR substantially reduces the burden of thoracotomy and cross-clamping but adds endograft-specific anatomical constraints and concerns about extensive segmental vessel coverage, arch embolisation, branch occlusion and spinal cord injury. The 2026 ESVS descending thoracic guidelines provide the current framework for selecting open, endovascular, staged or hybrid approaches [3].

For thoracic repair, an apparently normal initial neurological exam does **not** exclude delayed spinal cord injury. Monitor lower-limb power as soon as possible and repeatedly, and avoid hypotension and anaemia during the high-risk postoperative period. Left subclavian revascularisation, preservation of hypogastric flow and staged extensive coverage help preserve collateral supply. The protective strategy is detailed in Chapter 5.

## 4.6 Complications after endovascular aortic repair and how to respond

A patient can collapse from retroperitoneal bleeding without obvious drain output. Sudden hypotension, Hb fall, abdominal/back pain, groin swelling or metabolic acidosis after a large-bore femoral sheath should trigger assessment for aortic/iliac perforation or access-site bleeding, resuscitation and immediate procedural control. New acute leg pain or loss of pulses may be iliac-graft kinking, thrombosis, dissection or embolisation; Doppler and urgent vascular imaging/intervention follow. Severe AKI may reflect renal artery coverage or thrombosis. New paraplegia after TEVAR is an emergency: raise spinal perfusion pressure, consider urgent rescue CSF drainage and assess graft, bleeding and neurological alternatives without delay. New focal cortical deficit prompts stroke pathway and haemodynamic/embolism assessment.

A contrast reaction may be non-allergic physiological (nausea, heat, vasovagal bradycardia) or anaphylactic. Hypotension with bronchospasm, airway swelling or circulatory compromise requires **immediate adrenaline and resuscitation** rather than a delayed antihistamine-first approach. Continue standard perioperative anaphylaxis investigation, including timed tryptase and specialist follow-up. Contrast extravasation causes soft tissue injury; manage according to severity, check compartment/neurovascular status and refer urgently if severe. High radiation exposures can produce delayed skin injury and need disclosure, dose review, documentation and specialist follow-up. Equipment-related and access injuries deserve the same incident review as theatre complications.

## Distinguish postoperative kidney injury from branch malperfusion

Oliguria immediately after fenestrated or branched EVAR can reflect renal ostial coverage, branch-stent kinking or thrombosis, dissection, embolism, haemorrhage, low output, venous congestion or urinary obstruction. Contrast-associated AKI describes a temporal relationship. Review completion imaging and seek vascular input early if a salvageable renal artery may be compromised. Essential imaging or reintervention should be weighed against the risk of delay. Do a volume and perfusion assessment before giving repeated fluid boluses.

ESUR separates first-pass intra-arterial contrast exposure, where the kidneys receive relatively undiluted agent, from IV and second-pass intra-arterial exposure. In its renal guidance the illustrative risk cutoffs are eGFR below 45 for first-pass exposure and below 30 for IV/second-pass exposure. AKI and acute illness change the assessment. Tailor hydration to cardiac and kidney reserve, use the lowest diagnostic contrast dose and consider metformin decisions separately from the risk of kidney injury itself.

[ESUR contrast manual 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/) · [ESVS abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/)

items.title: 5. Spinal cord protection in open aortic repair and TEVAR
items.priority: P1 CORE (3 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
### Why legs can become weak even when the aortic stent looks perfect

The spinal cord does not receive its blood from one protected vessel. It is supplied by the longitudinal anterior and posterior spinal arteries, reinforced by a network from intercostal, lumbar, subclavian/vertebral and pelvic arteries. A long thoracic endograft can cover several intercostal supplies simultaneously. The cord may initially cope through collaterals and later become ischaemic if hypotension, anaemia or altered CSF pressure reduces remaining perfusion.

![Spinal cord perfusion pressure is a balance between arterial driving pressure and CSF/venous back-pressure.](set14-ch5-1.png)

**MAP** is the arterial force driving blood towards the cord. **CSF pressure** is one of the pressures the arriving blood must overcome. Thus spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCPP) is approximated by MAP minus the higher of CSF or relevant venous pressure. This makes two interventions intelligible: (1) raise MAP when cord perfusion is threatened, and (2) in selected patients carefully drain CSF to lower the opposing pressure. Neither treatment compensates for an occluded arterial graft or massive anaemia.

A **lumbar CSF drain** is a thin catheter into the lumbar subarachnoid space. It is not a spinal anaesthetic. The staff measure CSF pressure and withdraw fluid under a strict rate/volume protocol. Too much or too rapid drainage can cause intracranial haemorrhage, while heparin and coagulopathy create a spinal haematoma hazard. It therefore has to be coordinated with the aortic and anaesthetic teams.

**Monitoring:** motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) assess descending motor pathways and are sensitive to neuromuscular block and anaesthetic technique; somatosensory-evoked potentials (SSEPs) assess ascending sensory pathways. Neither is a replacement for an actual leg-power examination after surgery. New bilateral leg weakness after TEVAR is a perfusion emergency until proven otherwise.

**Rescue thought process:** call the team, check a real motor deficit, correct hypotension and poor cardiac output, optimise Hb and oxygenation, check CSF-drain pressure/function or consider rescue drain when safe, and rule out stroke, spinal haematoma and graft/arterial obstruction. Do not “observe until morning” because the neurological deficit may still be reversible.

## 5.1 Anatomy explains delayed as well as immediate paraplegia

The spinal cord receives longitudinal supply from the anterior spinal artery (approximately anterior two-thirds) and paired posterior spinal arteries, supplemented by segmental radiculomedullary vessels. The dominant anterior radiculomedullary artery, often called the artery of Adamkiewicz, is variable but commonly arises on the left between T8 and L1. However, no single artery carries the entire burden; a network of intercostal, lumbar, vertebral/subclavian, internal iliac and paraspinal collaterals maintains flow. This network can remodel after staged vessel occlusion. Extensive aortic coverage or high cross-clamping can suddenly eliminate several inflows, while hypotension, anaemia and venous/CSF pressure reduce the residual network's effectiveness.

The clinically useful equation is **spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCPP) ≈ MAP − max(CSF pressure, relevant venous pressure)**. Raising MAP may not improve SCPP when CSF pressure is also markedly elevated. Equally, aggressive CSF drainage can cause subdural or intracranial bleeding. This explains why spinal protection is a bundle of haemodynamic, anatomical, monitoring and drainage decisions rather than a mandate to insert a lumbar drain in everyone.

## 5.2 Identify risk before the stent or clamp

Risk increases with long-segment thoracic coverage, extent I–III thoracoabdominal aneurysm, prior infrarenal AAA repair (loss of lumbar collaterals), planned left subclavian coverage without revascularisation, poor internal iliac circulation, prolonged hypotension, anaemia, CKD, emergency repair, extensive segmental vessel sacrifice and long cross-clamp or operative times. Previous spinal cord injury and advanced atherosclerosis add vulnerability. Document baseline neurological function and existing motor deficits, and discuss expected spinal risk with the vascular team and patient.

### Core protocolised protective measures

- **Preserve collateral circulation:** consider left subclavian revascularisation when coverage is required, preserve internal iliac flow when feasible, consider intercostal reimplantation during open TAAA, minimise unnecessary aortic coverage and use staged repair for extensive endovascular reconstructions.
- **Protect oxygen delivery:** prevent prolonged hypotension and major anaemia. For high-risk thoraco-abdominal repair, an example protocol is MAP about 90–100 mmHg (or higher when rescue is required), haemoglobin ≥100 g/L, adequate oxygenation and temperature control. These are strategy-based targets rather than arbitrary thresholds for every small infrarenal EVAR.
- **Reduce surrounding pressure when appropriate:** lumbar CSF drainage in selected patients according to centre protocol, typically maintaining CSF pressure around ≤10–12 mmHg; drainage rate and daily maximum must be controlled to avoid intracranial haemorrhage.
- **Monitor:** early wake-up and frequent lower-limb motor examinations; MEPs and SSEPs in appropriate open/complex procedures, with anaesthesia tailored to maintain useful signals.
- **Rescue immediately:** an acute deficit is not something to “review on morning rounds.” Raise MAP, correct Hb/O₂, optimise cardiac output, urgently assess CSF pressure/drain feasibility and exclude graft occlusion, spinal haematoma or other structural causes.

## 5.3 The 2026 evidence changes who routinely receives a drain

The 2026 ESVS guideline **strongly recommends prophylactic CSF drainage for open thoracic or thoraco-abdominal repair** (Class I, level A) but states that **selective reactive (rescue) drainage may be preferable to routine prophylactic drainage for extensive endovascular repair** (Class IIb, level C). This distinction reflects the RCT benefit in open TAAA repair and the real complication rate of lumbar drains in endovascular populations [3]. It is incorrect to interpret “CSF drains prevent paraplegia” as proof that every TEVAR patient benefits from a prophylactic catheter. For selected very-high-risk endovascular anatomy, local protocols may still favour prophylaxis after multidisciplinary review.

Why the difference? In the classic open TAAA trial, prophylactic drainage reduced permanent neurological injury, while modern endovascular strategies preserve or allow adaptation of collaterals by staging and often permit close neurological examination. Drain complications include bloody insertion, spinal/epidural haematoma, subdural/intracranial haemorrhage, overdrainage headache, infection, CSF leak and catheter failure. Anticoagulation is common in aortic repair, so insertion and removal require explicit antithrombotic timing and neurological surveillance. **A bloody or traumatic lumbar drain is a safety event**: reconsider systemic heparin timing, consult relevant teams and do not assume the catheter can safely function as planned.

## 5.4 Practical rescue algorithm for postoperative paraplegia

**Recognition:** assess both lower limbs immediately after emergence and serially for at least the early high-risk period (often 48–72 h or longer for extensive repairs). A change in leg power, saddle sensation or sphincter function demands immediate action. Inspect hypotension episodes, Hb, oxygenation, temperature, K⁺/glucose, anticoagulation and drainage status. Rule out residual neuromuscular blockade and positioning injury, but do not delay perfusion rescue while deciding among diagnoses.

**Action:** communicate with vascular, anaesthesia and ICU teams; restore MAP promptly (commonly ≥90 mmHg, often higher with deficit according to protocol), optimise CO and oxygenation, correct severe anaemia (many protocols target Hb ≥100 g/L), and ensure venous drainage is not obstructed. If a CSF catheter is already present, check pressure, blockage and controlled drainage against the prescribed target; if absent, urgently assess suitability for rescue insertion, taking anticoagulation and coagulopathy into account. Arrange spinal imaging as indicated to exclude compressive haematoma or structural pathology, and confirm graft and collateral vessel patency. Avoid excessively deep sedation that prevents serial motor examination. Repeated reassessment is essential: a rapidly improving deficit after raising SCPP suggests a potentially reversible perfusion problem, but does not eliminate later deterioration.

### Worked examination stem

A patient develops bilateral leg weakness six hours after TEVAR covering 22 cm of aorta; Hb is 78 g/L, MAP 63 mmHg and no prophylactic drain was used. This should be approached as probable spinal cord hypoperfusion until proven otherwise, not attributed to residual anaesthetic. Simultaneously support MAP, correct oxygen delivery/anaemia, call the aortic team, assess the need and safety of rescue CSF drainage, and investigate alternative structural or vascular causes. **Do not give a large crystalloid bolus without considering myocardial function:** inadequate CO, bleeding and vasoplegia require different treatments.

## Examination focus: open and endovascular cord protection

2010.2 Q2 first tests the supply territories of the single anterior and paired posterior spinal arteries, then segmental reinforcement through radiculomedullary arteries, including the variable Adamkiewicz artery. Explain how distal perfusion, sequential clamping, segmental preservation or reimplantation, selected temperature strategies, oxygen delivery and CSF drainage address different mechanisms. If using evoked potentials, state what you will do when signals change.

2016.1 Q6 asks for endovascular risk factors and a prevention plan. Describe loss of several collateral territories, prior aortic repair and perioperative hypotension, anaemia and comorbidity. Discuss staging and collateral preservation where appropriate. The newer ESVS guidance differentiates prophylactic drainage in open repair from considering a rescue-first strategy in extensive TEVAR. A delayed deficit needs simultaneous perfusion rescue and assessment for other causes such as limb malperfusion, stroke or spinal haematoma.

[ESVS thoracic and thoracoabdominal guideline 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/) · [Coselli open TAAA randomised trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11932655/) · [ANZCA 2010.2 report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106419) · [ANZCA 2016.1 report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106430)

items.title: 6. Acute aortic syndromes and aortic dissection: diagnosis, anti-impulse therapy and repair
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (3 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.los: SS_VS 1.10; SS_VS 1.12; IT_RT 1.2; SS_VS 1.7; SS_VS 1.19; SS_IC 1.34; SS_CS 1.6
items.body:
### Aortic anatomy before memorising type A and type B

The aorta leaves the left ventricle as the **ascending aorta**, curves as the **arch** (giving rise to the head/arm vessels), continues as the **descending thoracic aorta**, and becomes the **abdominal aorta** through the diaphragm. In a dissection, a tear allows blood to track between aortic wall layers, creating a false lumen alongside the normal true lumen. The false lumen can compress the true lumen or block a branch artery, causing brain, kidney, gut or limb ischaemia.

- **Type A:** ANY ascending aortic involvement. Risks include rupture into the pericardium → tamponade; coronary artery involvement → myocardial ischaemia; disruption of aortic-valve support → acute aortic regurgitation. These explain why it is generally a cardiac surgical emergency requiring cardiopulmonary bypass, rather than a routine peripheral vascular case.

- **Type B:** descending aorta without ascending involvement. If uncomplicated and perfusion is preserved, treatment commonly starts with analgesia, HR/BP control and imaging surveillance. If there is rupture, uncontrolled pain/BP, rapid progression or branch malperfusion, TEVAR or other intervention may be required.

**Anti-impulse therapy explained:** each heartbeat adds pulsatile force to the diseased wall. Beta blockade reduces heart rate and ventricular ejection force (dP/dt); a vasodilator alone can cause reflex tachycardia and worsen the very impulse you are trying to limit. Hence in a stable hypertensive dissection, control pain and rate first, then reduce pressure while maintaining organ perfusion. Shock, tamponade and acute severe AR are important exceptions: the patient does not need an inflexible rate-lowering protocol.

If a type A patient requires emergency surgery, expect median sternotomy, cannulation and cardiopulmonary bypass, possible deep cooling/cerebral perfusion if the arch is involved, graft replacement of the ascending aorta and sometimes aortic-valve/root work. Anaesthetic priorities are preserving circulation until bypass, detecting tamponade/AR with TOE, managing severe bleeding and confirming myocardial/cerebral/visceral perfusion after repair.

## 6.1 A dissection is not a ruptured aneurysm

The immediate threat in **aortic dissection** is propagation of an intimal tear and false lumen under pulsatile stress. Complications depend on what that false lumen compresses or ruptures into: haemopericardium/tamponade, acute aortic regurgitation, coronary malperfusion, stroke, renal or mesenteric ischaemia, limb ischaemia and free rupture. The affected aortic segment changes the treatment. **Stanford type A** involves the ascending aorta, even if the entry tear is elsewhere; it is a cardiothoracic emergency. **Type B** does not involve the ascending aorta and is usually initially treated with anti-impulse therapy unless there is rupture, malperfusion, progression or other complication. A patient with uncomplicated acute type B dissection and BP 190/110 mmHg should not receive a major emergency operation simply because the diagnosis sounds dramatic. This is the exact error highlighted in the 2022.2 ANZCA examiner report [14].

Distinguish classical dissection from **intramural haematoma** (bleeding into media without an obvious intimal flap) and **penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer** (ulceration through intima into media). These can progress to rupture or dissection. The same early impulse-control principles apply while anatomy and urgency are defined. Aortic aneurysm can coexist with any of these syndromes, but its presence does not convert the medical management of an uncomplicated type B dissection into permissive hypotension.

## 6.2 Clinical diagnosis: maintain suspicion while excluding competing catastrophes

Classically there is abrupt severe chest or interscapular pain, sometimes tearing or migrating; abdominal pain, limb pain, syncope, stroke or acute paraplegia may dominate. Aortic regurgitation can present as a new diastolic murmur and shock; pericardial tamponade as sudden collapse. Differences in limb BP, pulse deficits, focal neurological signs and signs of visceral malperfusion support the diagnosis, but absence does not exclude it. Risk factors include chronic hypertension, connective tissue aortopathy (e.g. Marfan/Loeys–Dietz), bicuspid aortic valve/aneurysm, prior instrumentation, aortic surgery, stimulant use and pregnancy in susceptible patients.

**CTA from chest through abdomen/pelvis**, according to local protocol, is the usual definitive test in a stable patient: identify ascending involvement, entry/re-entry, true/false lumen, branch-vessel perfusion, aneurysm and rupture. TEE is valuable when unstable or in theatre and can identify proximal flap, tamponade, acute AR and coronary involvement, but distal extent may be incompletely seen. TTE may detect tamponade or ascending dilatation but a negative examination does not exclude dissection. ECG and troponin may suggest ACS because dissection itself can cause coronary malperfusion; uncritical thrombolysis or anticoagulation for presumed ACS could be catastrophic. Chest radiography is neither sensitive nor specific. Blood counts, creatinine, lactate, blood group and coagulation guide complications and treatment, not exclusion of the diagnosis.

## 6.3 Initial anti-impulse therapy: control the slope of pressure rise as well as the pressure

Aortic wall stress is driven not only by peak pressure but by the speed and force of LV ejection (**dP/dt**). Vasodilating a patient before rate control may provoke reflex tachycardia and increase shear stress even if the monitor shows a lower BP. Therefore, give titrated IV β-blockade first unless contraindicated, analgesia early, and add an arterial vasodilator only if the target pressure remains high. Provide invasive pressure monitoring and an appropriate high-dependency/ICU environment. The 2022 ACC/AHA aortic guideline recommends an **SBP below 120 mmHg, or the lowest pressure preserving organ perfusion, and HR 60–80/min** in acute aortic syndromes [4]. In many stable patients a lower HR near 60 is desirable, but a fixed HR or SBP must not worsen shock or critical malperfusion.

### Drugs and physiology

- **IV esmolol:** readily titratable, short acting; for example 500 micrograms/kg loading over a minute if tolerated followed by 50 micrograms/kg/min, adjusted in steps (sometimes to 200–300 micrograms/kg/min) to HR and perfusion. A bolus is often omitted in a frail or marginally perfused patient.
- **IV labetalol:** combined β- and α-blockade with longer effect; e.g. initial 5–20 mg IV bolus repeated judiciously or a protocolised infusion; avoid overshoot bradycardia and low-output shock.
- **If β-blockers contraindicated:** non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker (e.g. IV diltiazem) for rate control in selected patients, avoiding use in severe LV systolic failure or conduction disease.
- **Once rate controlled:** add nicardipine, clevidipine or carefully titrated sodium nitroprusside for persistent hypertension, balancing cyanide/thiocyanate accumulation risk if prolonged nitroprusside is used in renal/hepatic failure. Do **not** give a potent direct vasodilator in isolation when tachycardia remains uncontrolled.
- **Analgesia and nausea relief:** IV opioid titrated to pain and haemodynamics reduces sympathetic drive; avoid agitation, repeated coughing, severe hypercapnia and large procedural stress.

For a 75-year-old with type B dissection and BP 190/110, establish arterial pressure and monitoring, treat severe pain, titrate esmolol toward HR near 60–80 and subsequently lower SBP toward <120 if organ perfusion tolerates it; assess creatinine, urine output, pulses, lactate and neurological findings. Aggressive lowering to SBP 90 in a patient with critical renal/visceral malperfusion may worsen injury, so targets are individualised with the aortic team. If the patient is already hypotensive, rapidly evaluate rupture, tamponade, severe AR or malperfusion; **do not follow a hypertension algorithm when the presentation has changed to shock**.

## 6.4 Indications and timing for intervention

**Type A:** urgent operative repair after focused stabilisation. Typical surgical steps are median sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass via a safe arterial inflow site, cooling/cerebral protection as required, replacement of the ascending aorta ± hemiarch/arch and repair/replacement of the aortic valve/root when involved. The team may use antegrade cerebral perfusion and hypothermic circulatory arrest depending on arch anatomy. The anaesthetist anticipates major bleeding, malperfusion, dynamic AR, tamponade, coagulopathy, cerebral injury and prolonged postoperative organ support. Cannulation strategy and aortic pathology must be known before induction. Haemodynamically unstable type A disease needs urgent surgery rather than prolonged optimisation.

**Type B uncomplicated:** initial medical management with imaging, analgesia and impulse control; repeat assessment for progression or high-risk anatomy and determine a follow-up plan. **Complicated type B:** rupture, refractory pain or hypertension despite treatment, rapid expansion, end-organ malperfusion or threatened organ/limb viability generally prompts urgent intervention, commonly TEVAR where anatomically suitable. Selected uncomplicated but high-risk type B patients may undergo delayed/subacute TEVAR following multidisciplinary assessment; the goal is not to rush every type B dissection to stent before the acute inflammatory phase has evolved. The 2026 ESVS descending aorta guideline distinguishes uncomplicated, high-risk and complicated disease and supports anatomy- and risk-dependent timing [3].

### True-lumen and branch-vessel obstruction

Static obstruction occurs when the dissection flap extends into a branch and fixes a stenosis/occlusion; dynamic obstruction occurs when high false-lumen pressure compresses the true lumen or covers a branch opening. TEVAR sealing of the proximal entry tear may depressurise the false lumen and expand true-lumen flow, relieving dynamic malperfusion. Persistent static obstruction can still require branch stenting/fenestration or additional intervention. This explains why a successful-looking thoracic stent does not eliminate the need to recheck renal, bowel and leg perfusion.

## 6.5 Anaesthesia for TEVAR in type B dissection

Before anaesthesia, confirm anticipated left subclavian coverage, access anatomy, rupture/malperfusion status, need for lumbar drain, heparin policy and the intended landing zone. Preserve haemodynamic stability during induction and ensure arterial access and ready vasopressor/vasodilator infusions. Avoid uncontrolled hypertension (risk of propagation) and prolonged hypotension (spinal, renal or cerebral malperfusion). The deployment phase may require transient reduction in pulsatility; restore MAP promptly after deployment. Assess pulses, urine output and metabolic status. Carefully consider **systemic heparin in a patient with active bleeding, traumatic brain injury or expanding haematoma**; this is an individualised vascular–anaesthetic decision, not an automatic 100 units/kg instruction.

Complications specifically worth anticipating include access rupture, retrograde type A dissection, endograft-induced new entry tear, stroke, spinal cord injury, left arm ischaemia or posterior-circulation stroke after subclavian coverage, renal/visceral malperfusion, contrast-associated AKI and persistent false-lumen pressurisation. The initial postoperative plan should include serial neurovascular observations, sustained appropriate BP, renal/lactate assessment and follow-up imaging.

## 6.6 Open type A dissection repair: surgical sequence and anaesthetic responsibilities

**This section closes the explicit SS_CS 1.5 surgical-steps and SS_CS 1.6 anaesthetic-principles components.** A ruptured aneurysm, stable uncomplicated type B dissection, and unstable ascending type A dissection have different induction and circulatory goals. In type A, tamponade, coronary malperfusion, acute severe aortic regurgitation (AR) or end-organ hypoperfusion may make standard antihypertensive/β-blocker titration dangerous. Summon cardiothoracic surgery, perfusion, blood bank and critical care early; time to definitive repair is the priority.

### Typical operative sequence (extent is anatomy-dependent)

1. Review CTA/TEE for the proximal tear, true lumen, arch branch vessels, root/valve involvement, coronary ostia and pericardial blood; choose an arterial inflow site that avoids cannulating the false lumen or worsening malperfusion. Axillary, innominate, direct aortic or femoral strategies are selected by anatomy and expertise, not automatically by a single rule [4].

2. Establish arterial/venous cannulation and cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), using systemic heparinisation and confirming adequate oxygen delivery and perfusion. Sternotomy and decompression of tamponade are dangerous before control is available; in extremis, the team may require selected cannulation or support before opening.

3. Cool and protect the brain/viscera as required; cross-clamp and arrest the heart to inspect the tear and proximal aorta. Replace the ascending segment with a vascular graft; perform valve resuspension, root reconstruction or valve/root replacement if dictated by severe AR, root destruction or coronary involvement.

4. For an open distal anastomosis and/or arch extension, use a team-selected period of circulatory arrest with appropriate temperature and antegrade/other cerebral perfusion where indicated. Hemiarch is often sufficient when the arch has no relevant tear or aneurysm; total arch/frozen elephant trunk is reserved for appropriate anatomy or malperfusion [4].

5. Re-establish distal flow, de-air the graft and heart, rewarm and wean from CPB; assess repair, aortic valve, LV/RV function and regional perfusion by TEE, then reverse heparin with protamine, manage coagulopathy and achieve surgical haemostasis before transfer to ICU.

### Anaesthetic priorities by phase

**Before induction:** plan two reliable arterial pressure sites when limb/arch branch malperfusion may make one misleading; large-bore access, crossmatched blood, rapid transfusion, vasoactives, TEE, cerebral oximetry where used, defibrillation and full CPB readiness. In severe tamponade or low-output shock, preserve spontaneous circulation and sympathetic compensation during carefully titrated induction while surgeons are immediately ready for rescue. Severe acute AR favours avoiding marked bradycardia and high afterload, whereas uncontrolled hypertension in a stable patient requires impulse control. These competing lesions demand a physiology-led rather than protocol-only induction.

**During CPB/repair:** confirm adequate arterial inflow and systemic/cerebral perfusion (including arch branch considerations), communicate the planned temperature/flow/cerebral-protection strategy, monitor acid–base, lactate, potassium, Hb, glucose and temperature, and anticipate massive blood loss and complex coagulopathy. TEE can clarify AR, ventricular function, tamponade and postoperative repair but does not alone guarantee distal organ or cerebral protection. **Weaning and ICU:** assess residual AR, regional wall-motion abnormalities/coronary malperfusion, stroke, bleeding and tamponade, malperfusion of kidneys/bowel/limbs, vasoplegia, rhythm disturbance and postoperative mechanical circulatory support needs. Plan sedation, ventilation, anticoagulant restart and an explicit organ-perfusion surveillance schedule.

### Arch perfusion is not assured by a radial pressure

During ascending/arch dissection repair, arterial cannulation may be axillary/innominate, femoral or direct aortic according to true-lumen and branch perfusion. TEE can help confirm guidewire/cannula position in the true lumen; right radial versus left radial and/or femoral pressure can diverge when an arch branch is compromised, but neither pressure alone establishes cerebral or distal oxygen delivery. Plan cerebral oximetry, EEG or other brain monitoring as locally available; know whether the surgeon will use selective antegrade cerebral perfusion during circulatory arrest. Cooling reduces metabolic demand but does not guarantee a fixed “safe” arrest time. Controlled rewarming, restoration of flow and haemostatic assessment after CPB are integral to preventing neurological injury and major coagulopathic bleeding .

## Set 14 dissection study scope

Keep the diagnosis, medical stabilisation, malperfusion assessment, Type A repair and Type B treatment decisions together in Set 14. Type A repair requires a true-lumen perfusion plan, protection of the brain and myocardium, replacement of the diseased ascending segment and a root or arch strategy determined by the tear and operative findings. Type B management depends on complications and anatomy. In a hypertensive patient with adequate perfusion, control the impulse with IV beta blockade before adding a vasodilator when appropriate. In tamponade, shock or severe acute aortic regurgitation, first preserve coronary and systemic perfusion and expedite definitive care.

[ACC/AHA aortic disease guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9860464/) · [ESVS thoracic and thoracoabdominal guideline 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: 7. Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm: an integrated emergency operation
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
### First understand the emergency: a contained leak can suddenly become an uncontrolled bleed

A ruptured AAA often bleeds into the retroperitoneum. The surrounding tissues may temporarily confine the bleeding, so a patient can be awake with a low but measurable systolic pressure despite enormous risk. Giving litres of crystalloid to make the BP look normal may increase bleeding, dilute clotting factors and remove the fragile tamponade. The central priority is **rapid aortic control**, not perfect preoperative numbers.

The approach changes in distinct phases. **Before control:** minimise transfer delay, call senior help and blood bank, make blood available, assess consciousness/perfusion and accept a lower pressure in appropriately selected conscious patients rather than forcing normotension. **At induction:** sympathetic tone and venous return may be lost abruptly, causing arrest; coordinate induction with the vascular surgeon and haemorrhage-control plan. **After control:** restore appropriate organ perfusion and treat shock, coagulopathy and reperfusion effects.

- **Why local infiltration can be attractive for emergency EVAR:** the patient remains breathing spontaneously, with less abrupt sympathetic withdrawal. But the patient must tolerate groin access and lying still; movement, agitation, severe pain or loss of consciousness may force a carefully controlled conversion to GA.

- **If GA is required:** this is an emergency haemorrhage induction, not a routine elective case. Have immediately available blood products, vasopressors and surgical capability for proximal control. Use haemodynamically tailored doses and airway management appropriate for aspiration risk; no induction agent can compensate for uncontrolled exsanguination.

- **If bleeding is now controlled but hypotension persists:** check for ongoing internal bleeding or access injury, low preload, myocardial dysfunction, vasoplegia and reperfusion acidosis/hyperkalaemia. Surgical reclamping, further repair, blood products and vasoactives are considered according to the demonstrated cause.

The classic IMPROVE trial assessed an endovascular **strategy** for suspected rupture, not an obligation that every patient receive EVAR. Anatomical suitability, available devices, surgeon expertise and haemodynamic stability determine the actual repair. The BJA Education review by Berry, Gudgeon and Taylor is especially useful for this exact peri-induction decision.

## 7.1 The natural history is rapid haemorrhage, not a routine elective pathway

Rupture often presents with abdominal/back/flank pain, hypotension, collapse or a pulsatile mass, but the classic triad is frequently incomplete. Contained retroperitoneal rupture may allow brief relative stability; loss of tamponade can cause sudden exsanguination. Maintain a broad differential including other sources of haemorrhage, ACS, renal colic and intra-abdominal catastrophe. Bedside ultrasound may identify an aneurysm but **cannot reliably prove or exclude rupture**; CTA usually guides repair in a patient who can tolerate the transfer and rapid study, whereas the patient in extremis may go directly to the prepared hybrid theatre or operating room by local protocol.

Early survival depends on prompt definitive proximal control, realistic resuscitation and a well-coordinated vascular–anaesthetic–radiology–blood-bank team. Avoid numerous transfers, investigations or invasive procedures that delay haemorrhage control. Reversal of anticoagulation and activation of MHP may be life-saving; obtain two large-bore IVs or appropriate rapid access, arterial pressure monitoring only if it does not delay control, temperature control, crossmatched blood and a clear plan for rescue aortic occlusion.

## 7.2 Controlled resuscitation: permissive hypotension before haemostasis

Before proximal control, aggressive crystalloid-induced “normalisation” of BP can disrupt tamponade, increase bleeding, dilute coagulation factors and worsen acidosis/hypothermia. The 2024 ESVS guideline recommends permissive hypotension in conscious, adequately perfused patients with rupture, suggesting an SBP of approximately **70–90 mmHg**, with evidence graded level C [2]. This is not a target for a deteriorating unconscious patient, a patient with catastrophic coronary hypoperfusion or after aortic control; it is an approach that tolerates lower pressure while prioritising rapid definitive repair and haemostatic blood resuscitation. Consciousness and ability to speak can indicate tolerable cerebral perfusion but are imperfect. Avoid deliberately lowering BP with nitrates outside a specific specialist protocol.

Give blood and components early when needed. A major haemorrhage pack supplies RBCs, plasma and platelets with ratio-led early therapy until results permit targeted replacement; follow local practice. Reassess fibrinogen, ionised calcium, temperature, pH, K⁺, Hb and viscoelastic results. Avoid large crystalloid volumes except for an immediately demonstrated volume need when blood is unavailable. Reconcile the conflict: **before control avoid over-resuscitation; after control aim for adequate organ perfusion and oxygen delivery**.

## 7.3 Why the induction or conversion to GA is a dangerous moment

With active retroperitoneal tamponade, the patient's sympathetic tone supports perfusion. Loss of this tone at induction can cause profound hypotension, and intubation/positive-pressure ventilation reduce venous return. Invasive monitoring and ideal airway optimisation are valuable only to the extent that they do not delay sealing the rupture. Have surgeons scrubbed and vascular access/control ready before induction when possible. Discuss whether a proximal occlusion balloon may be required and who will deploy it.

If anatomy and cooperation permit, **emergency EVAR under local infiltration with minimal sedation** may preserve haemodynamics and is favoured by contemporary ESVS guidance when tolerated. Deep sedation may paradoxically recreate the problems of GA without a secured airway. Conversion to GA may be necessary for agitation, severe pain, loss of consciousness, airway compromise, access difficulty or prolonged complicated repair. If GA is required, use a carefully titrated low-dose haemodynamically appropriate induction (for example, reduced-dose ketamine or etomidate, or small titrated propofol doses where physiology permits) with vasopressor and blood already running. Do not interpret the named drug as protective against the consequences of uncontrolled haemorrhage. Use RSI principles appropriate to aspiration risk, with minimal delay and immediate surgeon readiness.

## 7.4 Surgical and haemodynamic sequence

**Open repair:** emergency laparotomy → obtain proximal aortic control (sometimes suprarenal/supraceliac initially) → distal control → open sac and repair with graft → correct bleeding/coagulopathy → staged release and reassess perfusion. **EVAR:** bilateral access → guidewire/sheath placement → proximal endograft deployment and exclusion of rupture → iliac limbs/ballooning → completion imaging and limb/graft check. Some patients require an endovascular aortic occlusion balloon while access or deployment is achieved. Balloon occlusion can stabilise central pressure, but it causes distal ischaemia and major reperfusion stress; use it only within the team's explicit protocol and minimise occlusion time.

During haemorrhage, the principal target is sustained coronary/cerebral perfusion sufficient to reach definitive control—not an attractive printed MAP obtained with excessive vasoconstriction and negligible flow. After control, correct hypovolaemia, rewarming, calcium and coagulopathy, and then reassess the circulation. In open repair, clamp release may add a major fall in SVR/preload and a hyperkalaemic load; the principles in Chapter 2 are essential. Patients who remain shocked should be evaluated for persistent blood loss, cardiogenic dysfunction, vasoplegia, abdominal compartment syndrome and malperfusion.

## 7.5 Evidence and postoperative consequences

The pragmatic IMPROVE randomised trial compared an **endovascular strategy** (EVAR when anatomy permitted) with an open strategy for suspected rAAA. Thirty-day mortality was 35.4% versus 37.4%, a non-significant difference; the endovascular strategy permitted more direct discharge home among survivors [17]. This is not evidence that an EVAR graft is intrinsically equivalent or superior in every anatomical subgroup; it is evidence for the strategy as delivered in emergency vascular centres. Choice still depends on anatomy, haemodynamics, device availability and team expertise. RCT findings should not be replaced by a simplistic claim that EVAR halves mortality.

Postoperative complications include ongoing haemorrhage, abdominal compartment syndrome, colonic/mesenteric ischaemia, myocardial ischaemia, stroke, AKI, reperfusion acidosis/hyperkalaemia, respiratory failure, limb/graft ischaemia and multiorgan dysfunction. Serial abdominal pressure assessment may be appropriate after large-volume resuscitation or tense abdomen with deteriorating ventilation/renal function; abdominal compartment syndrome is sustained intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction. Colonic ischaemia after rAAA repair can be catastrophic and requires a low threshold for investigation and surgical review. Adequate analgesia, nutrition, temperature, anticoagulant planning and carefully titrated fluid balance remain important after haemostasis has been achieved.

### Integrated decision example

A 79-year-old with contained rAAA is awake, SBP 82 mmHg, tachycardic, Hb 90 g/L, taking apixaban and scheduled for emergency EVAR. Before control, do not give 2 L crystalloid to target MAP 75: activate blood and reversal pathways, arrange the prepared hybrid room, assess consciousness/perfusion and minimise delay. If local anaesthesia is feasible, preserve cooperation and have an RSI/GA rescue plan. After the graft seals, the same SBP of 82 may now indicate under-resuscitation and organ injury, requiring reassessment of bleeding, CO and peripheral perfusion. **The appropriate BP strategy changes because the bleeding anatomy has changed.**

## Use the Blue Book cardiac and vascular bleeding algorithm as a framework

Start surgical control, warming and initial haemostatic resuscitation together. A fibrin-based trace can indicate poor fibrin clot strength. Weak whole-blood strength despite preserved fibrin contribution suggests a platelet contribution. Interpret clotting time with drug exposure, factor deficiency and heparin effects. Recheck after targeted treatment. The Blue Book figure illustrates the decision sequence and is useful for a viva. Use thresholds validated for the local device and bleeding policy. Normalising a tracing does not correct an uncontrolled vascular lesion.

[ANZCA Blue Book 2025](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [ESVS abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/)
