items.body:
### First visualise a carotid endarterectomy: clearing plaque without losing brain flow

The common carotid artery divides into the **internal carotid artery**, supplying much of the anterior brain, and the **external carotid**, supplying face/scalp structures. Plaque often sits at this bifurcation. A carotid endarterectomy (CEA) opens the artery, removes the plaque and closes the artery—often with a patch. The procedure is intended to reduce future embolic stroke risk.

![CEA schematic: carotid clamp temporarily interrupts direct ipsilateral internal carotid flow, making collateral circulation and cerebral monitoring essential.](set14-ch8-1.png)

- **Expose and heparinise:** the surgeon incises along the sternocleidomastoid, identifies cranial nerves, exposes carotid branches and gives heparin before clamping.

- **Clamp the carotid vessels:** direct internal carotid flow stops temporarily. The hemisphere then depends on blood from the contralateral carotid and vertebrobasilar circulation through the Circle of Willis. If these collaterals are inadequate, cerebral function can deteriorate within minutes.

- **Remove plaque / patch / restore flow:** the surgeon opens the vessel, shells out the plaque, may use a temporary shunt if perfusion is inadequate, closes with a patch and carefully flushes/de-airs before unclamping.

- **Check the brain and neck:** early neurological examination looks for embolic or low-flow stroke; the neck is checked for expanding haematoma; blood pressure is managed to avoid both low flow and hyperperfusion.

**Two anaesthetic approaches:** under awake local/regional anaesthesia the patient can speak, squeeze the opposite hand and obey commands during clamping—arguably the most direct functional test of cerebral perfusion. GA improves immobility and airway control but relies on indirect monitors such as EEG, evoked potentials, cerebral oximetry and sometimes transcranial Doppler. Neither technique consistently wins on hard outcomes; choice is patient and service-specific.

**Two opposite pressure problems:** during clamping, overly low MAP may prevent blood crossing collateral channels. After release, excessive hypertension can overwhelm chronically dilated cerebral vessels and contribute to cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome or haemorrhage. Therefore a single unchanging BP target through the whole operation makes little sense.

**Carotid sinus physiology:** at the bifurcation are stretch receptors that can trigger vagal bradycardia or even sinus arrest if manipulated. Ask the surgeon to stop traction, then treat the haemodynamic effect. An expanding post-CEA neck haematoma is an immediate airway emergency even if the patient initially has normal oxygen saturation.

## 8.1 Pathophysiology and the question of whether to intervene

Carotid atherosclerosis causes cerebral ischaemia through (1) plaque rupture and artery-to-artery embolism, most commonly; (2) progressive flow limitation with inadequate collateral supply, particularly when the contralateral carotid is occluded; and (3) perioperative haemodynamic instability in a circulation with impaired autoregulation. A carotid bruit suggests turbulent flow but is an unreliable measure of stenosis severity, and a normal examination does not exclude significant disease. Symptoms must be localised: ipsilateral transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax), contralateral weakness, sensory deficit or speech disturbance suggest carotid territory ischaemia. Posterior-circulation symptoms alone do not establish ipsilateral carotid causation.

**Symptomatic versus asymptomatic disease is a crucial distinction.** Patients with recent ipsilateral retinal/hemispheric TIA or nondisabling stroke and severe (70–99%) stenosis often benefit from timely CEA where procedural risk is acceptable. Selected symptomatic 50–69% disease can also benefit depending on sex, age, timing, anatomy and risk. The greatest preventable recurrent-stroke risk is often early after symptoms, so suitable patients are usually considered for intervention **within about two weeks** after a nondisabling event, with timing modified after major infarction, haemorrhagic transformation or thrombolysis. A large disabling stroke with extensive infarction is not a routine indication for immediate CEA. Review brain imaging, carotid duplex/CTA and the latest stroke-team recommendation.

For **asymptomatic stenosis**, modern intensive medical management changes the benefit–harm equation. The parallel CREST-2 trials published in late 2025 randomised patients with ≥70% asymptomatic stenosis to intensive medical therapy with or without stenting, or (in a separate trial) with or without CEA. At four years, stenting reduced the trial's composite primary outcome (6.0% medical versus 2.8% stent; P=0.02), whereas CEA did not significantly reduce it (5.3% medical versus 3.7% CEA; P=0.24) [15]. These are separate randomised comparisons, **not a direct head-to-head proof that stenting is universally superior to CEA**. Periprocedural risk remains real and patient selection, anatomy, durability, centre outcomes and expected lifespan matter. A historical assertion that “every asymptomatic severe stenosis should undergo CEA” is now untenable.

Statin-based lipid reduction, smoking cessation, BP control, diabetes optimisation and appropriate antiplatelet therapy underpin management irrespective of intervention. For symptomatic disease the 2023 ESVS carotid guideline is an important reference [5]. A recent coronary stent or complex antiplatelet requirement may shape carotid approach and the feasibility of a regional block; do not withdraw antiplatelets merely to make an anaesthetic technique convenient if that delays or endangers urgent stroke prevention.

## 8.2 CEA surgical sequence and why the clamp is dangerous

CEA exposes the common, internal and external carotid arteries through an incision along the anterior sternocleidomastoid. After identifying nerves, vessels and the plaque, the surgeon gives systemic heparin, clamps the carotid arteries, opens the artery, removes the plaque, may insert an intraluminal shunt and closes with a patch or primary repair. Flow restoration requires controlled de-airing and flushing before final unclamping. Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus can generate vagal/bradycardic responses, while plaque dislodgement, shunt manipulation and clamp-induced low flow can cause stroke. A dissection or thrombosis at closure can impair flow after apparently uncomplicated repair.

Carotid clamping changes the balance between **cerebral metabolic demand** and collateral supply from the opposite carotid via the anterior communicating artery, vertebrobasilar circulation via posterior communicating arteries and external carotid collaterals. If autoregulation is intact and collateral flow is adequate, flow may be maintained. If severe ipsilateral disease, poor circle-of-Willis collaterals or contralateral occlusion are present, distal carotid pressure and cerebral blood flow can fall abruptly. Following unclamping, a chronically underperfused hemisphere may have exhausted autoregulatory vasoconstriction and become susceptible to hyperperfusion, brain oedema or haemorrhage when systemic BP rises.

## 8.3 Choosing awake regional versus general anaesthesia

**Awake CEA** permits continuous, direct testing of speech, consciousness and contralateral hand/leg movement during the clamp. The disadvantage is that the patient must cooperate, remain still and tolerate a neck incision and near-face drapes; inadequate anaesthesia, anxiety, airway obstruction or seizure may require conversion to GA in a constrained position. A **general anaesthetic** offers airway control, immobility and comfort but neurological function is inferred through monitors rather than tested directly. An unanticipated difficult airway may be hazardous during emergency conversion; even an awake patient needs an explicit conversion plan.

The GALA randomised trial (3526 patients) showed no significant difference in 30-day stroke/MI/death between general and locoregional anaesthesia (4.8% versus 4.5%) [18]. A subsequent Cochrane review also found no convincing stroke/death advantage for either technique [19]. Select the technique according to awake cooperation, airway, neurological risk, anticoagulation, team expertise, patient preference and speed of surgery; neither approach is an exam-worthy guarantee of stroke prevention.

## 8.4 A practical ultrasound-guided superficial/intermediate cervical plexus technique

The cervical plexus derives from the anterior rami of C1–C4. Cutaneous branches emerge along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) near its midpoint, classically termed the nerve point of the neck (Erb's point). Superficial branches include the lesser occipital (C2), great auricular (C2–3), transverse cervical (C2–3) and supraclavicular (C3–4) nerves. They supply neck skin but do **not** reliably anaesthetise all deep dissection and carotid sheath structures. The surgeon often must infiltrate the deep incision, carotid sheath and sensitive areas; the patient should be warned that additional local anaesthesia may be needed. This distinction between providing anaesthesia and merely skin analgesia was central to the 2025.1 Final SAQ [12].

**Preparation:** obtain informed consent including the possibility of conversion to GA, inability to tolerate position, local-anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), nerve injury, haematoma and incomplete block. Review antiplatelets/anticoagulants; superficial, intermediate and deep techniques carry different bleeding consequences. Position supine with comfortable head rotation away from the side to be blocked (avoid severe extension in vertebrobasilar insufficiency). Use full monitoring, IV access, oxygen as needed, equipment for resuscitation/LAST treatment and communication with the surgeon. Mark SCM, mastoid, clavicle and the posterior SCM midpoint; identify the internal jugular vein, carotid and relevant fascial planes with ultrasound.

**Superficial cervical plexus block:** under sterile ultrasound guidance place a high-frequency linear transducer transversely at the midpoint of the SCM posterior border. The investing fascia and superficial cervical sensory branches are seen near the posterior SCM, with vascular structures deep/anterior. With an in-plane needle directed to the plane just superficial to investing fascia at the posterior SCM border, aspirate carefully and inject aliquots of local anaesthetic (a representative total volume 10–15 mL of ropivacaine 0.375–0.5%, adjusted to size and total additional surgeon infiltration). Observe controlled spread cranially and caudally along the fascial plane. Landmark subcutaneous fan infiltration along the posterior SCM border is an alternative when ultrasound is not available and anatomical landmarks are reliable. For an **intermediate cervical plexus block**, local anaesthetic is placed deeper to the investing fascia but superficial to prevertebral fascia—technique and nomenclature vary among practices; it may provide more deep spread than purely subcutaneous injection, but may carry increased risk near the carotid and neural structures. A deep cervical plexus block at the C2–C4 transverse process level is more invasive and may lead to phrenic nerve block, vertebral artery injection, neuraxial spread or injury, especially hazardous in severe lung disease.

**Dose calculation matters:** 15 mL ropivacaine 0.5% contains **75 mg**; if the surgeon subsequently infiltrates 20 mL lidocaine 1% (200 mg), cumulative systemic local-anaesthetic exposure must be considered even though the drugs differ. Do not simply apply each drug's maximum as an independent allowance; concurrent local anaesthetics have additive toxicity. Common reference single-drug maximums are approximately ropivacaine 3 mg/kg, lidocaine 4.5 mg/kg without adrenaline or 7 mg/kg with adrenaline, but patient fragility, vascularity and institutional policies warrant lower totals. Inject incrementally with repeated aspiration and ultrasound observation. The technique is successful only if the patient can comfortably tolerate incision and deeper dissection while remaining able to perform neurological examination.

**Sedation:** use no sedation or minimal titrated short-acting sedation such as small-dose dexmedetomidine or remifentanil/propofol, maintaining spontaneous ventilation and immediate rousability. Deep sedation defeats the principal advantage of an awake neurological monitor and may hide stroke, hypoventilation and hypercapnia. Agree on a simple neurological task (e.g., conversation, contralateral hand squeeze, toe movement) before the clamp and recheck at intervals. If inadequate block becomes evident, request surgical infiltration or limited dose addition rather than escalating to an unresponsive patient under the drapes. Prepare a difficult-access airway rescue plan with immediate ability to stop the procedure and uncover the face.

### Identify the actual fascial plane

An intermediate cervical plexus block places local anaesthetic beneath SCM but superficial to prevertebral fascia, typically at about the C4 level under ultrasound. This must not be conflated with a truly superficial subcutaneous fan infiltration along the posterior SCM border. Both approaches may require supplementary surgeon infiltration for deep carotid-sheath manipulation. Deeper cervical injections increase the possibility of phrenic/recurrent laryngeal or brachial plexus effects, and root-level deep blocks add vascular/neuraxial hazards . The best answer describes the chosen plane, ultrasound landmarks, incremental injection, LAST precautions, awake assessment and a safe GA conversion plan—not an indiscriminate mixture of named techniques.

## 8.5 General anaesthesia and cerebral protection

Under GA, insert an arterial line before induction when practical. Use a stable induction that avoids hypotension and tachycardia; sudden falls in BP may reduce flow to a stenosis-dependent hemisphere, while severe hypertension risks plaque/vascular injury and myocardial demand. Maintain oxygenation, normocapnia, stable temperature and adequate Hb. Many teams aim to keep MAP close to awake baseline before clamping and **at or modestly above baseline (often up to 10–20%) during carotid clamping** if neurologically and cardiologically tolerated. This is a practical target, not proof that every patient requires a 20% rise. Increased CO₂ produces cerebral vasodilation but may divert flow (“steal”) from maximally dilated compromised regions; hyperventilation causes vasoconstriction, so avoid unplanned CO₂ extremes.

A selective or routine carotid shunt may be used according to the surgeon's policy and monitoring. Shunting can restore distal perfusion but introduces embolic, dissection and intimal trauma risks. Under awake anaesthesia, new neurological symptoms with clamping are an immediate reason to discuss MAP elevation, shunt insertion or clamp release. Under GA, interpretation relies on multimodal monitoring and the surgeon's judgement.

### Comparing cerebral perfusion monitors

| **Monitor**                       | **What it measures**                                                             | **Strength**                                                           | **Important limitation**                                                                                     |
|-----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Awake neurological examination    | Real-time speech, cognition and contralateral motor function                     | Most clinically direct indication of clamp intolerance                 | Requires conscious, cooperative patient; subtle regional deficits may be missed                              |
| EEG (continuous/raw or processed) | Cortical electrical activity                                                     | Detects hemispheric slowing or loss of fast frequencies with ischaemia | Affected by volatile/IV drugs, hypothermia and deep anaesthesia; does not detect all subcortical ischaemia   |
| Somatosensory evoked potentials   | Cortical response to peripheral nerve stimulation                                | Useful in some centres under GA                                        | Sensitive to drugs, temperature and technical artefact; incomplete detection                                 |
| Transcranial Doppler              | MCA flow velocity and microembolic signals                                       | Can detect reduced flow and emboli during manipulation                 | Requires good temporal acoustic window; velocity not absolute CBF and operator dependence                    |
| Near-infrared cerebral oximetry   | Regional mixed arterial/venous oxygen saturation from superficial frontal tissue | Continuous, quick, trend-based                                         | Extracranial contamination, probe variation, frontal-only coverage; thresholds are not universally validated |
| Carotid stump pressure            | Back-pressure distal to clamp                                                    | Simple surrogate of collateral pressure                                | A pressure is not a direct measure of tissue flow or oxygenation; thresholds vary by institution             |

Treat a concordant change promptly: confirm electrode/probe and anaesthetic depth, restore oxygenation and adequate MAP, check CO₂/Hb, communicate with surgeon and consider shunt. It is poor practice to rely on one number (for example stump pressure 50 mmHg or NIRS drop 20%) as a definitive binary indicator without context. During unclamping, identify air or solid embolic events, avoid abrupt severe hypertension and ensure carotid flow and haemostasis are confirmed before closing.

## 8.6 Carotid sinus reflex, reperfusion and postoperative blood pressure

The carotid sinus at the bifurcation contains stretch-sensitive baroreceptors. Mechanical stimulation may trigger vagal bradycardia, sinus arrest or hypotension; the first step is to inform the surgeon and stop traction. Treat persistent symptomatic bradycardia with atropine (e.g. 0.5–0.6 mg IV in an adult, following local resuscitation guidance) and appropriate haemodynamic support. Local infiltration around the sinus may reduce recurrence, undertaken by the surgeon. Conversely, clamping and denervation alter baroreflex responses; postoperative labile hypertension or hypotension can follow. Persistently high BP after unclamping threatens a brain with impaired autoregulation and may cause **cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome**, while excessive BP reduction can precipitate ipsilateral ischaemia or myocardial injury.

### PACU: a new headache after CEA is not routine postoperative pain

**Neck haematoma/airway compression:** progressively tense swelling, dysphagia, voice change, stridor or respiratory distress may progress to impossible airway access. Call for help/vascular surgeon immediately, give oxygen and prepare for emergency release of the wound if airway is compromised; do not send the patient for routine imaging while obstructing. Rescue intubation can be difficult because haematoma distorts anatomy. An awake-oxygenation strategy with the surgeon ready to decompress may be necessary, with surgical airway backup.

**New neurological deficit:** test speech, gaze, face and limb strength early and serially; an abrupt deficit may be thromboembolism, carotid thrombosis, low perfusion, intracranial haemorrhage or hyperperfusion. Urgent stroke-team/vascular evaluation and imaging are required. A new seizure or severe ipsilateral headache with hypertension may herald hyperperfusion, oedema or haemorrhage; manage BP in a controlled monitored environment while evaluating the cause. **Hyperperfusion syndrome can be delayed** several days; safety-net discharge information is essential.

**Haemodynamic instability:** new severe hypertension may reflect pain, agitation, baroreceptor impairment or cerebral hyperperfusion; treat with a titratable IV agent (e.g. labetalol or nicardipine) according to institutional targets without inducing hypoperfusion. Hypotension can arise from carotid sinus dysfunction, anaesthetic drugs, hypovolaemia or myocardial dysfunction. Assess ECG, troponin when indicated, volume status and neurological signs before giving fluid or vasopressors indiscriminately.

**Cranial nerve injury:** hypoglossal XII injury causes tongue deviation; vagal/recurrent laryngeal X dysfunction causes hoarseness and aspiration, potentially serious with contralateral vocal cord dysfunction; marginal mandibular VII injury causes lower facial asymmetry; accessory XI injury impairs shoulder elevation. Distinguish these from a central stroke. Wound infection, bleeding and myocardial injury remain common non-neurological hazards.

## 8.7 Carotid artery stenting (CAS): same artery, different physiology and antiplatelets

CAS introduces a stent via transfemoral, transradial or transcarotid access (including flow-reversal approaches); distal filters or flow reversal may be used to reduce emboli. It avoids a neck incision and direct cranial nerve injury but requires catheter manipulation through diseased vessels and commonly dual antiplatelet therapy. Ballooning/stenting can strongly stimulate the carotid sinus, causing profound bradycardia and hypotension during or after deployment. Have atropine, vasopressors and cardiac pacing capability according to risk. Monitor for stroke from atheroemboli, stent thrombosis, contrast-associated AKI, access complications and later restenosis.

The choice between CEA and CAS reflects symptomatic status, patient age, anatomy, previous neck radiation or surgery, arch tortuosity, antiplatelet constraints and centre outcomes. CREST-1 and other trials demonstrated different periprocedural profiles: stenting tended toward more periprocedural stroke, CEA toward more MI, with long-term event outcomes influenced by patient selection. CREST-2's 2025 asymptomatic results should be included in discussion rather than repeated older guidance that ignores current medical management. A trial result for asymptomatic intervention must not be transplanted uncritically to symptomatic high-risk anatomy.

## 8.8 New intraoperative neurological deficit: discriminate ischaemia from embolism

During awake CEA, sudden speech arrest, altered consciousness or contralateral weakness on clamping suggests inadequate collateral flow until proven otherwise; immediately alert the surgeon, restore agreed cerebral perfusion pressure and consider clamp release or shunting. A deficit during plaque manipulation, shunting or declamping may instead reflect embolisation, dissection or thrombosis. Under GA, an abrupt concordant EEG/SSEP/NIRS/TCD change warrants a rapid equipment/drug check, restoration of oxygenation, CO₂, Hb and haemodynamic support, followed by direct surgical evaluation. No monitoring modality can exclude all stroke. Record the time and mechanism of suspected injury, activate the local stroke/vascular pathway, and coordinate urgent imaging/re-exploration or endovascular options according to whether there is carotid occlusion, intracranial vessel occlusion, bleeding or another cause. Recent surgery and anticoagulation make routine systemic thrombolysis hazardous; it is never an automatic response. Continue targeted neurological monitoring after emergence, even if intraoperative signals recover.

## Matching the immediate stroke response to the mechanism

A new focal deficit after CEA may reflect carotid thrombosis, a distal embolus, intracranial haemorrhage or hyperperfusion. Check the last normal assessment, glucose and oxygenation, consult both vascular and stroke teams early and arrange urgent examination and imaging. Recent surgery may make IV thrombolysis unsafe. Selected large-vessel occlusions can still be treated with thrombectomy. The 2026 AHA/ASA update expanded selection for some large-core and basilar cases and advises against automatic intensive SBP lowering below 140 after successful thrombectomy. Post-CEA hyperperfusion and intracranial haemorrhage have their own BP strategy.

[AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke guideline 2026](https://doi.org/10.1161/STR.0000000000000513) · [CREST-2 primary report](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2508800)
