items.body:
### Anatomy first: how surgeons revascularise the leg

Blood reaches the leg from the abdominal aorta through the iliac arteries, then the common femoral artery in the groin. This divides into deep femoral and superficial femoral branches; the superficial femoral artery becomes the popliteal behind the knee and then tibial arteries supplying the foot. Disease at each level creates different symptoms and determines where the surgeon must restore inflow.

![Lower-limb revascularisation: an open bypass routes blood around a blocked segment; angioplasty/stenting enlarges the existing vessel lumen.](set14-ch9-1.png)

- **Femoral–popliteal bypass:** vein or synthetic graft is sewn from a femoral inflow artery to the popliteal artery beyond the blockage. **Femoral–distal bypass** ends farther down, for example on a tibial artery; this targets severe limb-threatening disease and may be technically delicate.

- **Aorto-bifemoral bypass:** a Y-shaped graft carries blood from the aorta to both femoral arteries; it may require abdominal exposure and an aortic clamp. **Femoro-femoral crossover:** a graft passes from one groin to the other, useful if one iliac inflow remains sound. **Axillo-femoral bypass:** extra-anatomical graft from axillary artery to femoral artery, sometimes used when abdominal aortic reconstruction is undesirable.

- **Endarterectomy:** plaque is removed from a surgically opened artery, often the common femoral. **Angioplasty/stenting:** a balloon widens a narrowed artery and a stent may scaffold it open. These are not the same operation as a bypass and have different access/antiplatelet implications.

Why the anaesthetic differs: an uncomplicated femoral endarterectomy may be done under GA or regional with modest fluid shifts; a long distal bypass may need systemic heparinisation, prolonged limb ischaemia and careful positioning; aorto-bifemoral reconstruction behaves like open aortic surgery. Postoperative pulses and Doppler signals matter because **graft thrombosis can happen despite normal systemic BP**.

In **acute limb ischaemia** (ALI), the issue is sudden loss of arterial flow with insufficient time for collaterals. Motor weakness is more alarming than pain alone because it signals threatened neuromuscular viability. Revascularisation itself can trigger a systemic reperfusion problem: K+, acid and myoglobin are released; muscle swells in fixed fascial compartments; compartment syndrome can cause further tissue loss even when a distal pulse returns.

**Anaesthetic technique:** choose GA, neuraxial or a peripheral block based on surgical access, anticoagulation/thrombolysis, physiological reserve and the need for serial neurological examinations. A dense block can make new compartment pain or sensory deficits harder to recognise, so document baseline findings and a surveillance plan.

## 9.1 The haemodynamic consequences of a leg lesion depend on collateral flow

Atherosclerotic obstruction in the aortoiliac, femoropopliteal or tibial vessels reduces resting and exercise perfusion. At rest, an adequate collateral network can conceal a high-grade stenosis. During exercise demand exceeds flow and claudication occurs. In CLTI, reduced resting flow causes constant ischaemic rest pain, ulceration, gangrene and susceptibility to infection. Diabetes, ESRD and neuropathy modify symptoms: ulceration may be more obvious than pain. Severity assessment considers the **WIfI classification** (wound, ischaemia and foot infection) as well as limb anatomy, patient risk and available vein conduit. A major goal is limb salvage with acceptable morbidity, not simply reopening the largest visible stenosis.

Risk-reducing medical therapy continues after an intervention: tobacco cessation, statins, antiplatelets, diabetes management, supervised exercise where appropriate, wound/foot care and cardiovascular risk modification. After lower-limb revascularisation, selected patients may benefit from low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin, as demonstrated in VOYAGER-PAD, but bleeding risk, renal function, planned procedures and neuraxial analgesia are essential constraints. It is not suitable for every patient nor interchangeable with full-dose anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation.

## 9.2 Bypass versus endovascular strategy: the operation reflects anatomy

Aorto-femoral or aorto-bifemoral bypass routes flow around major aortoiliac occlusion using a prosthetic graft and may require an infrarenal aortic clamp and laparotomy. A femoro-femoral crossover graft may avoid abdominal clamping when one iliac inflow is patent. Infrainguinal bypass (femoral–popliteal/tibial) uses autologous great saphenous vein or an alternative conduit to cross long occlusions and reach a suitable distal target. Endarterectomy removes plaque from a local segment; balloon angioplasty, atherectomy and stenting treat suitable lesions endovascularly. The chosen technique changes blood loss, anticoagulation, ischaemic time, surgical position, postoperative analgesia and graft surveillance.

The BEST-CLI trial found that in CLTI patients with an adequate single-segment great saphenous vein, a bypass-first strategy reduced major adverse limb events or death relative to endovascular treatment; in those without suitable vein, the advantage was not the same. BASIL-2, involving predominantly infrapopliteal intervention, yielded findings more favourable to an endovascular-first strategy for its trial population. The apparently conflicting results demonstrate why lesion anatomy, vein availability, frailty, wound status and operator expertise matter more than a universal assertion of “bypass is best” or “stents are less invasive” [20,21].

### Extra-anatomical bypass is not a minor groin-only operation

An axillo-bifemoral bypass uses an axillary artery inflow graft tunnelled subcutaneously down the chest/abdominal wall and connected to one or both femoral arteries. It avoids laparotomy and aortic cross-clamping in a patient unsuitable for major transabdominal reconstruction, but introduces a long graft with potential thrombosis, infection, kinking and compromised inflow. Map the axillary and bilateral groin surgical fields, plan arm/shoulder positioning and padding, and document perfusion to both legs and the donor arm. Because the arterial reconstruction still requires anticoagulation and may be prolonged, “no aortic clamp” does not mean trivial haemodynamic or bleeding risk .

## 9.3 Preoperative assessment and optimisation for limb surgery

Establish whether the operation is elective for claudication, urgent for tissue loss/infection or emergency for acute limb ischaemia. The same patient may be chronically ischaemic but develop abrupt occlusion from embolism or graft thrombosis. Evaluate symptoms, vascular ultrasound/CTA or angiography, limb viability, pulses, skin integrity and neurological status. Document a detailed **baseline lower-limb exam** (capillary refill, Doppler signal, temperature, sensation, dorsiflexion/plantar flexion) so postoperative graft occlusion is not missed.

Comorbidities are central: CAD with limited exercise tolerance that cannot be tested because of leg pain, chronic HF, CKD/dialysis, COPD, diabetes and frailty. A patient's inability to walk a kilometre may reflect limb disease rather than poor cardiac fitness, so functional history alone can misclassify risk. Assess cardiac symptoms and ventricular function, ECG and risk-directed biomarkers/echo, anaemia, potassium, glucose and coagulation. Document whether the patient is taking aspirin, clopidogrel, anticoagulants, SGLT2 inhibitors and analgesics for ischaemic pain. Screen for active foot sepsis and need for antibiotics/source control.

## 9.4 Intraoperative anaesthesia for bypass/revascularisation

General anaesthesia, neuraxial anaesthesia and peripheral nerve blocks may each be suitable depending on surgical site, antithrombotic regimen, need for heparin, patient respiratory reserve and expected duration. **Neuraxial sympathectomy** may cause useful peripheral vasodilation but can reduce coronary and cerebral perfusion if it produces hypotension; it is not an automatic way to improve graft flow. A peripheral nerve block or regional catheter can provide excellent analgesia without complete sympathectomy but may impair postoperative motor/sensory assessment; document the degree and duration of block and a plan to detect compartment syndrome or new limb ischaemia.

For an aortobifemoral graft, use the major aortic principles in Chapter 3. For infrainguinal bypass, invasive arterial pressure monitoring is reasonable in extensive or high-risk cases. Avoid prolonged systemic hypotension, hypoxia, hypothermia and severe anaemia that could impair graft and myocardial perfusion. Systemic UFH is commonly administered before arterial clamping; discuss expected dose, ACT monitoring, timing relative to neuraxial placement and surgical preference for protamine. Distal anastomosis may require prolonged leg ischaemia. A Doppler signal after the final anastomosis should be documented; absence of a signal requires immediate vascular assessment rather than waiting for the patient to wake up.

The operative field may involve supine, lateral or prone positioning for posterior targets. Protect the opposite ischaemic leg from compression, avoid traction on neuropathic limbs and cushion areas of fragile skin or ulceration. In long operations, assess access, temperature and distal pressure injury. Fluid therapy balances coronary perfusion and graft flow against HF and CKD; treat a significant fall in MAP promptly, evaluate the cause, use small assessed boluses only when volume responsive, and employ vasopressors when distributive hypotension is dominant. Avoid using distal vasoconstriction as a substitute for fixing a compromised arterial graft.

## 9.5 Acute limb ischaemia: the Rutherford examination determines urgency

Sudden occlusion may result from cardioembolic disease (e.g. AF), in-situ thrombosis of a severely stenosed artery, graft/stent occlusion, dissection, trauma or iatrogenic catheter injury. The classic six Ps—pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paraesthesia and paralysis—are useful but not always all present. The key high-risk progression is **sensory loss extending beyond toes and motor weakness**: nerves and muscle become nonviable rapidly. Evaluate arterial and venous Doppler signals and make a Rutherford classification before choosing imaging or revascularisation.

| **Rutherford class**         | **Clinical findings**                                                | **Doppler findings**                           | **Treatment urgency**                                                                                           |
|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| I — viable                   | No sensory or motor loss                                             | Arterial and venous signals present            | Urgent vascular assessment, anticoagulation and planned revascularisation if indicated                          |
| IIa — marginally threatened  | Minimal sensory deficit (often toes), no motor loss                  | Arterial may be absent; venous present         | Rapid revascularisation, often with time for imaging                                                            |
| IIb — immediately threatened | Sensory loss beyond toes, mild–moderate weakness                     | Arterial absent; venous present                | **Emergent** revascularisation; do not delay for prolonged imaging/work-up                                      |
| III — irreversible           | Profound anaesthesia and paralysis/rigidity, absent capillary refill | Both arterial and venous signals may be absent | Reperfusion may cause catastrophic systemic toxicity; primary amputation/palliation after specialist assessment |

**Immediate medical management** is systemic unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated, as recommended by the 2024 ACC/AHA PAD guideline [6]. A typical acute therapeutic regimen is an IV UFH bolus (often around 70–80 units/kg or a local fixed-dose 5000-unit approach) followed by infusion titrated to aPTT/anti-Xa, but use the local ALI protocol; active bleeding, major trauma or aortic dissection can make anticoagulation inappropriate. Give adequate analgesia, correct hypovolaemia, keep the limb neutral and warm (not with direct high heat), and obtain ECG/vascular imaging as time allows. Avoid tight dressings and local injections into an already threatened compartment. Type IIb requires surgical/endo-team mobilisation concurrently with resuscitation, not sequentially after CT.

### Revascularisation and anaesthetic consequences

Options include open embolectomy (e.g. Fogarty catheter), catheter-directed thrombolysis, aspiration thrombectomy, angioplasty/stenting and bypass. Thrombolysis is unsuitable with major recent bleeding, intracranial pathology or very urgent IIb disease when delay threatens muscle viability; it also constrains neuraxial techniques. Endovascular wire/catheter manipulation and open thrombectomy both carry distal embolic and reperfusion risks. Obtain pre-reperfusion blood gas, electrolytes and renal function; continuous ECG, appropriate arterial monitoring and ready calcium/insulin-dextrose therapy are prudent for prolonged severe ischaemia.

**When reperfusion begins**, lactate, K⁺, myoglobin and inflammatory mediators return centrally. Sudden hyperkalaemia can cause ventricular arrhythmia or arrest; acidaemia can reduce myocardial contractility and amplify vasodilatory shock. Correct life-threatening ECG-toxic hyperkalaemia immediately with IV calcium, insulin/dextrose and other measures according to standard emergency practice, but understand that definitive resolution also requires control of tissue injury and renal excretion or dialysis. Monitor serial K⁺, pH, lactate, CK, calcium, urine output and ECG. Reperfused tissue swells; capillary leak can cause **compartment syndrome** even when arterial flow has been restored.

### Compartment syndrome after reperfusion

Classically there is pain disproportionate to the injury, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling, paraesthesia and later weakness; pulse loss is late and may be absent. A dense regional block, sedation or neuropathy can obscure pain. Clinical suspicion takes priority; if needed, measure compartment pressure (an often used warning is diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure ≤30 mmHg, interpreted in context). Fasciotomy is a time-critical decompressive procedure that should not be postponed for a normal pulse examination. Discuss prophylactic fasciotomy in prolonged ischaemia or severe swelling before revascularisation.

## 9.6 Postoperative vascular and systemic surveillance

Monitor graft/limb flow serially with colour, warmth, capillary refill, Doppler signal, pain, motor and sensory examination—compare with the documented baseline. A new severe pain, cold foot or absent Doppler requires immediate vascular review and possible urgent return to theatre. Also monitor haematoma/bleeding (systemic heparin and antiplatelets), distal emboli, renal dysfunction and reperfusion injury, postoperative MI/stroke, infection and wound dehiscence. Continue appropriate antithrombotics following the chosen intervention once haemostasis and neuraxial constraints permit. ABI/duplex follow-up and wound/foot care are part of long-term limb salvage; “graft patent on the day” does not complete treatment.

## 9.7 Post-revascularisation rhabdomyolysis: diagnose and treat beyond “check CK”

Reperfusion of a prolonged or critically ischaemic limb can cause skeletal-muscle necrosis and release of CK, potassium, phosphate and myoglobin. Suspect this when the limb becomes tense/swollen, dark urine develops, or hyperkalaemia, rising creatinine and acidaemia persist after apparent restoration of arterial flow. Follow serial CK, K⁺, Ca²⁺, phosphate, bicarbonate, creatinine, urine output and ECG, while urgently assessing for compartment syndrome: fasciotomy is time-critical and intact pulses do not exclude it [6,30].

**Immediate management:** control hyperkalaemia and any ECG toxicity promptly; correct shock, maintain oxygenation and discuss the adequacy of revascularisation and need for fasciotomy with the vascular team. Isotonic crystalloid may reduce pigment-associated AKI when circulating volume and kidney function permit; titrate to perfusion, urine output and pulmonary congestion rather than prescribing litres automatically to an elderly patient with HF or oliguric CKD. Published trauma consensus discusses a urine-output goal around 1–3 mL/kg/h (not over 300 mL/h) where feasible, but this is not a compulsory target in anuric/overloaded vascular patients. Stop escalating fluid if it causes overload without urine clearance. Routine bicarbonate for urine alkalinisation and routine mannitol/loop diuretics do **not** have established AKI-prevention benefit [30].

**Escalate:** persistent severe hyperkalaemia, pulmonary oedema, refractory acid–base disturbance or uraemia may require renal replacement therapy on usual indications. Monitor for DIC, hypocalcaemia changes and recurrent compartment pressure. Rehabilitation and limb viability assessment continue after the acute metabolic threat resolves; an amputated or irreversible limb may remain a source of systemic injury and requires multidisciplinary decisions.

items.title: 10. Amputation: surgical and anaesthetic choices, with a focused pain SAQ
items.priority: P1 CORE (3 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
### What actually happens during an amputation, and why the level matters

**Below-knee amputation (BKA):** the surgeon removes the distal leg while preserving the knee. Skin and muscle flaps are fashioned, blood vessels are ligated, bones cut and nerves divided appropriately, then flaps closed to permit later prosthetic fitting. **Above-knee amputation (AKA):** the femur and more proximal thigh tissues are divided; the remaining stump is shorter and subsequent mobility often requires more energy. Advanced infection and severe ischaemia can increase blood loss and contamination.

The nerve supply is not one single nerve. For BKA, the sciatic nerve supplies most of the lower leg, but saphenous (from the femoral nerve) supplies medial skin. AKA involves femoral, obturator, sciatic/posterior cutaneous and other proximal contributions. This is why “just a femoral block” cannot provide complete AKA anaesthesia, and why a combined block or neuraxial/GA approach may be needed.

## 10.1 Preoperative: recognise the pain phenotype and the threatened patient

Critical limb-threatening ischaemia creates severe rest pain and often infection, tissue loss, diabetic neuropathy, opioid tolerance, sleep loss and psychological distress. Document pain distribution/severity at rest and movement, neuropathic symptoms, current opioid equivalents and response, prior analgesia, renal function and the patient’s goals. Correct distressing pain before surgery where possible without delaying source control. Liaise early with the acute pain team if opioid tolerant or poorly controlled; detailed acute-pain drug selection and titration are taught in Set 15, and persistent-pain mechanisms in Set 16.

## 10.2 Intraoperative: match the block or GA to surgical level and anticoagulation

For BKA, sciatic plus saphenous (femoral) territories generally need coverage; a popliteal/proximal sciatic and saphenous/femoral strategy may suit the incision. AKA involves more proximal sciatic, femoral, obturator and other thigh/groin contributions, so a femoral block alone is not adequate surgical anaesthesia. Choose general, neuraxial, regional or combined anaesthesia according to amputation level, sepsis and haemodynamics, airway, patient preference, antithrombotics and expertise. A peripheral catheter may extend useful analgesia, but systemic heparinisation, thrombolysis and coagulopathy may make neuraxial/deep-plexus approaches inappropriate .

For the actual operation, plan reliable multimodal analgesia alongside haemodynamic management; consider a safe peripheral catheter when useful to reduce systemic opioids. Avoid neuraxial sympathetic blockade in a poorly perfused patient without a convincing benefit and a safe antithrombotic/removal plan. Do not promise that a particular block prevents phantom-limb pain: evidence is uncertain. Set 24–25 covers block anatomy, local anaesthetic dose and technical execution.

Pre/intra/post framework for the 2025.2 SAQ: PRE—take a focused pain/medication history, continue baseline opioid requirement to avoid withdrawal, begin or optimise multimodal treatment and seek pain-team input if appropriate. INTRA—choose and justify GA/neuraxial/peripheral technique; consider catheter-based analgesia with anticoagulant safety and a haemodynamically suitable systemic regimen. POST—regular simple analgesia and titrated opioid rescue (PCA only when indicated), selected anti-neuropathic therapy if appropriate, early physiotherapy/prosthetic and psychological support, and acute-pain follow-up. Adjust all treatment for renal impairment, bleeding risk and respiratory sedation; the full prescribing algorithms live in Set 15.

## 10.3 Postoperative: do not mistake a surgical complication for phantom pain

| **Syndrome**             | **Typical features**                                                              | **Differential and response**                                                                                      |
|--------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Residual-limb/stump pain | Surgical site tenderness, deep wound pain, swelling or mechanical prosthetic pain | Normal acute healing versus infection, haematoma, ischaemia, neuroma, bone pathology; inspect and treat cause      |
| Phantom-limb sensation   | Non-painful perception of absent limb position, movement or itching               | Common and not pathological by itself; explain and reassure                                                        |
| Phantom-limb pain        | Burning, stabbing, cramping or electric pain perceived in the absent limb         | Multifactorial peripheral nerve and central mechanisms; neuropathic treatment and interdisciplinary rehabilitation |

Distinguish residual-limb/stump pain (wound, infection, haematoma, ischaemia, neuroma), non-painful phantom sensation and phantom-limb pain. New pain, bleeding, malodour, wound failure or compromised perfusion needs surgical assessment rather than simply escalation of neuropathic medication. Screen for persistent/phantom pain and arrange multidisciplinary review when needed; mechanisms, long-term pharmacological strategies and non-drug rehabilitation are addressed in Set 16. A block treats acute pain but is not proven to abolish future phantom pain.

Examiner calibration (2025.2 FEx, SAQ 6): “Justify your perioperative analgesic strategy for a patient with critical ischaemic leg pain requiring an above-knee amputation.” The minimum standard was an appropriate and safe regional option, multimodal analgesia and recognition of persistent/phantom pain risk. Strong responses explicitly addressed PRE/INTRA/POST phases; common omissions were pre-amputation pain assessment/treatment and postoperative anti-neuropathic and multidisciplinary support. This focused framework earns marks without duplicating Set 15/16 pain chapters.

## Use the amputation pain evidence in clinical context

The 2026 BJA Education review supports early pain assessment, multimodal treatment and targeted regional analgesia. A femoral or sciatic block alone may leave substantial transfemoral territory uncovered. Match the plan to the actual incision, including obturator, lateral femoral cutaneous or posterior cutaneous territories where relevant, using surgical supplementation or catheters as appropriate. Consider anticoagulation, total local anaesthetic dosing and whether a block might complicate postoperative examination. Regional analgesia can reduce acute opioid requirements. Evidence for reliably preventing persistent or phantom pain remains uncertain.

[BJA Education pain after lower limb amputation, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.11.006) · [ASRA antithrombotics and regional anaesthesia](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39880411/)

items.title: 11. Vascular interventional radiology beyond aneurysm stent-grafts
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
### First picture what the interventional radiologist is doing

An interventional radiology (IR) procedure is usually performed using ultrasound, CT or fluoroscopy rather than direct open surgical vision. For **angioplasty**, a guidewire crosses a stenosis, a balloon is inflated and sometimes a stent is left behind. For **embolisation**, tiny coils, plugs or particles deliberately stop blood flow to a bleeding vessel or lesion. For **thrombectomy**, a catheter retrieves or aspirates clot. A technically “small” puncture can therefore affect a major artery, a spinal branch or a bleeding pelvic vessel.

The suite may be remote, with the C-arm, screens and sterile drapes limiting access to the patient’s head. Decide early whether the procedure requires an awake neurological exam, complete immobility, breath-holding or prolonged painful embolisation. **Sedation is not benign if airway access is lost**. Plan monitors, capnography, emergency airway equipment, blood products, warming, radiation protection and rapid conversion to surgery.

- **A useful procedure briefing:** Which artery are you entering? Which territory will be deliberately blocked? Is heparin or thrombolysis planned? What complication could cause sudden hypotension? Can the patient safely move or speak during deployment? How will we recognise distal ischaemia?

**Haemodynamic collapse after angioplasty:** think occult retroperitoneal bleeding or vessel rupture, contrast anaphylaxis/vasovagal event, cardiac ischaemia, arrhythmia or acute vessel occlusion. Look at the angiographic field, pressure trace, ECG, ETCO2, pulses, Hb and surgical access. Do not simply assume “sedation-related hypotension”.

## 11.1 Procedural requirements are as important as the patient's medical history

Interventional radiology encompasses peripheral angioplasty/stenting, embolisation for haemorrhage or vascular malformation, renal and mesenteric interventions, dialysis access interventions, aortic branch procedures and image-guided biopsy. Each has a different balance of analgesia, immobility, anticoagulation, haemorrhage and airway risk. An embolisation in a shocked patient with ongoing GI or pelvic bleeding is not physiologically comparable to elective stenting in a cooperative patient with stable claudication, even though both occur in a fluoroscopy suite.

Before transport, confirm the purpose of intervention (diagnostic angiography, vessel recanalisation, haemostasis or device insertion), anatomical site, access (femoral/radial/brachial/transjugular), anticipated duration, positioning and whether balloon inflation or deliberate transient interruption of organ flow is required. Ask about contrast volume, radiologist's heparin policy, planned thrombolysis, need for transvenous pacing, risk of intraprocedural rupture and whether urgent surgical conversion is possible at that facility. Check haemoglobin/coagulation, platelet count, renal function, antithrombotics, pregnancy status when relevant, allergy history and haemodynamic reserve. A radial arterial line inserted into the same artery planned for access may complicate the procedure; coordinate line sites with the interventionalist.

## 11.2 Sedation versus GA is a balance between access and immobility

Many peripheral angiograms or small biopsies can be managed with local anaesthesia ± mild sedation; use capnography and preserve verbal responsiveness, oxygenation and airway access. Strong analgesia and stillness may be required during prolonged iliac recanalisation, painful embolic delivery or tumour ablation. Sedation can deteriorate rapidly when the patient's face is inaccessible behind the C-arm and drapes. A patient with OSA, morbid obesity, severe COPD or an anticipated difficult airway may be safer with GA from the outset than with deep sedation in a remote area. Conversely, profound hypotension after induction can be disastrous during ongoing haemorrhage before embolic control. Choose the least physiologically disruptive technique that still permits a controlled, safe procedure.

### Image-guided biopsy

A biopsy under CT/ultrasound is a tissue-sampling procedure, but its risks depend on site: pneumothorax/haemothorax after lung biopsy, major vascular or intra-abdominal bleeding after visceral biopsy, liver/pancreatic bleeding or infection, and rare tumour-seeding concerns. Review anticoagulation, platelets and site-specific safe thresholds with the operator; the indication for stopping anticoagulation differs substantially between low-risk superficial biopsy and high-risk deep-organ biopsy. Decide if breath-holding is required; GA/positive-pressure ventilation can change the position or motion of a lung lesion, while spontaneous respiratory motion can frustrate precise needle access. Prepare a rescue pathway for tension pneumothorax or massive haemorrhage, especially in a remote CT suite.

### Vascular embolisation

Embolisation delivers particles, coils, plugs, glue or other agents to reduce flow to a bleeding vessel or lesion. For bleeding, the patient may already have severe shock and coagulopathy; resuscitation must run **in parallel with definitive control**. For elective embolisation (e.g. a vascular malformation), intended ischaemia can produce severe procedural and post-embolisation pain, fever and inflammatory response. Non-target embolisation can cause stroke, spinal cord infarction, bowel/skin necrosis or limb ischaemia. Intra-arterial injection may provoke vasospasm or dissection; missed distal perfusion cannot be identified solely from a stable systemic BP. The anaesthetic plan includes acute analgesia, vascular access, blood availability and post-procedure organ surveillance.

### Angioplasty and vascular stenting

Balloon inflation can temporarily occlude flow and cause pain, organ ischaemia or arrhythmia depending on site. Stents may require systemic heparin, antiplatelet loading and antiplatelet continuation after the procedure. The patient at highest risk is often one whose antiplatelets must be held for another operation soon afterward: discuss before deployment. Access complications include haematoma, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, embolisation, retroperitoneal bleeding and limb occlusion. Monitor new pain and loss of pulses in addition to BP/haemoglobin. A covered stent can rescue perforation but may compromise branch flow; repair strategy rests with the procedural team.

## 11.3 Contrast reactions and other complications

**Immediate contrast-associated physiological reactions** include warmth, nausea and transient vasovagal hypotension/bradycardia; treat the mechanism rather than labelling every symptom “iodine allergy.” True immediate hypersensitivity can cause rash, bronchospasm, angioedema and shock, with severe reactions requiring rapid IV adrenaline, airway/oxygen and circulating-volume support according to the perioperative anaphylaxis guideline. “Shellfish allergy” is not a biologically meaningful predictor of iodinated contrast anaphylaxis; a history of a previous reaction to contrast is far more informative. Document the specific agent and reaction and refer for formal assessment where indicated.

**Renal injury** is multifactorial: chronic CKD, hypotension, atheroembolism, obstruction of a renal artery, sepsis and contrast exposures all matter. Prevent prolonged low perfusion, minimise necessary contrast and avoid needless nephrotoxins. **Arterial occlusion** after a procedure can present with absent pulse, acute organ dysfunction or severe pain; it is time-critical and warrants vascular assessment. **Spinal cord ischaemia** can follow embolisation of a segmental spinal supplier or extensive aortic coverage and is managed with immediate perfusion rescue. **Haemorrhage** may be hidden in the retroperitoneum or pelvis; a sudden reduction in ETCO₂, BP and Hb without visible blood should prompt focused imaging and procedural discussion. **High radiation dose** may cause delayed erythema, skin injury or cataract risk; document dose, incident threshold, counselling and follow-up according to the radiology physics/safety team. **Device migration/embolism** may require urgent extraction or surgery.

## 11.4 Radiology-suite safety and rescue plan

The service must have a clear protocol for failed oxygen supply, loss of wall suction, difficult airway under drapes, loss of IV access, haemorrhage, cardiac arrest and conversion to emergency surgery. Arrange the bed and C-arm so the anaesthetist can access the face and chest, with a plan to move equipment rapidly for CPR. Blood product transport and radiology-suite storage times matter. The effective time to help may be longer than in an operating theatre, so check who responds, from where, and how they are called. Use complete monitoring through transfers, observe temperature, avoid long infusion lines with unmeasured dead-space and control radiation exposure. A patient receiving deep sedation and vasoactive drugs in IR deserves the same standards as a patient receiving them in theatre.

### A five-point hybrid-suite briefing that prevents avoidable rescue delay

Before the patient is draped, physically trace the airway circuit, infusion extensions and emergency IV access through every planned table/C-arm/gantry position. Identify whether the IR table can tilt, who can move the C-arm out of the way, where a full anaesthesia/resuscitation trolley and defibrillator are located, who summons major haemorrhage and vascular surgery, and where an appropriately staffed recovery or ICU destination is available. If GA or urgent conversion becomes necessary, decide whether induction occurs on a tilting transfer trolley rather than an immobile IR table. Sedation with inaccessible airway, long tubing, compromised suction and delayed blood supply is a systems hazard, not simply a drug-choice problem (ANZCA PS55/PG18).

## 11.5 Inadvertent aortic occlusion: the specifically examinable IR complication

**Mechanisms:** graft malposition/migration, thrombosis, device or balloon obstruction, dissection/true-lumen collapse, failed iliac limbs, or intentional temporary aortic balloon occlusion that is prolonged. Full aortic obstruction produces abrupt bilateral lower-body hypoperfusion; partial or branch obstruction may initially appear as a new pulseless leg, gut ischaemia, anuria or hypertension proximal to an obstruction. It can occur with a satisfactory radial BP: a proximal pressure does not demonstrate distal flow. After TEVAR, abrupt leg weakness may arise from spinal hypoperfusion even if femoral pulses remain present.

**Diagnosis during deployment:** announce the concern, check distal pulses/Doppler, femoral sheath waveforms or distal pressure when available, bilateral limb temperature, ECG, acid–base, lactate and urine output. Request immediate aortic/graft angiography or direct procedural imaging to identify a blocked lumen or branch. Exclude major haemorrhage and cardiogenic shock as coexisting causes of falling ETCO₂/MAP. **Management:** the interventionalist must promptly restore flow by balloon deflation, device repositioning, thrombectomy, branch stenting, endovascular salvage or urgent open conversion as anatomy dictates. Maintain cerebral/coronary perfusion while the obstruction is corrected; avoid blindly increasing proximal afterload for a distal-flow problem. Prepare for profound reperfusion hypotension, hyperkalaemia, bowel/renal injury and compartment syndrome after restored flow. Serial distal-organ observations are mandatory after the angiographic result appears satisfactory.

**PS55 application in IR:** before the case, confirm a dedicated anaesthetic assistant, appropriate oxygen/suction, machine and monitors, difficult-airway and resuscitation equipment, essential emergency drugs, enough trained staff to reposition/resuscitate, rapid access to blood and surgery, appropriate recovery facilities and safe transfer logistics. Physical remoteness, heavy imaging equipment and delayed help change the minimum safe plan; they do not justify lowering standards of care [7].

## Escalation for contrast reactions and unexpected distal occlusion

After suspected contrast anaphylaxis document agent, timing, alternatives such as occult bleeding and the treatment response. Arrange acute and baseline tryptase according to ANZAAG and referral to an appropriate allergy service. For unexpected bilateral loss of femoral signals, tell the operator immediately and check for balloon, sheath or graft obstruction, thrombus or dissection. A normal radial waveform can coexist with distal malperfusion. Restore distal circulation with the procedural team and reassess potassium, acid–base balance, haemodynamics and compartments after flow returns. Keep a means of moving the gantry and accessing the airway immediately.

[ANZCA professional documents including PS55 and PG09](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents) · [ESUR contrast manual 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/) · [Multisociety PAD guideline 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013) · [ANZCA Blue Book catalogue](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

items.title: 12. Less common but explicitly examinable elective vascular procedures
items.priority: P1 CORE (3 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (2 parent LOs)
items.los: SS_VS 1.4; SS_VS 1.5; SS_VS 1.17; SS_VS 1.7; SS_VS 1.3; SS_VS 1.6
items.body:
### A fistula explained in one minute

A haemodialysis fistula is a deliberate connection between an artery and a vein (often at wrist or elbow) so the vein develops the high flow and robust wall needed for repeated dialysis needles. A palpable vibration (**thrill**) and audible **bruit** indicate flow. Too little flow means thrombosis/fistula failure; too much flow can increase venous return and eventually contribute to high-output heart failure in susceptible patients. Distal “steal” means hand perfusion is diverted through the fistula, causing pain or coldness.

The anaesthetist checks last dialysis, electrolytes/K+, volume status, uraemic bleeding tendency and whether heparin was used during dialysis. In addition to local anaesthesia, a brachial plexus block can provide analgesia and sympathetic vasodilation; avoid needless intravascular fluid loading in an oliguric patient. Postoperative examination must establish both fistula patency **and** hand perfusion.

## 12.1 Haemodialysis vascular access: the fistula changes the circulation

An arteriovenous fistula (AVF) surgically joins an artery and vein, producing a high-flow low-resistance circuit that enlarges and matures over weeks to months. This creates a **left-to-right systemic shunt** (not intracardiac) that increases venous return and cardiac workload; a very high-flow fistula can contribute to high-output heart failure in susceptible patients. Complications include fistula thrombosis, steal syndrome (distal hand ischaemia), venous hypertension, aneurysmal dilation, infection, bleeding and nerve injury. AV grafts and tunneled dialysis catheters have different infection and patency profiles. The surgical goal may be creation, superficialisation, revision, thrombectomy or ligation, each with different access and blood-loss requirements.

**Preoperative:** assess CKD/ESRD, last dialysis, dry weight, potassium, calcium, acid–base state, uraemic platelet dysfunction, access history, infection and baseline hand perfusion. Examine for a bruit and thrill and document distal pulses and hand function. Discuss whether the surgical target is the dominant arm, whether previous central venous catheters caused stenosis and whether there are signs of heart failure. Avoid BP cuffs and unnecessary IV cannulation in a functioning fistula arm.

**Anaesthesia:** local infiltration with sedation, brachial plexus regional anaesthesia or GA are reasonable. Ultrasound-guided infraclavicular, supraclavicular or axillary blocks can provide excellent anaesthesia and reduce sympathetically mediated vasoconstriction, promoting access flow; block choice follows incision site and respiratory risk (e.g. phrenic blockade with some proximal approaches). Maintain haemodynamic stability and protect the surgical limb from pressure. Local anaesthetic drug clearance may be altered by severe systemic disease; carefully calculate dose. Antithrombotic exposure from dialysis heparin, uraemic coagulopathy and perioperative anticoagulation must be considered before a deep plexus block. Sedation should be adjusted for drug clearance, OSA and airway risk. Postoperatively check thrill/bruit and distal perfusion, bleeding, hand pain/coldness and neurologic function; provide analgesia appropriate to a fresh access site and plan safe next dialysis.

### Sympathectomy explained before the anaesthetic considerations

Thoracoscopic sympathectomy treats selected severe hyperhidrosis or sympathetic vascular disorders by interrupting part of the sympathetic chain alongside the thoracic vertebral bodies. The surgeon needs a small thoracic working space, often by allowing a lung to deflate or insufflating CO2 into the chest. This can raise intrathoracic pressure, reduce venous return, impair oxygenation and cause vagal or sympathetic haemodynamic changes.

The key intraoperative complication is capnothorax or tension physiology: rising airway pressures, falling SpO2 and hypotension. Stop/release insufflation and evaluate lung expansion before treating an unexplained fall in BP as simple vasodilation. After surgery, ensure lung reinflation and assess for pneumothorax/haemothorax; expect modest port pain but counsel about compensatory sweating and possible Horner syndrome.

## 12.2 Thoracoscopic sympathectomy: a short procedure with potentially major cardiopulmonary effects

Thoracoscopic sympathectomy is most often performed for severe refractory palmar/axillary hyperhidrosis and occasionally selected vasospastic conditions. The surgeon introduces ports into the thorax and interrupts targeted sympathetic chain levels. Anaesthesia generally requires GA with reliable lung deflation or appropriate thoracoscopic exposure, often using a double-lumen tube, bronchial blocker or single-lumen technique with surgical CO₂ insufflation depending on centre practice and scope. Anticipate a controlled pneumothorax with reduced venous return, altered lung compliance and increased intrathoracic pressure; use protective ventilation and limit excessive insufflation pressures. Bilateral procedures may involve sequential side changes.

**Key physiological considerations:** sympathetic interruption can reduce HR and systemic vascular tone; manipulation may provoke vagal bradycardia. New pneumothorax or capnothorax causes increased airway pressures, reduced lung expansion and possible haemodynamic compromise; if sudden hypotension, desaturation or high airway pressure occurs, ask the surgeon to release insufflation and exclude tension physiology. Adequate analgesia usually involves acetaminophen, appropriate opioid and local intercostal/port-site infiltration. Postoperative problems include residual pneumothorax, haemothorax, pleuritic pain, subcutaneous emphysema, Horner syndrome from high-level injury and later compensatory sweating—often the most bothersome long-term adverse effect. Discuss these potential outcomes during consent and ensure lung reinflation and postoperative chest imaging when indicated.

## 12.3 Miscellaneous emergency vascular operations: arterial laceration and vessel occlusion

A patient with penetrating injury to the femoral artery may need immediate proximal and distal control, shunt placement, primary repair or interposition graft. Before definitive control, avoid “normalising” BP at the expense of bleeding, correct coagulopathy and preserve oxygen delivery; a contained haematoma can decompress suddenly during dissection. Once flow is restored, monitor distal pulses, potassium/CK and compartment status. Aortic/iliac injury demands the same MHP and clamp-release preparedness as ruptured aneurysm. Damage-control surgery or temporary vascular shunting may be essential in a shocked multiply injured patient.

If the procedure is for major **arterial occlusion rather than haemorrhage**, the principal concern is prolonged organ ischaemia and reperfusion injury. The contrast between these two emergency presentations matters: a hypotensive actively bleeding patient needs haemostatic resuscitation, while an occluded limb without bleeding may require immediate therapeutic UFH, rapid imaging and reperfusion. Applying the wrong generic “vascular” algorithm can cause catastrophic harm.

## 12.4 Emergency vascular procedures: six distinct pre/intra/post strategies

**SS_VS 1.7 requires perioperative management including fluids and analgesia for every named emergency.** An emergency aneurysm rupture cannot share the same BP and anticoagulant algorithm as an occluded but non-bleeding artery. These are exam frameworks; procedure-specific local protocols and available expertise determine actual targets.

| **Emergency operation**                        | **Haemodynamic/operative plan and fluids**                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | **Analgesia and recovery**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Ruptured AAA                                   | Before proximal control: rapid transfer, blood-based haemostatic resuscitation, cautious permissive pressure if awake/perfused, avoid large crystalloid. Prepare occlusion/EVAR or open repair, then correct volume and reperfusion shock after haemostasis. | Carefully titrated analgesia avoiding circulatory collapse; postoperative ICU, abdominal/renal/bowel/limb monitoring and dynamic multimodal analgesia. Epidural usually unsuitable in the unstable anticoagulated phase.                                                                               |
| Acute type A dissection                        | Treat pain and impulse in a stable patient, but shock/tamponade/acute severe AR alter priorities. Prepare bypass and massive transfusion; use TEE and lesion-specific pressure/flow decisions throughout surgery.                                            | Provide titrated opioid analgesia before repair; expect sternotomy/CPB recovery, ICU ventilation, dynamic analgesia and surveillance for neurological, bleeding and organ-malperfusion complications.                                                                                                  |
| Major vessel occlusion (aortic/iliac or graft) | Document perfusion deficit and threatened territory, urgently restore flow by catheter/open surgery, usually with UFH if no major bleeding contraindication. Reassess fluid/CO and treat K⁺/acidosis on reperfusion; avoid forcing fluids into HF/CKD.       | Severe ischaemic pain needs titrated systemic opioid ± safe regional option. Continue postoperative Doppler, bowel/limb/renal/compartment checks and analgesia as vascular status changes.                                                                                                             |
| Acute limb ischaemia                           | Classify Rutherford viability, commence UFH if appropriate, expedite revascularisation for IIb and monitor abrupt K⁺/acid/CK return. Replace genuine deficits, support perfusion and watch for fasciotomy requirements.                                      | Treat severe pain early. A dense regional block can mask evolving neurological loss/compartment syndrome; postoperative neurovascular surveillance, multimodal pain care and rhabdomyolysis management are essential.                                                                                  |
| Emergency limb amputation                      | Assess severe sepsis, infected/irreversible muscle, bleeding, AKI and electrolyte toxicity; source control and adequate perfusion outweigh elective optimisation. Fluid/blood/vasopressors follow observed shock physiology.                                 | Record existing ischaemic/neuropathic pain and baseline opioids; use appropriate neuraxial/peripheral/GA technique with anticoagulant constraints. Plan acute analgesia, residual-limb/phantom pain prevention strategies and rehabilitation, without claiming a block reliably prevents chronic pain. |
| Arterial laceration/major bleeding             | Obtain proximal/distal vascular control with MHP, warming, calcium and targeted haemostasis. Temporary shunt/damage control may be needed. After repair confirm distal flow and prepare for reperfusion/compartment complications.                           | Small, carefully titrated opioid doses before haemorrhage control; once haemostatically stable use multimodal/local or regional strategies if anticoagulation permits. Monitor graft/limb perfusion, occult bleeding and nerve injury.                                                                 |

A useful oral answer always specifies **which territory is threatened, whether active haemorrhage is present, whether systemic heparin is safe, when definitive control happens, and what reperfusion injury must be watched for**. The fluid prescription and postoperative pain plan then follow those decisions.

## Two emergency decisions worth rehearsing

In suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia obtain urgent CT angiography with arterial and venous phases even when renal impairment is present. A normal lactate early does not exclude ischaemia. Start resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics in parallel, discuss heparin where appropriate and decide whether revascularisation also requires laparotomy, bowel resection or a second look. Pain out of proportion and atrial fibrillation are useful cues, not required findings. Have a plan for metabolic washout after reperfusion.

After fistula creation, distinguish absent thrill from a painful or cool hand with distal ischaemia. New severe weakness or sensory loss may indicate ischaemic monomelic neuropathy even when skin perfusion looks relatively preserved. Interpret against preoperative findings and block effects and obtain early vascular review. If a high-flow access worsens breathlessness, assess the shunt contribution alongside volume, RV function and pulmonary hypertension.

[ESVS mesenteric and renal artery guidance 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejvs.2025.06.010) · [KDOQI vascular access guidance](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32778223/) · [Multisociety PAD guideline 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013)

items.title: 13. Putting complication prevention, fluid therapy and regional choices together
items.priority: P1 CORE (5 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (2 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.los: SS_VS 1.5; SS_VS 1.18; SS_VS 1.13; SS_VS 1.10; SS_VS 1.12; SS_VS 1.3; SS_VS 1.6; SS_VS 1.8
items.body:
### How to make decisions rather than memorise a complications list

Before giving a drug or fluid bolus, ask: **is there a fall in circulating volume, arterial tone, forward cardiac output, or blood flow through a specific vessel?** These are different problems. A hypotensive patient after EVAR with retroperitoneal bleeding needs source control and blood; vasodilatory shock after reperfusion may need noradrenaline; LV failure during cross-clamping may require afterload adjustment and inotropy; a newly cold foot with normal MAP needs vascular reassessment, not an empiric fluid bolus.

Think separately about three endpoints: (1) **whole-patient survival**—airway, circulation, haemorrhage; (2) **organ perfusion**—brain, heart, kidneys, bowel and spinal cord; and (3) **technical vascular success**—graft/stent patency, distal Doppler signals and absence of embolisation. A high systemic BP cannot prove success at levels 2 or 3.

## 13.1 Intraoperative complications: recognise and treat mechanisms

| **Event**                        | **Possible mechanism and early clues**                                                              | **Immediate response**                                                                                                                                                |
|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Major haemorrhage                | Anastomotic disruption, rupture, access injury; falling BP/ETCO₂, rapid transfusion requirement     | Surgical control; MHP; warmed blood, fibrinogen/platelet/viscoelastic guidance, calcium and temperature correction; investigate occult bleeding                       |
| Myocardial ischaemia             | Afterload surge, tachycardia, anaemia, hypotension; ST change, new wall motion abnormality, CO fall | Correct supply–demand imbalance; assess ECG, rhythm, Hb, BP/CO, bleeding; coordinate cardiac management and troponin surveillance                                     |
| Carotid sinus bradycardia        | Baroreceptor stimulation, brady/asystole                                                            | Stop traction, atropine and resuscitation as needed; consider local infiltration, appropriate pacing readiness                                                        |
| Clamp-related cerebral ischaemia | Inadequate collateral flow; EEG/NIRS/TCD or awake neurological change                               | Confirm monitoring, raise MAP to agreed target, review CO₂/Hb, communicate about selective shunt or clamp release                                                     |
| Acute arrhythmia                 | Myocardial ischaemia, K⁺/Ca²⁺ disturbance, reperfusion, myocardial disease                          | Treat instability via standard resuscitation algorithms, correct cause, avoid repeated futile antiarrhythmic therapy without correcting electrolyte/perfusion problem |
| Spinal cord ischaemia            | Extensive segmental coverage, low MAP, high CSF pressure or anaemia                                 | Immediate SCPP rescue bundle: MAP, Hb/O₂, controlled drainage or urgent rescue insertion, vascular assessment                                                         |
| Embolic event                    | Aortic plaque, stent or wire manipulation; limb loss of pulse, focal stroke                         | Stop manipulation, restore flow/perfusion, stroke/vascular rescue pathway                                                                                             |
| Reperfusion syndrome             | Return of acid/K⁺/myoglobin; hypotension, ECG changes, acidaemia                                    | Gradual reperfusion when feasible, aggressive monitoring, calcium and potassium treatment, assess CO/volume/vasoplegia                                                |
| Acute renal impairment           | Ischaemia, emboli, access-related renal occlusion, contrast or low CO                               | Check inflow and renal stents, maintain perfusion, avoid nephrotoxins, correct volume carefully and request renal support as indicated                                |
| Contrast anaphylaxis             | Acute shock, bronchospasm, angioedema after contrast                                                | Immediate adrenaline, oxygen, fluids/vasopressors as needed, stop exposure, investigation and allergy referral                                                        |

## 13.2 When does vascular anaesthesia need different fluid decisions?

A common error is to apply a single universal “give fluids to a CVP target” policy to every part of a vascular case. **Fluid responsiveness** means that a bolus will increase stroke volume; it does not necessarily mean fluid is beneficial if the patient has pulmonary oedema or severe venous congestion. Use small challenges or dynamic tests where valid, and interpret them with CO, BP, capillary refill, echo, blood loss and urine output. Dynamic pulse-pressure variation is unreliable during spontaneous breathing, arrhythmia, low tidal volumes, high intra-abdominal pressure or markedly altered RV afterload. Low urine output during renal artery clamping is not evidence that the correct response is another litre of saline.

| **Phase or condition**          | **Physiological problem**                                            | **Reasoned initial strategy**                                                                                            |
|---------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Bleeding before rupture control | Blood loss with risk of losing tamponade if pressure forced too high | Controlled blood-based resuscitation, rapid source control; permissive pressure only while adequately perfused           |
| Elective pre-clamp              | Need enough circulatory reserve without LV overload                  | Replace demonstrable deficit; check flow and congestion; avoid fixed large preload                                       |
| High aortic clamp               | Rising LV impedance, possible myocardial dysfunction                 | Avoid tachycardia, titrate vasodilator/inotrope by CO and ischaemia rather than BP alone                                 |
| Immediately before release      | Expected vasodilation and distal venous pooling                      | Check volume responsiveness and blood loss, prepare noradrenaline, correct significant K/Ca derangements, staged release |
| After reperfusion               | Vasoplegia, myocardial depression, ongoing bleeding, acid/K⁺ washout | Differentiate cause, reassess CO/echo and lactate, use appropriate fluid/blood and vasopressors                          |
| Carotid clamping                | Threatened hemispheric perfusion                                     | Maintain adequate baseline or higher MAP, avoid CO₂ extremes, use selective shunt policy                                 |
| Spinal protection               | Maintain spinal perfusion pressure                                   | Adequate MAP/Hb, prevent low CO and excessive CSF pressure; rescue promptly                                              |
| CKD/heart failure               | High risk of both overload and inadequate organ perfusion            | Assess individual flow, avoid nephrotoxins and large indiscriminate fluid loads                                          |

Postoperative fluid prescribing should have an indication for each infusion: maintenance if genuinely unable to drink, replacement of ongoing losses, or resuscitation for a documented deficit. Record urine output, daily weight, fluid balance, creatinine, electrolytes and clinical evidence of congestion; these data are complementary, not interchangeable. Intraoperative blood conservation and correct early haemostatic resuscitation reduce the downstream need for high-volume crystalloids and their associated bowel, pulmonary and wound oedema.

## 13.3 Regional anaesthesia: an evaluation, not a simple preference

Regional techniques can avoid airway manipulation, reduce opioid requirements, facilitate neurological assessment and improve analgesia. Specific techniques—awake cervical plexus block for CEA, brachial plexus block for AVF, peripheral catheter for amputation or neuraxial analgesia for open AAA—have distinct advantages. Their risks rise when vascular procedures require systemic heparin, thrombolysis or dual antiplatelet therapy. A block that provides dense analgesia may obscure an evolving limb compartment syndrome or nerve deficit. Neuraxial sympathectomy can destabilise a patient with severe CAD and fixed stroke-volume physiology. Local anaesthetic toxicity and vascular puncture are particularly consequential in a hypoperfused patient. The decision should always answer: **Does the technique change the safety and outcomes of this specific operation, and can its complications be rescued?**

For epidural/neuraxial and deep plexus procedures, comply with current ANZCA/ASRA/ESAIC–ESRA antithrombotic timing guidance, including safe catheter removal. Avoid fabricating a single universal number of hours for every anticoagulant: the timing depends on drug, dose, renal clearance, bleeding/traumatic insertion and concurrent agents. If anticoagulants cannot be interrupted because of critical limb ischaemia, recent stenting or aortic rupture, use an alternative technique and optimise multimodal analgesia. The patient must have a postoperative monitoring plan that detects nerve compression or neuraxial haematoma early.

## 13.4 Postoperative surveillance: exactly what should be checked in recovery?

Immediately communicate the **operation, clamp/occlusion times, blood loss/transfusion, heparin/protamine, graft location, known organ ischaemia, drain status and vascular/neurological baselines**. Obtain adequate analgesia before emergence while avoiding masking a required neurological examination. In PACU/ICU assess airway, breathing, circulation, temperature, glucose, ECG and urine output, then perform targeted neurological and perfusion checks: distal pulses after bypass/EVAR, motor power after TEVAR and carotid surgery, neck wound and voice after CEA, abdominal pain/lactate after aortic repair, renal output after suprarenal clamp and surgical site haematoma after access procedures. Any unexplained deterioration must trigger early surgical review and not merely “repeat bloods in an hour.”

**A common high-risk error** is the assumption that a normal BP or arterial saturation rules out organ-specific injury. A stroke can occur with normal MAP; bowel ischaemia after aortic repair can exist while systemic SpO₂ is 100%; graft thrombosis causes a limb emergency despite normal HR; spinal cord ischaemia can first appear hours after apparently perfect TEVAR. Successful vascular anaesthesia is measured by neurological, renal, bowel and limb outcomes as well as intraoperative stability.

## 13.5 Vascular-specific fluid/perfusion choices and a brief analgesia crosswalk

This table completes SS_VS 1.5 without reproducing Set 15 drug/PCA/epidural protocols or Set 16 persistent-pain treatment. The emphasis is WHAT is different in each vascular operation: cardiac/organ perfusion, bleeding, renal reserve, anticoagulation, postoperative neurovascular examination and the feasibility of a catheter or block. There is no fixed vascular fluid target or default analgesic technique. Explain the mechanism of hypotension before giving fluid, blood or vasoactive medication.

| **Procedure**                                | **Perioperative fluid / perfusion approach**                                                                                                                                                                                                         | **Postoperative analgesia and specific precautions**                                                                                                                                                                            |
|----------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Open infrarenal AAA / aorto-bifemoral bypass | Anticipate bleeding and rapid clamp/release changes; restore blood loss with appropriate components, use fluid responsiveness and CO rather than CVP alone, prepare vasodilator/inotrope for clamp and noradrenaline for release.                    | Thoracic epidural if antithrombotic timing and haemodynamics permit; otherwise opioid PCA plus acetaminophen and wound/abdominal-wall catheter or plane block. Watch epidural hypotension and delayed neuraxial bleed.          |
| Open descending thoracic/TAAA repair         | Plan for high clamp, distal perfusion, possible left-heart bypass, larger blood loss and prolonged lung/spinal/renal ischaemia. Maintain oxygen delivery and SCPP without causing pulmonary congestion.                                              | Thoracic epidural/paravertebral/erector-spinae or systemic multimodal regimen selected against full heparinisation and CSF-drain constraints. Pain control must support cough, mobilisation and respiratory recovery.           |
| EVAR / TEVAR / complex FBEVAR                | Avoid unnecessary prophylactic fluid loading for contrast; maintain BP/CO for kidney, spinal cord and limb flow, respond immediately to access bleeding. TEVAR with spinal risk may need protocolised higher MAP postoperatively.                    | Often local/groin infiltration and acetaminophen ± low-dose opioid; extensive complex grafts may need PCA and monitored sedation weaning. Avoid excess opioid sedation when frequent motor examinations are essential.          |
| Carotid endarterectomy / stent               | Before/during clamp prevent hypotension that threatens cerebral collateral supply; avoid indiscriminate fluid boluses in heart failure. After release carefully control hypertension/hypotension and watch for neck bleeding or neurological change. | Usually local infiltration, acetaminophen and small titrated opioid if needed; avoid deep sedation that masks neurological deficit or airway haematoma. Assess cranial nerve function, voice and swallowing before oral intake. |
| Peripheral bypass / endarterectomy           | Protect myocardium and distal graft perfusion while avoiding oedema in CKD/HF. Replace documented blood loss; treat vasodilation with vasoactives when appropriate and recheck graft Doppler.                                                        | Acetaminophen ± PCA/oral opioid, carefully selected peripheral nerve catheter or neuraxial analgesia. Define neurovascular-monitoring plan because a dense block can conceal compartment syndrome or recurrent occlusion.       |
| Haemodialysis fistula creation/revision      | Aim for usual dry weight and a circulation adequate for fistula patency, not fluid loading in an oliguric patient. Watch for regional-block sympathectomy, HF and potassium/acid–base changes. Protect fistula arm.                                  | Often local infiltration or brachial plexus block with acetaminophen; use renally appropriate opioid rescue, avoid routine NSAIDs in advanced CKD. Recheck thrill, bleeding, steal/hand perfusion and time to dialysis.         |
| Thoracoscopic sympathectomy                  | Usually modest losses; avoid large boluses for insufflation-related reduced venous return until capnothorax/tension physiology and other causes are considered. Re-expand lung and restore normal ventilation.                                       | Port-site infiltration, acetaminophen and brief opioid as required; assess pleuritic pain, residual pneumothorax/haemothorax and lung expansion. Epidural is generally disproportionate for a short uncomplicated procedure.    |

Postoperative handover check: can the patient breathe deeply, cough and mobilise; does analgesia allow serial limb/spinal/neurological examinations; will antithrombotic restart or anticoagulant exposure affect catheter removal; and is renal function adequate for the chosen medicines? A good pain score cannot compensate for missed graft thrombosis, compartment syndrome or spinal cord ischaemia. For generic opioid/PCA/epidural monitoring, refer to Set 15.
