items.body:
### A repeatable ANZCA viva framework for any new vascular operation

- Name the **artery, disease and surgical intention**: relief of stenosis, bypass of occlusion, aneurysm exclusion, plaque removal, or haemorrhage control.

- Describe the **surgical sequence** in plain English: access/incision → heparin/cross-clamp or wire/stent → repair/deployment → return of flow → haemostasis. Mention whether clamping/reperfusion affects kidney, gut, leg, brain or spinal cord.

- Describe **preoperative** assessment that changes management: cardiac and pulmonary reserve; kidney function; neurological/limb baseline; recent MI/stent; antithrombotics; surgical imaging; urgency.

- Describe **intraoperative** technique/monitoring and why: GA versus regional or awake; arterial line and large-bore access where indicated; blood/heparin plan; haemodynamic target specific to the procedural phase; temperature, acid–base and electrolytes.

- Describe **postoperative** organ-specific surveillance: neurological exam, graft pulses, abdominal symptoms/bleeding, renal function and myocardial injury. Add an explicit analgesia and anticoagulant-restart plan.

This structure is more reproducible than starting by listing induction agents. For example, in a carotid operation the biggest unique problem is brain flow during clamping, while in ruptured AAA it is avoiding collapse before haemorrhage control. Both use general anaesthesia sometimes, but the correct answer differs because the operation differs.

## 14.1 Open, endovascular and conservative treatment are different risk distributions

To evaluate an operation, first identify the disease's untreated natural history, then compare the short-term operative hazard with the durability, recovery, surveillance and late-failure risk of each available strategy. The lowest immediate-risk operation is not necessarily the best lifelong intervention, and the most anatomically comprehensive operation may be inappropriate for an individual with limited reserve.

| **Decision**                                         | **Open surgical treatment**                                                                                                           | **Endovascular treatment**                                                                                                                          | **Conservative / medical strategy**                                                                                                                         |
|------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Infrarenal AAA**                                   | Durable surgical graft with abdominal exposure, clamp-related LV afterload changes, major haemorrhage and pulmonary/renal injury      | Less physiological insult initially; dependent on sealing zones and access; endoleak, migration and late rupture demand surveillance                | Appropriate for small stable aneurysm or when intervention is not beneficial; control BP, smoking and other vascular risks, scheduled imaging               |
| **Descending thoracic aneurysm / type B dissection** | Open thoracotomy with major blood loss, one-lung ventilation, aortic cross-clamping and distal-organ ischaemia                        | TEVAR avoids many open stresses but can cover intercostal/arch branches, causing SCI, stroke, retrograde type A dissection and access complications | Anti-impulse treatment and surveillance for uncomplicated type B dissection; intervention with complications/high-risk progression                          |
| **Symptomatic carotid stenosis**                     | CEA directly removes plaque; neck surgery with cranial nerve, haematoma and baroreflex risks; awake neurological examination possible | CAS avoids neck incision but adds catheter/arch embolism, stent-thrombosis and mandatory antiplatelet implications                                  | Intensive stroke risk reduction always necessary; may be sole treatment for low-grade stenosis or patients whose procedural risks exceed benefit            |
| **CLTI/infrainguinal arterial disease**              | Durable vein bypass in suitable anatomy and conduit, with wound and graft risks                                                       | Lower initial tissue trauma; may require repeated interventions, and distal anatomy affects durability                                              | Cardiovascular therapy, infection control and foot care remain mandatory; tissue loss usually still needs perfusion restoration if limb salvage is feasible |
| **Acute limb ischaemia**                             | Immediate embolectomy, bypass or repair when threatened limb demands rapid flow restoration                                           | Catheter thrombectomy or thrombolysis in selected viable/marginally threatened limbs; reperfusion is not without hazard                             | Anticoagulation while arranging definitive care; palliation/primary amputation if irreversibly ischaemic                                                    |

### Interpreting the apparently conflicting limb revascularisation trials

The **BEST-CLI** study was not a universal victory for bypass. In its cohort with a usable single-segment great saphenous vein, the composite of major adverse limb event or death occurred in 42.6% after surgery versus 57.4% after endovascular treatment at a median 2.7 years; when no suitable vein existed, the difference was not clearly significant [20]. The **BASIL-2** study enrolled patients requiring an infrapopliteal (with or without more proximal) procedure and found more major amputation or death with a vein-bypass-first than a best-endovascular-first strategy (63% vs 53%) [21]. These studies included different anatomic distributions, procedural strategies and patients. For the anaesthetist, that is a lesson about multidisciplinary selection and individual physiological risk, not a reason to insist that all diabetic legs must have one type of surgery.

After successful lower-limb revascularisation, **VOYAGER PAD** found fewer acute limb/cardiovascular composite events with rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin than with aspirin alone, at the expense of increased bleeding risk [22]. This is a vascular secondary prevention regimen, not the full-dose anticoagulation used for atrial fibrillation or acute embolus. It influences the timing of subsequent surgery and regional techniques. The local vascular team must specify antithrombotic duration and how a later procedure will be handled.

## 14.2 A worked open AAA case: haemodynamics from induction through unclamping

A 73-year-old with a 6.4 cm infrarenal AAA, treated hypertension, moderate LV hypertrophy and stable angina undergoes elective open repair. The plan is an arterial line, large-bore access, temperature control, crossmatched blood, cell salvage and GA; an epidural is considered only after antithrombotic and postoperative anticoagulation planning. Before induction, ask what LVH means physiologically: a relatively stiff ventricle requires adequate diastolic filling, sinus rhythm and an appropriate perfusion pressure. Avoid both excessive vasodilation and large empiric fluid loads.

**Induction and dissection.** Give balanced, titrated anaesthesia, preventing tachycardia, sustained hypotension and an abrupt fall in coronary diastolic perfusion. If hypotension develops, differentiate vasodilation from bleeding, LV dysfunction and hypovolaemia: inspect the surgical field, ETCO₂ and pressure trace, use echo if uncertainty persists, and titrate an appropriate vasopressor or blood product. The pre-clamp goal is not an arbitrarily high CVP; it is adequate organ flow with a reasonable tolerance for the impending clamp.

**Clamp on.** Aortic pressure and LV afterload may rise; the magnitude depends on clamp level, collateral flow, intravascular volume and LV function. Watch for new ST depression, rising filling pressures, worsening CO and arrhythmias. Increase anaesthetic depth if the response is primarily sympathetic stimulation, but do not treat every pressure rise with an indiscriminate vasodilator. If the myocardium is failing, adjust afterload with a short-acting vasodilator and consider inotropy with echocardiographic guidance. Maintain distal ischaemia time awareness and communicate the anticipated release.

**Before unclamping.** Ask the surgeon to give warning. Reassess estimated blood loss, available product, ionised calcium, K⁺, temperature, lactate and acid–base status. Correct demonstrable volume loss and have titratable noradrenaline ready. Lower-body vascular capacitance expands when flow returns, and vasodilatory metabolites wash centrally. A stepwise release allows measured reassessment and reduces the abrupt collapse risk.

**Clamp off.** If MAP falls and ETCO₂ changes, examine CO and bleeding, not just a single pressure. A preload-responsive patient may need blood or small crystalloid aliquots; vasoplegia needs vasopressor; new LV impairment requires targeted support. Check potassium and ionised calcium and interpret a rising lactate in the context of reperfusion and perfusion. Sudden abdominal distension or blood loss changes the diagnosis. After operation, monitor troponin/ECG if risk warrants, renal function, bowel perfusion and graft pulses. Ischaemic colitis can present with pain, bloody diarrhoea, acidosis or unexplained shock and must not be dismissed as routine postoperative ileus.

## 14.3 A worked ruptured AAA case: the pre-control exception

A 79-year-old with an 8 cm AAA presents with back pain, pallor and SBP 78 mmHg. He is awake and answering questions but has a distended abdomen and falling Hb. The appropriate immediate questions are: can definitive proximal control be achieved rapidly, is endovascular repair anatomically possible, is blood immediately available, and will intubation remove the small remaining sympathetic compensation? Activate the haemorrhage pathway, establish reliable vascular access, minimise transfer delays and brief the surgeon before induction.

While he remains awake and adequately perfused, carefully tolerated hypotension may limit free bleeding. Once he loses consciousness, has worsening ischaemia or becomes profoundly hypoperfused, perfusion priorities change; permissive hypotension does not mean abandoning resuscitation. Aortic balloon occlusion is not a routine first-line mortality-improving substitute for definitive control. GA induction is a particularly dangerous moment: venodilation, loss of catecholamines and positive-pressure ventilation can cause collapse. Prepare blood, vasopressors and immediate vascular control, use small titrated doses and avoid prolonged delay to secure the airway. A local-anaesthetic-first rEVAR is possible in selected awake patients with an experienced team. After control, the management focus shifts to oxygen delivery, coagulopathy, hypocalcaemia, rewarming and surveillance for abdominal compartment, renal failure, mesenteric ischaemia and limb hypoperfusion.

## 14.4 A carotid case: recognising an immediately life-threatening neck haematoma

A 68-year-old with recent left hemispheric TIA and high-grade left ICA stenosis has CEA under GA. Intraoperatively, the team avoids prolonged hypotension during clamping, maintains adequate oxygenation and normocapnia, and treats bradycardia due to carotid sinus manipulation while assessing perfusion. Thirty minutes after extubation, the patient becomes agitated, dysphonic and develops neck swelling and stridor. This is an **airway and surgical emergency**: call the surgeon and theatre/airway assistance immediately, deliver oxygen, prepare for prompt wound opening/haematoma evacuation according to local emergency protocol, and anticipate rapid difficult re-intubation from distorted anatomy and venous engorgement. Attempts at prolonged non-invasive oxygenation without definitive decompression are dangerous.

The same patient develops hypertension after the wound is cleared. Search for pain, hypoxia, urinary retention and other triggers, but remember that loss of baroreflex buffering can precipitate cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome with headache, seizure and intracerebral haemorrhage. Maintain a surgical-unit BP plan and monitor for neurological deterioration. A new focal deficit demands the local stroke and graft thrombosis pathway; it is not necessarily an anaesthetic emergence phenomenon. These complications can coexist with a normal peripheral oxygen saturation.

## 14.5 A TEVAR case: delayed bilateral leg weakness

A 77-year-old undergoes long-segment descending TEVAR with partial left subclavian coverage. Six hours later, new bilateral lower-limb weakness appears despite an unremarkable earlier examination. Suspect **spinal cord ischaemia until proven otherwise**, while also excluding neuraxial haematoma and an acute intracranial event as clinically indicated. Escalate immediately. Check MAP and CO, raise spinal cord perfusion pressure using a multidisciplinary rescue protocol, correct hypoxaemia, anaemia and hypovolaemia, and assess whether a functioning CSF drain is in place. If absent, urgent rescue drainage is a consideration after coagulation/antithrombotic review, not a blind insertion at the bedside. Reassess limb strength repeatedly and seek vascular imaging if branch obstruction or graft complication is possible.

The case illustrates why intraoperative haemodynamic stability is not sufficient proof that the aortic procedure was neurologically safe. Delayed ischaemia can follow postoperative hypotension, anaemia or loss of collateral arterial supply. The 2026 ESVS guidance supports routine prophylactic drainage for open thoracoabdominal aortic repair but does not require a prophylactic drain for every TEVAR [3,23].

## 14.6 Acute limb ischaemia case: threatened but not yet irreversible

A 64-year-old with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden severe left foot pain and a cool, pale leg. Sensation is reduced in the toes and ankle dorsiflexion is weak. Weakness means that the limb is **immediately threatened (Rutherford IIb)** until assessed otherwise; calling it stable because the patient is normotensive would be a major error. Involve vascular surgery immediately, provide analgesia, confirm the time of symptom onset and evaluate arterial Doppler signals. Begin IV UFH unless contraindicated, and obtain imaging if it will not delay required revascularisation. The anaesthetic plan anticipates rapid conversion between endovascular and open surgery, systemic heparin, major reperfusion derangements and potential fasciotomy.

Once perfusion returns, monitor K⁺, ECG, acid–base status, CK, urine output, swelling, pain and compartment signs. New hypotension may result from reperfusion vasodilation; hyperkalaemia and rhabdomyolysis can be life-threatening even though distal pulses have returned. A fixed neurologic deficit despite flow restoration may indicate irreversible muscle/nerve injury. Discuss the chance of amputation without suggesting that “successful thrombectomy” guarantees limb salvage.

## 14.7 Endovascular case: sudden haemodynamic collapse during angioplasty

A patient under monitored anaesthesia care for iliac angioplasty becomes hypotensive and tachycardic. The operator reports difficulty advancing the wire and then severe lower-back pain. Consider **retroperitoneal haemorrhage from iliac perforation** rather than reflexively giving antiemetics or more sedation. Call for definitive vascular control, check access sites and imaging, start haemostatic resuscitation and prepare for GA if airway control, agitation, haemodynamic instability or urgent conversion makes that necessary. A covered stent or balloon tamponade may be an immediate bridge to repair. The counterexample is abrupt bradycardia and hypotension after contrast injection with urticaria and wheeze: that pattern points to anaphylaxis, where timely adrenaline and airway management are essential. Different mechanisms can produce the same BP, and treatment must follow mechanism.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
An important Final Examination skill is to connect clinical decisions to the correct patient population and outcome, without substituting an attractive trial headline for the relevant anatomy or physiological mechanism.

| **Study / guidance**               | **Pivotal observation**                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | **Clinical interpretation and limitation**                                                                                                                                 |
|------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **EVAR-1** [16]                  | Early advantages of elective infrarenal EVAR did not produce a durable late all-cause survival advantage; late aneurysm-related mortality/rupture and reinterventions remained relevant                                                     | EVAR is less invasive initially, not maintenance-free; surveillance and anatomy remain decisive                                                                            |
| **IMPROVE** [17]                 | Emergency endovascular-strategy versus open repair: 30-day mortality 35.4% vs 37.4%, not significantly different                                                                                                                          | Do not present this pragmatic strategy trial as proof that EVAR always reduces rupture mortality; anatomy and team capability matter                                       |
| **CREST-2** [15]                 | In parallel trials of ≥70% **asymptomatic** stenosis, a stenting-plus-intensive-medical arm reduced the four-year composite versus its own medical arm, whereas CEA did not show a statistically significant effect against its own control | It was not a head-to-head randomised comparison of CEA versus CAS; historical symptomatic-carotid benefit must not be extrapolated wholesale to modern asymptomatic care |
| **GALA** [18]                    | No statistically clear stroke/MI/death advantage for regional versus GA during CEA                                                                                                                                                          | Awake neurological assessment is valuable but does not by itself establish superiority of an anaesthetic modality                                                          |
| **Cochrane CEA review** [19]     | No convincing mortality/stroke difference with LA versus GA in available trials                                                                                                                                                             | Technique choice is driven by cooperation, block/sedation safety, monitoring, surgeons and local expertise                                                                 |
| **BEST-CLI** [20]                | With a suitable single-segment vein, bypass-first improved major adverse limb-event/death composite against endovascular-first                                                                                                              | Applicability hinges on usable vein and specific disease/operative strategy                                                                                                |
| **BASIL-2** [21]                 | In infrapopliteal CLTI, vein-bypass-first increased major amputation or death versus endovascular-first                                                                                                                                     | Different population and artery anatomy from BEST-CLI; avoid falsely declaring one method best in all legs                                                                 |
| **VOYAGER PAD** [22]             | Low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin after revascularisation reduced limb/CV composite events with added bleeding risk                                                                                                                            | Balance limb benefit against bleeding and future neuraxial/procedural plans; not a substitute for full anticoagulation when indicated                                      |
| **Coselli CSF-drain trial** [23] | Randomised evidence supports CSF drainage during open thoracoabdominal repair                                                                                                                                                             | The evidence does not automatically justify routine prophylactic drains for every TEVAR; use the newer 2026 ESVS distinction                                               |

items.body:

Reaffirms the unchanged substantive recommendations of the 2024 guideline; formally replaces that edition.

- **6.** **ACC/AHA.** [2024 Guideline for the Management of Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12782132/). PAD, CLTI and acute limb ischaemia.

items.title: How do you assess cardiac risk before major vascular surgery?
items.q: How do you assess cardiac risk before major vascular surgery?
items.a:
- Functional capacity (limited by claudication), RCRI or vascular-specific score.
- ECG and indicated biomarkers; echo/CPET or stress testing selectively, rather than routinely for all.
- Further testing only if it changes management.
- Continue aspirin, statin and beta-blocker.

> **Closing point:** Plan around what will change management.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [AoA/BIHS pre-operative blood pressure guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082) · [ADS–ANZCA perioperative diabetes guidelines](https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/guideline/ads-anzca-perioperative-diabetes-and-hyperglycaemia-guidelines-adults-november-2022/)

items.title: What preoperative optimisation do high-risk vascular patients need?
items.q: What preoperative optimisation do high-risk vascular patients need?
items.a:
- Treat hypertension, heart failure, anaemia, diabetes and CKD.
- Smoking cessation and prehabilitation.
- Medication review (SGLT2 inhibitor, anticoagulants).
- Shared decision-making and critical care bed.

> **Closing point:** Optimise what is modifiable.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [AoA/BIHS pre-operative blood pressure guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082) · [ADS–ANZCA perioperative diabetes guidelines](https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/guideline/ads-anzca-perioperative-diabetes-and-hyperglycaemia-guidelines-adults-november-2022/)

Past exam: 2026.1 Q15

items.title: Which medications should be continued or stopped in vascular surgery?
items.q: Which medications should be continued or stopped in vascular surgery?
items.a:
- Continue aspirin, statin and beta-blocker.
- Hold SGLT2 inhibitor for 3 to 4 days.
- Plan clopidogrel and anticoagulants individually.
- ACE inhibitor or ARB: follow local policy.

> **Closing point:** Do not stop antiplatelets without a reason.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [AoA/BIHS pre-operative blood pressure guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082) · [ADS–ANZCA perioperative diabetes guidelines](https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/guideline/ads-anzca-perioperative-diabetes-and-hyperglycaemia-guidelines-adults-november-2022/)

items.title: Should surgery be postponed for a day-of-surgery BP of 180/110?
items.q: Should surgery be postponed for a day-of-surgery BP of 180/110?
items.a:
- Repeat correctly, review usual BP and assess acute organ injury and surgical urgency.
- 2026 AoA/BIHS clinic guidance uses <180/120 to proceed; persistent SBP 180 reaches its systolic postponement threshold for planned surgery.
- Urgent cases need a documented individual decision; acute organ injury needs urgent treatment.
- Do not rapidly lower asymptomatic BP with IV drugs simply to proceed.

> **Closing point:** Give a justified decision using the relevant current pathway.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [AoA/BIHS pre-operative blood pressure guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082) · [ADS–ANZCA perioperative diabetes guidelines](https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/guideline/ads-anzca-perioperative-diabetes-and-hyperglycaemia-guidelines-adults-november-2022/)

Past exam: 2021.1 Q12

items.title: What must you check when a patient has severe hypertension before surgery?
items.q: What must you check when a patient has severe hypertension before surgery?
items.a:
- Reading accuracy and cuff size.
- Medications missed, withdrawal, drug use.
- Symptoms, ECG, renal function, fundi.
- Secondary causes such as phaeochromocytoma.

> **Closing point:** Grade, damage and cause.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [AoA/BIHS pre-operative blood pressure guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082) · [ADS–ANZCA perioperative diabetes guidelines](https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/guideline/ads-anzca-perioperative-diabetes-and-hyperglycaemia-guidelines-adults-november-2022/)

Past exam: 2021.1 Q12

items.title: What is the role of frailty assessment in vascular surgery?
items.q: What is the role of frailty assessment in vascular surgery?
items.a:
- Predicts mortality, delirium and complications.
- Clinical Frailty Scale.
- Informs shared decision-making and prehabilitation.
- Plan critical care and rehabilitation.

> **Closing point:** Frailty alters the goal of surgery.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [AoA/BIHS pre-operative blood pressure guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082) · [ADS–ANZCA perioperative diabetes guidelines](https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/guideline/ads-anzca-perioperative-diabetes-and-hyperglycaemia-guidelines-adults-november-2022/)

items.title: What is perioperative myocardial injury and how is it detected?
items.q: What is perioperative myocardial injury and how is it detected?
items.a:
Myocardial injury has troponin above the 99th percentile, with a rise or fall supporting acuity. MINS is attributed to an ischaemic mechanism after non-cardiac surgery and can be silent. An infarction also requires evidence of ischaemia. Consider sepsis, pulmonary embolism, arrhythmia and renal dysfunction, and assess ECG, symptoms and serial values. Use selective surveillance in high-risk patients.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative cardiovascular guidance, reaffirmed 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017)

items.title: What happens to the circulation when you clamp the aorta?
items.q: What happens to the circulation when you clamp the aorta?
items.a:
- SVR/afterload usually rise and proximal MAP increases.
- Preload redistribution varies with clamp level, collaterals and venous capacitance; LV filling pressure may rise.
- Output may fall, stay stable or rise; a diseased ventricle is vulnerable to distension/ischaemia.
- Direct flow below the clamp is interrupted; organ effects depend on its exact position.

> **Closing point:** Pressure is not flow.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

Past exam: 2025.1 Q8

items.title: What happens when the aortic clamp is released?
items.q: What happens when the aortic clamp is released?
items.a:
- SVR falls abruptly (vasodilator metabolites, reactive hyperaemia).
- Blood pools in the reperfused legs: relative hypovolaemia.
- Hypotension and reduced coronary perfusion.
- Acid, potassium and lactate wash out.

> **Closing point:** Expect a preload and afterload fall together.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

Past exam: 2025.1 Q8

items.title: Why does the clamp position matter in aortic surgery?
items.q: Why does the clamp position matter in aortic surgery?
items.a:
- Infrarenal clamping excludes the distal bed; haemodynamic responses still vary.
- Suprarenal clamping interrupts renal inflow; it does not automatically exclude the coeliac/SMA territories.
- Supracoeliac clamping adds visceral inflow interruption and a larger ischaemic load.
- Higher/longer clamps generally need more organ-protection planning.

> **Closing point:** Name the actual vessels excluded.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

Past exam: 2006.2 Q3

items.title: How do you prepare for unclamping?
items.q: How do you prepare for unclamping?
items.a:
- Coordinate release with the surgeon; anticipate vasodilation and distal pooling.
- Replace assessed volume/blood deficits before release without indiscriminate loading.
- Reduce vasodilators as appropriate, maintain adequate anaesthesia and prepare vasopressor support.
- Gradual release/partial re-clamping if needed; monitor gases, potassium, calcium and perfusion.

> **Closing point:** Prepare for reduced preload and SVR.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What monitoring do you use for open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair?
items.q: What monitoring do you use for open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair?
items.a:
- Arterial line, central venous access, ECG with ST analysis.
- Cardiac output monitoring (pulse contour, oesophageal Doppler or TOE).
- Urine output, temperature, ACT, blood gases, lactate and potassium.
- Neuromuscular and depth monitoring.

> **Closing point:** Blood pressure alone does not describe cardiac output.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: How do you protect the kidneys during aortic clamping?
items.q: How do you protect the kidneys during aortic clamping?
items.a:
- Optimise volume and perfusion before clamping and minimise renal ischaemic time.
- Use indicated distal/selective renal-perfusion strategies for the operation.
- Avoid nephrotoxins; identify embolism, obstruction and postoperative low flow.
- Do not use renal-dose dopamine; routine mannitol benefit is unproven.

> **Closing point:** Restore effective perfusion, not just a BP number.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

Past exam: 2006.2 Q3

items.title: What is the role of epidural analgesia in open aortic surgery?
items.q: What is the role of epidural analgesia in open aortic surgery?
items.a:
- Excellent analgesia with fewer respiratory complications.
- Sympathetic block causes vasodilation and hypotension, particularly at unclamping.
- Heparin and clopidogrel require timing rules for insertion and removal.
- Neurological checks after removal.

> **Closing point:** Benefit against haematoma risk.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: How do you minimise blood loss in elective open aortic repair?
items.q: How do you minimise blood loss in elective open aortic repair?
items.a:
- Preop: treat anaemia, manage antithrombotics and arrange blood/cell salvage.
- Intraop: surgical haemostasis, warmth, calcium and targeted fluid/component replacement.
- TXA is an individual protocol decision; POISE-3 reduced bleeding but did not establish prespecified cardiovascular noninferiority.
- Postop: detect ongoing bleeding early and re-explore when indicated.

> **Closing point:** Preserve organ perfusion while controlling bleeding.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What intraoperative complications can occur in major vascular surgery?
items.q: What intraoperative complications can occur in major vascular surgery?
items.a:
- Haemorrhage and coagulopathy.
- Myocardial ischaemia and arrhythmia.
- Embolism (air, thrombus, atheroma) and limb or gut ischaemia.
- Heparin issues, protamine reaction, hypothermia and positioning injury.

> **Closing point:** Anticipate, monitor and communicate.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What are the risks of heparin and protamine in vascular surgery?
items.q: What are the risks of heparin and protamine in vascular surgery?
items.a:
- Bleeding if excess; thrombosis if inadequate (check ACT).
- Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
- Protamine reaction: hypotension, pulmonary hypertension, anaphylaxis.
- Give protamine slowly and warn of the risk.

> **Closing point:** Monitor the ACT.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: Which patient factors increase risk in open AAA repair?
items.q: Which patient factors increase risk in open AAA repair?
items.a:
- Age, cardiac disease, heart failure, CKD, COPD and frailty.
- Ruptured or urgent presentation, suprarenal clamp.
- Large aneurysm, anaemia, long clamp time.
- Low volume centre.

> **Closing point:** Cardiac, renal and respiratory reserve decide risk.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What are the major postoperative complications after aortic surgery?
items.q: What are the major postoperative complications after aortic surgery?
items.a:
- Cardiac, renal and respiratory failure.
- Bleeding, colonic ischaemia, limb ischaemia.
- Stroke, delirium, infection and VTE.
- Persistent post-surgical pain.

> **Closing point:** Cardiac, renal, gut.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: How do you recognise colonic ischaemia after AAA repair?
items.q: How do you recognise colonic ischaemia after AAA repair?
items.a:
- Bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and distension.
- Rising lactate and acidosis.
- Risk rises with rupture, low flow, embolism and poor mesenteric/pelvic collaterals.
- Sigmoidoscopy and surgical review.

> **Closing point:** Think of it with unexplained acidosis.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What is abdominal compartment syndrome?
items.q: What is abdominal compartment syndrome?
items.a:
- Raised intra-abdominal pressure above 20 mmHg with organ dysfunction.
- Oliguria, high airway pressures, hypotension.
- Measure bladder pressure.
- Decompressive laparotomy.

> **Closing point:** Common after ruptured AAA.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: How do you provide analgesia after major vascular surgery?
items.q: How do you provide analgesia after major vascular surgery?
items.a:
- Multimodal: paracetamol, local infiltration, rectus sheath catheters.
- Epidural if clotting and antiplatelets allow.
- Avoid NSAIDs in CKD.
- Plan for persistent pain follow-up.

> **Closing point:** Balance benefit against haematoma risk.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: When would you choose an endovascular approach over open AAA repair?
items.q: When would you choose an endovascular approach over open AAA repair?
items.a:
- Suitable anatomy (neck, iliacs), high-risk patient.
- Less physiological stress, blood loss and early mortality.
- Needs lifelong surveillance and reintervention.
- Open repair remains for unsuitable anatomy.

> **Closing point:** Individualise by anatomy and fitness.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What are the anaesthetic options for endovascular aneurysm repair?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic options for endovascular aneurysm repair?
items.a:
- Elective infrarenal EVAR may use local/minimal sedation, regional or GA according to patient/procedure.
- Local anaesthesia is associated with better rEVAR outcomes in observational data; this is not proof of causation.
- GA supports immobility/apnoea and airway control; extensive thoracic repairs often need it.
- Cooperation, anticoagulation, duration and rescue/conversion capability guide choice.

> **Closing point:** Plan safe conversion before starting.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What are the complications of EVAR?
items.q: What are the complications of EVAR?
items.a:
- Access injury, aortic or iliac rupture, endoleak.
- Distal embolisation and limb ischaemia.
- Contrast-associated AKI and post-implantation syndrome.
- Spinal cord and colonic ischaemia; conversion to open repair.

> **Closing point:** Prepare blood and a conversion plan.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What is an endoleak?
items.q: What is an endoleak?
items.a:
- Persistent flow within the excluded aneurysm sac outside the graft is an endoleak.
- I: attachment-site leak; II: retrograde branch flow; III: component/fabric failure; IV: porosity.
- Types I/III usually need prompt correction; type II decisions depend on sac growth/persistence.
- Type V (“endotension”) is sac expansion without a demonstrable leak, rather than visible flow.

> **Closing point:** Surveillance assesses the sac and the graft.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: How is renal function protected during EVAR?
items.q: How is renal function protected during EVAR?
items.a:
- Minimise and dilute contrast.
- Hydration and avoidance of nephrotoxins.
- Maintain perfusion pressure.
- Check creatinine at 48 to 72 hours.

> **Closing point:** Contrast and hypotension are the main hazards.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What are the complications of TEVAR?
items.q: What are the complications of TEVAR?
items.a:
- Spinal cord ischaemia, stroke and visceral/limb malperfusion.
- Access injury, rupture, retrograde Type A dissection and endoleak.
- CA-AKI, contrast reaction and post-implantation inflammation.
- Use perfusion/collateral protection and an agreed drain-rescue pathway; no automatic prophylactic drain for every TEVAR.

> **Closing point:** Open and endovascular drain strategies differ.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

Past exam: 2022.2 Q11

items.title: Why use rapid pacing or adenosine during stent deployment?
items.q: Why use rapid pacing or adenosine during stent deployment?
items.a:
- Transient reduction of flow/pulse pressure can help precise deployment in selected cases.
- It is device/operator-specific, not obligatory for every TEVAR or EVAR.
- Agree the plan, invasive BP monitoring and pacing/defibrillation/resuscitation capability.
- Keep the intervention brief and restore perfusion immediately.

> **Closing point:** Use only when its deployment benefit justifies the risk.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What is post-implantation syndrome?
items.q: What is post-implantation syndrome?
items.a:
- Fever, inflammatory-marker elevation and leukocytosis after endograft placement.
- Usually a self-limited inflammatory syndrome, but severity varies.
- Exclude infection, end-organ ischaemia and other causes before attributing fever to it.
- Supportive treatment and observation according to clinical severity.

> **Closing point:** Do not label an unwell patient’s fever benign without assessment.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: Which patients are at risk of contrast-associated AKI?
items.q: Which patients are at risk of contrast-associated AKI?
items.a:
- AKI/severe CKD, especially with hypovolaemia, HF or other acute illness.
- ESUR high-risk thresholds: eGFR <30 for IV/IA second-pass, <45 for IA first-pass renal exposure.
- Large/repeated contrast loads and concurrent haemodynamic/nephrotoxic insults increase concern.
- Metformin is not nephrotoxic; its danger is accumulation/lactic acidosis if AKI occurs.

> **Closing point:** Association after contrast does not establish causation.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/)

items.title: Why is abrupt oliguria after complex EVAR a vascular emergency until assessed?
items.q: Why is abrupt oliguria after complex EVAR a vascular emergency until assessed?
items.a:
Renal branch occlusion, dissection, coverage or stent kinking can threaten salvageable renal perfusion. Review completion imaging and consult vascular surgery promptly. Check volume, output, bladder and bleeding in parallel. Contrast exposure alone does not explain an abrupt change.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/)

items.title: What is spinal cord perfusion pressure?
items.q: What is spinal cord perfusion pressure?
items.a:
- Approximate SCPP = MAP − the higher of CSF pressure and CVP.
- MAP 80 and CSF 15 give 65 mmHg, not 70.
- Targets follow the aortic service protocol and clinical response.
- Improve oxygen delivery, augment MAP and lower CSF pressure safely when indicated.

> **Closing point:** Consider arterial inflow and venous/CSF back pressure.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/)

items.title: How do you use a CSF drain in aortic repair?
items.q: How do you use a CSF drain in aortic repair?
items.a:
- 2026 ESVS recommends prophylactic drainage for open thoracic/TAAA repair; extensive TEVAR may use a rescue-first strategy.
- Assess coagulation/antithrombotics; insert and manage with a trained team and strict levelling/pressure/volume protocol.
- Targets commonly include CSF ≤10–12 mmHg; hourly limits are protocol-specific, often 10–15 mL/h, not unlimited drainage.
- Monitor neurology and headache/bleeding; drainage can cause intracranial or neuraxial haemorrhage.

> **Closing point:** Do not generalise open-repair trial benefit to all TEVAR.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/)

items.title: Which patients are at highest risk of spinal cord ischaemia?
items.q: Which patients are at highest risk of spinal cord ischaemia?
items.a:
- Extensive thoracoabdominal repair or long coverage in TEVAR.
- Previous aortic surgery, left subclavian coverage.
- Hypotension, anaemia, renal impairment.
- Closed internal iliac arteries.

> **Closing point:** Extent of aortic coverage decides risk.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/)

items.title: How do you respond to a new lower limb weakness after aortic repair?
items.q: How do you respond to a new lower limb weakness after aortic repair?
items.a:
- Activate the aortic/spinal rescue team immediately and document motor findings.
- Augment MAP promptly, often ≥90–100 mmHg, while correcting hypoxaemia, anaemia and low output.
- Check an existing drain or arrange expert rescue drainage if safe; respect volume and anticoagulation limits.
- Exclude residual block, limb malperfusion and spinal/epidural haematoma; urgent imaging/intervention as indicated.

> **Closing point:** Act immediately with the specialist rescue pathway.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/)

items.title: What intraoperative monitoring can detect spinal cord ischaemia?
items.q: What intraoperative monitoring can detect spinal cord ischaemia?
items.a:
- Motor and somatosensory evoked potentials.
- Avoid long-acting neuromuscular blockade and high-dose volatile.
- Loss of signal triggers raising MAP and shunt or reimplantation.
- Awake neurological assessment on emergence.

> **Closing point:** MEPs assess motor pathways; exclude technical/anaesthetic causes of signal loss.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/)

items.title: Which drugs have been used for spinal cord protection?
items.q: Which drugs have been used for spinal cord protection?
items.a:
- Thiopentone, steroids, magnesium and lidocaine.
- Naloxone and others.
- Evidence is weak.
- Physiological measures matter more.

> **Closing point:** Do not rely on drugs.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/)

items.title: Which vessels reinforce the spinal arteries during aortic repair?
items.q: Which vessels reinforce the spinal arteries during aortic repair?
items.a:
Segmental intercostal and lumbar branches supply radiculomedullary arteries, including Adamkiewicz. The cord also has collateral inflow from the subclavian/vertebral and pelvic territories. Extensive coverage, prior repair and systemic hypotension can exhaust that reserve.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic/thoracoabdominal guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: How is acute Type B aortic dissection treated medically?
items.q: How is acute Type B aortic dissection treated medically?
items.a:
- Monitored anti-impulse therapy: analgesia and titrated IV beta-blocker if tolerated.
- Aim HR 60–80/min and SBP <120 or lowest maintaining organ perfusion; add vasodilator after rate control if needed.
- Use non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel rate control when beta-blockade is contraindicated and appropriate.
- Intervene for complications; selected high-risk uncomplicated cases may undergo planned subacute TEVAR.

> **Closing point:** Avoid compromising perfusion while reducing aortic stress.

**Sources:** [ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9860464/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

Past exam: 2022.2 Q11

items.title: Why give a beta-blocker before a vasodilator in aortic dissection?
items.q: Why give a beta-blocker before a vasodilator in aortic dissection?
items.a:
- A vasodilator causes reflex tachycardia.
- Tachycardia raises dP/dt and extends the dissection.
- Lower rate then lower pressure.
- Avoid over-treatment if malperfusion.

> **Closing point:** Rate before pressure.

**Sources:** [ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9860464/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

Past exam: 2022.2 Q11

items.title: What are the indications for intervention in Type B dissection?
items.q: What are the indications for intervention in Type B dissection?
items.a:
- Malperfusion (renal, mesenteric, limb, spinal).
- Rupture or impending rupture.
- Refractory pain or hypertension.
- Rapid expansion.

> **Closing point:** Uncomplicated cases are managed medically.

**Sources:** [ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9860464/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

Past exam: 2022.2 Q11

items.title: What are the main problems of Type A dissection?
items.q: What are the main problems of Type A dissection?
items.a:
- Rupture/tamponade, severe acute AR and coronary malperfusion.
- Cerebral, visceral, renal and limb malperfusion.
- Emergency repair with CPB; arch work may need circulatory arrest/cerebral perfusion, but not every repair requires deep arrest.
- Induce with the surgeon/perfusion team ready; shock/acute AR may preclude routine anti-impulse drugs.

> **Closing point:** Support perfusion and expedite definitive repair.

**Sources:** [ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9860464/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: Why are arterial lines in both arms useful in dissection?
items.q: Why are arterial lines in both arms useful in dissection?
items.a:
- Branch-vessel involvement can make arm pressures discordant or misleading.
- Neither the higher nor lower reading alone proves true systemic/organ perfusion.
- Interpret sites with CTA/TOE, pulses and cannulation/perfusion strategy; femoral monitoring may add information.
- Watch changes during CPB and repair.

> **Closing point:** Know the anatomy behind each pressure trace.

**Sources:** [ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9860464/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: How do you confirm dissection, and what can focused echo miss?
items.q: How do you confirm dissection, and what can focused echo miss?
items.a:
- CTA defines aorta and branches in a sufficiently stable patient.
- TTE/TOE show root, AR, effusion and ventricular consequences; expert TOE can support an unstable patient.
- Distal ascending aorta has a TOE blind spot; a negative focused study does not exclude dissection.
- Contact the aortic team early; avoid redundant imaging delays.

items.title: Why can dissection shock make routine beta-blockade unsafe?
items.q: Why can dissection shock make routine beta-blockade unsafe?
items.a:
- Shock may reflect rupture, tamponade, coronary malperfusion or severe acute AR.
- Support perfusion and arrange immediate definitive repair rather than mandatory BP reduction.
- Marked bradycardia worsens acute AR; titrate with specialist input.
- Avoid IABP; controlled pericardial rescue is exceptional, not routine complete drainage.

items.title: How do aortic dissection or atheroma alter your cannulation plan?
items.q: How do aortic dissection or atheroma alter your cannulation plan?
items.a:
- Review imaging and use epiaortic ultrasound/TOE appropriately; TOE does not visualise every ascending-aortic segment.
- Avoid plaque disruption and false-lumen perfusion. Consider axillary/innominate or imaging-guided central inflow; femoral may be needed urgently but risks retrograde malperfusion.
- Compare pressures and bilateral cerebral trends and inspect the true lumen during initiation.
- High line pressure or unilateral cerebral change demands immediate circuit/cannula/anatomical assessment, not simply more pump pressure.

items.title: What is permissive hypotension and why use it in ruptured AAA?
items.q: What is permissive hypotension and why use it in ruptured AAA?
items.a:
- Accept a systolic pressure of 70 to 90 mmHg while the patient is mentating.
- Avoids disrupting the clot and dilutional coagulopathy.
- Use blood products rather than large crystalloid volumes.
- Do not use in head injury or in prolonged hypotension.

> **Closing point:** Control bleeding before restoring normal pressure.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: How do you induce anaesthesia for a ruptured AAA?
items.q: How do you induce anaesthesia for a ruptured AAA?
items.a:
- Patient prepared, surgeon scrubbed and draped before induction.
- Titrate induction agents to effect; vasopressors drawn up.
- Arterial line first if it does not delay.
- Induction removes sympathetic tone: collapse can follow.

> **Closing point:** Be ready to clamp or inflate a balloon.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What problems follow repair of a ruptured aneurysm?
items.q: What problems follow repair of a ruptured aneurysm?
items.a:
- Abdominal compartment syndrome.
- AKI, colonic ischaemia, limb ischaemia.
- Coagulopathy and hypothermia.
- Multi-organ failure; ICU care.

> **Closing point:** Check bladder pressure and lactate.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What happens to cerebral perfusion when the carotid artery is clamped?
items.q: What happens to cerebral perfusion when the carotid artery is clamped?
items.a:
- Antegrade flow through the clamped ICA stops; the ipsilateral brain depends on collateral supply.
- Severe stenosis may have exhausted reserve/impaired autoregulation, but this is not universal.
- Maintain an individual MAP at/above credible baseline during clamping, balancing cardiac risk.
- Awake or multimodal monitoring guides intervention/shunting.

> **Closing point:** Protect collateral perfusion and prevent embolism.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

Past exam: 2024.1 Q12

items.title: What happens at carotid unclamping?
items.q: What happens at carotid unclamping?
items.a:
- Flow restoration risks air/plaque embolism and excessive reperfusion.
- Baroreflex changes may produce hypotension, bradycardia or hypertension; no fixed sequence is guaranteed.
- Titrate BP to avoid both cerebral hypoperfusion and hyperperfusion.
- Watch for new neurological deficits and later hyperperfusion syndrome.

> **Closing point:** Treat the observed response.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

Past exam: 2024.1 Q12

items.title: How can cerebral ischaemia be monitored during CEA?
items.q: How can cerebral ischaemia be monitored during CEA?
items.a:
- Awake speech, consciousness and contralateral hand testing provide direct functional assessment.
- Under GA, EEG/SSEP, TCD and NIRS offer complementary information with limitations.
- Stump-pressure thresholds vary, often around 40–50 mmHg; none guarantees adequate perfusion.
- Correct systemic causes and follow the agreed shunting strategy.

> **Closing point:** No GA monitor replaces the complete clinical picture.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

items.title: What are the advantages of regional anaesthesia for CEA?
items.q: What are the advantages of regional anaesthesia for CEA?
items.a:
- Direct awake neurological assessment may guide selective shunting.
- Avoids induction/intubation and some GA effects; BP instability can still occur.
- Needs cooperation, effective surgical blockade and a conversion/airway plan.
- GALA: 30-day stroke/MI/death 4.8% GA versus 4.5% local; difference not statistically significant.

> **Closing point:** No proven universal outcome superiority or equivalence.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

Past exam: 2010.2 Q12

items.title: What is the nerve supply that must be blocked for CEA?
items.q: What is the nerve supply that must be blocked for CEA?
items.a:
- Cervical plexus C1–C4; superficial cutaneous branches C2–C4.
- Lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical and supraclavicular supply the skin.
- Mandibular angle is great auricular territory; chin/lower lip are V3.
- Superficial/intermediate block often needs planned incision/deep surgical supplementation; test before starting.

> **Closing point:** Cutaneous analgesia alone may not cover deep dissection.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

Past exam: 2025.1 Q15

items.title: What are the complications of a deep cervical plexus block?
items.q: What are the complications of a deep cervical plexus block?
items.a:
- Phrenic, recurrent laryngeal, vagal or hypoglossal block and Horner syndrome.
- Vascular/vertebral artery injection, LAST, bleeding and neuraxial spread.
- Bilateral or contralateral nerve dysfunction may threaten ventilation/airway.
- Superficial/intermediate approaches avoid deliberate root injection but retain bleeding, toxicity and spread risks.

> **Closing point:** Select the least invasive effective technique with supplementation planned.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

Past exam: 2025.1 Q15

items.title: What local anaesthetic doses are safe for cervical plexus block?
items.q: What local anaesthetic doses are safe for cervical plexus block?
items.a:
- Calculate patient-specific total mg, concentration and volume before injection.
- Example: 10–15 mL ropivacaine 0.375–0.5% is 37.5–75 mg for a unilateral intermediate block, adjusted to spread/patient.
- Include all surgeon top-ups and mixed-agent additive toxicity; use product/local limits with frailty reductions.
- Incremental injection and visible spread reduce risk; aspiration/ultrasound cannot guarantee safety.

> **Closing point:** A quoted mg/kg maximum is not a promise of safety.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

items.title: What BP targets apply during CEA?
items.q: What BP targets apply during CEA?
items.a:
- Baseline from both arms.
- Keep MAP at or 10 to 20% above baseline during clamping.
- Treat hypertension on unclamping and in PACU.
- Avoid hypotension at induction.

> **Closing point:** Maintain collateral perfusion.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

Past exam: 2017.2 Q2

items.title: Why is hypertension common after CEA and what are the dangers?
items.q: Why is hypertension common after CEA and what are the dangers?
items.a:
- Baroreceptor dysfunction, pain, bladder distension and hypoxia.
- Neck haematoma, hyperperfusion syndrome and intracerebral haemorrhage.
- Myocardial ischaemia.
- Treat the cause, then titrated labetalol/nicardipine or the agreed agent; avoid abrupt BP reduction.

> **Closing point:** Control BP and check the neck and neurology.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

Past exam: 2017.2 Q2

items.title: How does a neck haematoma present after CEA and what do you do?
items.q: How does a neck haematoma present after CEA and what do you do?
items.a:
- Neck swelling/pressure, dysphagia, voice change or distress may precede stridor/hypoxaemia.
- Call surgical/airway help and give oxygen immediately.
- If the airway is threatened, urgent bedside wound decompression may be lifesaving; do not wait for theatre transfer.
- Plan difficult-airway control and definitive haemostasis; stable haematomas still need urgent review.

> **Closing point:** Airway compromise makes decompression time-critical.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

Past exam: 2015.2 Q11

items.title: Which cranial nerves can be injured in CEA?
items.q: Which cranial nerves can be injured in CEA?
items.a:
- Hypoglossal: tongue deviation.
- Vagus or recurrent laryngeal: hoarseness.
- Marginal mandibular: lip weakness.
- Glossopharyngeal: swallowing; aspiration risk.

> **Closing point:** Check swallow and voice.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

Past exam: 2015.2 Q11

items.title: What is cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome?
items.q: What is cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome?
items.a:
- Ipsilateral headache, hypertension, seizures, focal deficit.
- Follows reperfusion after CEA or stenting; usually day 2 to 7.
- Risk: severe stenosis and poor BP control.
- Treat BP, seizures and image.

> **Closing point:** Control the pressure.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

items.title: What are the principles of GA for CEA?
items.q: What are the principles of GA for CEA?
items.a:
- Pre: symptom timing, cardiac risk, medications, baseline BP.
- Intra: arterial line, haemodynamic stability, cerebral perfusion, heparin.
- Brain monitoring and shunt decisions.
- Post: smooth emergence, neurological check, BP control.

> **Closing point:** Perfusion pressure, cardiac protection and a rapid wake.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/)

Past exam: 2006.1 Q11

items.title: Which carotid lesions should be treated and when?
items.q: Which carotid lesions should be treated and when?
items.a:
- CEA benefits suitable recently symptomatic 70–99% stenosis; selected 50–69% lesions also benefit.
- Aim for intervention within 14 days where neurologically appropriate; large disabling/haemorrhagic infarction may change timing.
- All patients need intensive medical risk-factor therapy.
- Asymptomatic intervention remains selective; interpret CREST-2 as two parallel trials, not CAS versus CEA head-to-head.

> **Closing point:** The symptom history and neurological state determine urgency.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/) · [CREST-2 (2025)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41269206/)

items.title: When is carotid stenting used in preference to endarterectomy?
items.q: When is carotid stenting used in preference to endarterectomy?
items.a:
- Consider anatomy/hostile neck, restenosis, operative risk, age and team outcomes.
- Transfemoral CAS has more perioperative stroke in older patients; avoid assuming the same data apply to TCAR.
- DAPT, procedural heparin, carotid-sinus depression and postoperative BP/neurology need a plan.
- CREST-2’s asymptomatic stenting trial showed benefit over intensive medical therapy; its CEA trial did not reach significance.

> **Closing point:** CREST-2 did not directly compare stenting with CEA.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid and vertebral artery guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [BJA Education: The cervical plexus (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534922001512) · [GALA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/) · [CREST-2 (2025)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41269206/)

items.title: What anaesthetic challenges do patients having lower limb angioplasty present?
items.q: What anaesthetic challenges do patients having lower limb angioplasty present?
items.a:
- Cardiac, renal, diabetic and cerebrovascular comorbidity.
- Remote radiology suite and limited access.
- Antiplatelets, heparin and contrast.
- Local with sedation is often adequate.

> **Closing point:** Treat the patient, not the leg.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization (2015)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482) · [BJA Education: Pain after lower limb amputation (2026)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41727978/) · [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766)

Past exam: 2018.1 Q13

items.title: What are the complications of lower limb angioplasty and stenting?
items.q: What are the complications of lower limb angioplasty and stenting?
items.a:
- Vessel perforation and haematoma.
- Distal embolisation and acute thrombosis.
- Contrast reaction and contrast-associated AKI.
- Conversion to open surgery.

> **Closing point:** Have a bailout plan.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization (2015)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482) · [BJA Education: Pain after lower limb amputation (2026)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41727978/) · [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766)

Past exam: 2018.1 Q13

items.title: What are the anaesthetic options for femoropopliteal bypass?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic options for femoropopliteal bypass?
items.a:
- Spinal or epidural; GA; peripheral blocks.
- Sympathectomy increases flow.
- Neuraxial block depends on antiplatelets and heparin timing.
- Regional has no proven mortality benefit.

> **Closing point:** Choose by comorbidity and antithrombotics.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization (2015)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482) · [BJA Education: Pain after lower limb amputation (2026)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41727978/) · [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766)

items.title: How do you time neuraxial block with clopidogrel and heparin?
items.q: How do you time neuraxial block with clopidogrel and heparin?
items.a:
- Aspirin alone usually adds no interval; stop clopidogrel 5–7 days for neuraxial or deep plexus/deep peripheral blocks.
- Stop IV UFH 4–6 h and confirm normal coagulation before insertion/removal; check platelets if UFH >4 days.
- Wait ≥1 h after needle placement before heparin and ≥1 h after catheter removal before re-heparinisation.
- A bloody tap requires joint reassessment, not automatic cancellation; maintain neurological surveillance.

> **Closing point:** Deep peripheral blocks are not an anticoagulation loophole.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization (2015)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482) · [BJA Education: Pain after lower limb amputation (2026)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41727978/) · [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766)

items.title: What are the features of peripheral vascular disease that affect anaesthesia?
items.q: What are the features of peripheral vascular disease that affect anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Systemic atherosclerosis: coronary and carotid disease.
- Diabetes, CKD, COPD, hypertension.
- Silent ischaemia; limited exercise testing.
- Unreliable limb BP; polypharmacy.

> **Closing point:** A marker of high cardiovascular risk.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization (2015)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482) · [BJA Education: Pain after lower limb amputation (2026)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41727978/) · [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766)

items.title: What are the problems of acute limb ischaemia?
items.q: What are the problems of acute limb ischaemia?
items.a:
- Embolism or thrombosis; the six Ps.
- Urgent surgery in unfit patients.
- Reperfusion injury: hyperkalaemia, acidosis, myoglobinuria.
- Compartment syndrome.

> **Closing point:** Reperfusion causes systemic effects.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization (2015)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482) · [BJA Education: Pain after lower limb amputation (2026)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41727978/) · [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766)

items.title: How is diabetes managed around vascular surgery?
items.q: How is diabetes managed around vascular surgery?
items.a:
- Preop: assess control, CKD/neuropathy and urgency; poor HbA1c does not automatically delay limb salvage.
- Plan SGLT2 cessation, basal insulin and fasting/correction doses.
- Intraop: ADS–ANZCA target generally 5–10 mmol/L with regular/hourly checks where indicated.
- Postop: transition insulin safely; restart drugs according to intake, renal function and ketosis risk.

> **Closing point:** Avoid hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia and euglycaemic ketoacidosis.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [AoA/BIHS pre-operative blood pressure guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082) · [ADS–ANZCA perioperative diabetes guidelines](https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/guideline/ads-anzca-perioperative-diabetes-and-hyperglycaemia-guidelines-adults-november-2022/)

items.title: How do you manage a patient with CKD having vascular surgery?
items.q: How do you manage a patient with CKD having vascular surgery?
items.a:
- Stage, electrolytes, Hb and dialysis timing.
- Avoid nephrotoxins and contrast where possible.
- Avoid morphine; use cisatracurium.
- Maintain perfusion pressure.

> **Closing point:** Renal clearance guides drug choice.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [AoA/BIHS pre-operative blood pressure guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082) · [ADS–ANZCA perioperative diabetes guidelines](https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/guideline/ads-anzca-perioperative-diabetes-and-hyperglycaemia-guidelines-adults-november-2022/)

items.title: What finding makes acute limb ischaemia immediately limb-threatening?
items.q: What finding makes acute limb ischaemia immediately limb-threatening?
items.a:
New motor weakness with an absent arterial Doppler signal and retained venous Doppler suggests Rutherford IIb. Call vascular surgery and expedite revascularisation. Profound anaesthesia and paralysis with absent venous signals suggest irreversibility. Give systemic heparin unless contraindicated.

**Sources:** [2024 ACC/AHA multisociety lower-extremity PAD guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013)

items.title: What must you check before and after revascularising a profoundly ischaemic leg?
items.q: What must you check before and after revascularising a profoundly ischaemic leg?
items.a:
Before reperfusion check potassium, ECG, gas, volume and arterial pressure. Prepare for hypotension, hyperkalaemia and arrhythmia. After flow returns check motor/sensory status, pulses, compartments, CK, creatinine and urine output. A palpable pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome.

**Sources:** [2024 ACC/AHA multisociety lower-extremity PAD guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013)

items.title: What are the two types of pain after amputation?
items.q: What are the two types of pain after amputation?
items.a:
- Residual-limb pain occurs in the remaining limb: assess wound, ischaemia/infection, neuroma, bone and prosthetic causes.
- Phantom limb pain is pain perceived in the missing limb, often neuropathic.
- Phantom sensation can be painless and does not require automatic neuropathic-drug treatment.
- The syndromes may coexist and require individual assessment.

> **Closing point:** Differentiate the pain before choosing treatment.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization (2015)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482) · [BJA Education: Pain after lower limb amputation (2026)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41727978/) · [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766)

items.title: How might you reduce chronic pain after amputation?
items.q: How might you reduce chronic pain after amputation?
items.a:
- Treat pre-existing pain and plan acute multimodal/regional analgesia with early pain-team input.
- Perineural catheters help acute opioid-sparing care; reliable chronic phantom-pain prevention is not established.
- Do not routinely add gabapentinoids for prevention; consider renal accumulation, sedation and respiratory risk.
- Rehabilitation, psychological support and selected mirror/graded motor imagery support longer-term management.

> **Closing point:** Good acute analgesia is essential; chronic prevention remains uncertain.
