**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization (2015)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482) · [BJA Education: Pain after lower limb amputation (2026)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41727978/) · [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766)

items.title: What is REBOA?
items.q: What is REBOA?
items.a:
- Femoral-access aortic balloon occlusion can temporarily control selected bleeding distal to it.
- Zone I is descending thoracic; zone III infrarenal for pelvic bleeding; avoid zone II.
- It raises proximal afterload but causes distal ischaemia; minimise occlusion and never delay definitive control.
- UK-REBOA did not support routine trauma use; rAAA proximal balloon control is a distinct specialist context.

> **Closing point:** A bridge with major ischaemic and access risks.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What happens when the REBOA balloon is deflated?
items.q: What happens when the REBOA balloon is deflated?
items.a:
- Hypotension from vasodilation and blood pooling.
- Acidosis, hyperkalaemia and lactate wash out.
- Resuscitate before deflation and deflate slowly.
- Watch for bleeding recurrence.

> **Closing point:** Prepare as for aortic unclamping.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What are the advantages of interventional radiology procedures compared with open surgery?
items.q: What are the advantages of interventional radiology procedures compared with open surgery?
items.a:
- Less physiological stress and blood loss.
- Local anaesthesia or sedation often possible.
- Shorter stay; suits high-risk patients.
- Disadvantages: radiation, contrast, durability.

> **Closing point:** Good for the unfit, with limits.

**Sources:** [ANZCA anaphylaxis guideline 2022](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/professional-documents/endorsed-guidelines/anaphylaxis-guideline-2022.pdf) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/) · [ANZCA Blue Book](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

items.title: What are the requirements for safe anaesthesia in the radiology suite?
items.q: What are the requirements for safe anaesthesia in the radiology suite?
items.a:
- Same standard of monitoring and equipment as the main theatre.
- Trained assistant, recovery area, resuscitation equipment.
- Radiation protection and communication.
- Back-up from surgery and the blood bank.

> **Closing point:** Standards do not change with location.

**Sources:** [ANZCA anaphylaxis guideline 2022](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/professional-documents/endorsed-guidelines/anaphylaxis-guideline-2022.pdf) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/) · [ANZCA Blue Book](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

items.title: How do you treat anaphylaxis to contrast?
items.q: How do you treat anaphylaxis to contrast?
items.a:
- Stop possible triggers, call help, give oxygen and support airway; lie flat/raise legs when feasible.
- For life-threatening reactions with monitored IV expertise: adrenaline 50–100 micrograms IV titrated/repeated; moderate reactions start lower.
- If IV expertise/access unavailable, 500 micrograms IM thigh; repeat per protocol. Give fluid boluses and an infusion for persistent shock.
- Treat bronchospasm, monitor after stabilisation and arrange tryptase/allergy investigation.

> **Closing point:** Adrenaline and resuscitation precede investigations.

**Sources:** [ANZCA anaphylaxis guideline 2022](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/professional-documents/endorsed-guidelines/anaphylaxis-guideline-2022.pdf) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/) · [ANZCA Blue Book](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

items.title: When should tryptase be taken after suspected anaphylaxis?
items.q: When should tryptase be taken after suspected anaphylaxis?
items.a:
- ANZAAG/ANZCA: as soon as feasible after initial resuscitation.
- Repeat at 1 hour and 4 hours.
- Obtain baseline after 24 hours or at later follow-up.
- Record timings and refer for specialist investigation; do not delay treatment to sample.

> **Closing point:** Acute serial samples plus a baseline.

**Sources:** [ANZCA anaphylaxis guideline 2022](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/professional-documents/endorsed-guidelines/anaphylaxis-guideline-2022.pdf) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/) · [ANZCA Blue Book](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

items.title: How is contrast-associated AKI prevented?
items.q: How is contrast-associated AKI prevented?
items.a:
- Assess AKI/eGFR and route of renal exposure; minimise unnecessary contrast.
- Ensure euvolaemia; protocol IV saline for selected high-risk patients, avoiding overload.
- Avoid nonessential nephrotoxins and haemodynamic insults; plan metformin according to eGFR/AKI/route.
- No routine NAC; PRESERVE did not show bicarbonate superiority over saline.

> **Closing point:** CA-AKI is temporal association, not automatic contrast causation.

**Sources:** [ANZCA anaphylaxis guideline 2022](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/professional-documents/endorsed-guidelines/anaphylaxis-guideline-2022.pdf) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/) · [ANZCA Blue Book](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

items.title: How does the anaesthetist limit radiation exposure?
items.q: How does the anaesthetist limit radiation exposure?
items.a:
- Minimise exposure time, increase distance and use shielding; scatter geometry affects actual dose.
- Use suitable apron, thyroid/eye protection and a correctly positioned mobile/ceiling shield.
- Wear and review dosimetry according to the local programme.
- Pregnancy warrants confidential occupational advice and appropriate monitoring/workplace planning.

> **Closing point:** Distance helps substantially; inverse-square is an approximation for scatter exposure.

**Sources:** [ANZCA anaphylaxis guideline 2022](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/professional-documents/endorsed-guidelines/anaphylaxis-guideline-2022.pdf) · [ESUR contrast media guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/) · [ANZCA Blue Book](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

items.title: Why can both feet become ischaemic with a normal radial arterial pressure during IR?
items.q: Why can both feet become ischaemic with a normal radial arterial pressure during IR?
items.a:
A balloon, sheath, thrombus or dissection can block aorto-iliac flow below a normal proximal pressure. Alert the operator, verify femoral signals and obtain angiographic confirmation. Anticipate haemodynamic and metabolic changes when flow returns.

**Sources:** [2024 ACC/AHA multisociety lower-extremity PAD guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013)

items.title: What does thoracoscopic sympathectomy aim to achieve and what are its complications?
items.sub: Dialysis access, sympathectomy and other vascular emergencies
items.eyebrow: Dialysis access, sympathectomy and other vascular emergencies
items.q: What does thoracoscopic sympathectomy aim to achieve and what are its complications?
items.a:
- Interrupt sympathetic outflow for selected hyperhidrosis; palmar procedures commonly target rib R3/R4 levels.
- Compensatory sweating, Horner syndrome, pneumothorax, bleeding and neuralgia.
- Anticipate bradycardia, hypotension and insufflation effects.
- Use an agreed lung-isolation/ventilation plan and assess respiratory recovery before discharge.

> **Closing point:** Name the rib-level target and avoid stellate injury.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization (2015)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482) · [BJA Education: Pain after lower limb amputation (2026)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41727978/) · [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766)

items.title: How do you distinguish early fistula failure from access-related hand ischaemia?
items.sub: Dialysis access, sympathectomy and other vascular emergencies
items.eyebrow: Dialysis access, sympathectomy and other vascular emergencies
items.q: How do you distinguish early fistula failure from access-related hand ischaemia?
items.a:
An absent thrill suggests access failure. Pain, coolness, sensory change or weakness in the hand suggests compromised distal flow. Severe new neuropathy may occur with a warmer hand and preserved pulse. Check baseline and block effects, and obtain urgent vascular review for a new deficit.

**Sources:** [KDOQI vascular access guideline, 2019 update](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32778223/)

items.title: Why should a normal lactate or impaired renal function not defer imaging for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia?
items.sub: Dialysis access, sympathectomy and other vascular emergencies
items.eyebrow: Dialysis access, sympathectomy and other vascular emergencies
items.q: Why should a normal lactate or impaired renal function not defer imaging for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia?
items.a:
Lactate may be normal before extensive injury. Urgent arterial and venous phase CT angiography helps locate the lesion and evaluate bowel, even when kidney function is impaired. Treat sepsis and shock while involving surgical and endovascular teams.

**Sources:** [2025 ESVS mesenteric and renal guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejvs.2025.06.010)

items.title: How do you recognise stroke in the recovery room?
items.q: How do you recognise stroke in the recovery room?
items.a:
- New focal deficit, dysphasia, altered consciousness or failure to wake.
- Check ABCs/glucose and exclude mimics; establish last-known-well and activate stroke/vascular teams.
- Urgent brain/vascular imaging; assess thrombectomy eligibility.
- Recent major surgery often limits systemic thrombolysis; after CEA also consider thrombosis/re-exploration or hyperperfusion.

> **Closing point:** Use a time-critical cause-specific pathway.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What are the risk factors for perioperative stroke?
items.q: What are the risk factors for perioperative stroke?
items.a:
- Previous stroke, carotid stenosis, AF.
- Vascular or cardiac surgery.
- Hypotension and withdrawal of antithrombotics.
- Associated with substantially increased mortality and disability; the magnitude varies by cohort.

> **Closing point:** Mostly embolic.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: How do you prevent venous thromboembolism in vascular patients?
items.q: How do you prevent venous thromboembolism in vascular patients?
items.a:
- Assess thrombosis, bleeding, renal function and neuraxial/catheter timing.
- Give appropriate pharmacological prophylaxis when haemostasis permits.
- Assess arterial perfusion before compression: severe PAD can contraindicate stockings/devices on that limb.
- Mobilise early and reassess after bleeding or changes in treatment.

> **Closing point:** Match prophylaxis to both venous risk and arterial supply.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: What causes renal failure after aortic surgery?
items.q: What causes renal failure after aortic surgery?
items.a:
- Clamp ischaemia, hypovolaemia, contrast.
- Atheroembolism and nephrotoxins.
- Abdominal compartment syndrome.
- Prevent with volume and perfusion pressure.

> **Closing point:** Kidneys depend on perfusion pressure.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/)

items.title: 1. Cardiac risk assessment for open aortobifemoral bypass
items.q: A 68-year-old man with intermittent claudication, diabetes and a previous myocardial infarction is listed for open aortobifemoral bypass. How will you assess his perioperative cardiac risk and what measures will you take to reduce it?
items.a:
## Preop

### Risk assessment

Major vascular surgery is a **high-risk** operation (risk of major cardiac events above 5%) in a patient with systemic atherosclerosis and silent ischaemia.

- **History and functional capacity:** DASI or METs (claudication limits exercise, so an exercise history may mislead); angina, heart failure, arrhythmia, valve disease, stroke, diabetes, CKD.
- **Scores:** **RCRI** (high-risk surgery, IHD, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine >2 mg/dL (approximately 177 µmol/L)), or the **VSG-CRI** (vascular-specific); frailty and ASA grade.
- **Tests:** ECG; echo for new/worsening HF or suspected significant valve disease. CPET selectively assists risk discussion/planning; no single anaerobic-threshold cutoff determines suitability. BNP/NT-proBNP and troponin can refine elevated-risk assessment; stress testing/coronary angiography only for standard indications or when the result changes management.

### Risk reduction

- **Continue** aspirin, statin and beta-blocker; start a statin if not on one; do not start high-dose beta-blocker immediately before surgery ([POISE primary trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18479744/): reduced MI but more stroke/death with its acute high-dose regimen).
- **Revascularisation** (PCI/CABG) is indicated only by standard indications (not simply to reduce perioperative risk: [CARP primary trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15625331/) studied stable CAD and did not establish survival benefit from prophylactic revascularisation); if a recent stent, plan dual antiplatelets and timing.
- Optimise heart failure, hypertension, arrhythmia, diabetes (HbA1c, perioperative glucose generally 5–10 mmol/L under ADS–ANZCA guidance, with individualised targets), anaemia, CKD and COPD; smoking cessation.
- **Shared decision-making** on whether to proceed, or an endovascular alternative.
## Intraop

- arterial line, ST monitoring, avoid hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia and hypothermia; treat pain; consider cardiac output monitoring.
## Postop

- consider troponin at 24/48 hours in elevated-risk patients, ECG if indicated, monitored care and analgesia. MINS means presumed ischaemic myocardial injury, often asymptomatic; exclude sepsis/PE and other causes. Investigate/treat the mechanism, optimise secondary prevention and weigh antithrombotics against bleeding rather than automatically starting aspirin for every troponin rise.

## Apply the findings

A patient whose walking is limited by claudication cannot demonstrate cardiopulmonary reserve by simple distance alone. Ask about symptoms during activities they can perform, assess functional status and frailty and check for active or decompensated disease. Use results only when they could alter optimisation, surgery or monitoring. Discuss the relative cardiovascular burden of aortic clamping, less invasive alternatives and what operative benefit justifies the risk.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance: 2026 reaffirmation of 2024 recommendations](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017). · [AHA/ACC perioperative cardiovascular guidance, reaffirmed 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [ANZCA Blue Book catalogue, including 2023 radiation and aortic balloon occlusion chapters](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises major vascular surgery as high risk
- Assesses functional capacity and recognises limits in claudicants
- Uses RCRI or a vascular-specific score
- Selects investigations that will change management (echo, CPET, BNP)
- Continues aspirin, statin and beta-blocker; avoids new high-dose beta-blocker
- Limits revascularisation to usual indications
- Optimises diabetes, CKD, COPD and smoking
- Describes intraoperative and postoperative strategies including troponin surveillance
- Includes shared decision-making

items.title: 2. Pathophysiology of peripheral vascular disease and perioperative considerations
items.q: Describe the pathophysiology of peripheral vascular disease and its perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Pathophysiology

Here **peripheral arterial disease (PAD)** means atherosclerosis; “PVD” is a broader term that can also include venous disease. PAD involves atherosclerosis of the aorta and lower limb arteries: lipid deposition, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation and plaque rupture or thrombosis. Risk factors: **smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia**, age, CKD. Narrowing may cause exertional **claudication**. **Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI)** is PAD with chronic ischaemic rest pain, ulceration or gangrene (usually >2 weeks) supported by objective perfusion assessment. Most claudicants do not inevitably progress to CLTI. In **diabetics** there is also calcified medial disease (non-compressible vessels, falsely high ankle-brachial index), neuropathy and infection. Acute limb ischaemia arises from **embolism or thrombosis** (the six Ps).

## Preop

- **It is a marker of systemic atherosclerosis**: CAD and cerebrovascular disease are common and cardiac risk is substantial; exact prevalence depends on the population. Many have **silent ischaemia**, and exercise testing is limited by claudication.
- **Comorbidity**: diabetes, CKD, COPD (smokers), hypertension, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, frailty; **polypharmacy** with antiplatelets, statins and anticoagulants. Treat anaemia.
- **Procedure type** (angioplasty, bypass, amputation) guides technique and risk.

## Intraop

- **Arterial access and monitoring**: limb BP is unreliable (use the least diseased arm; bilateral differences with subclavian stenosis), difficult cannulation, and cuff placement on the affected limb.
- **Anaesthetic choice**: regional techniques are suitable but affected by anticoagulation; GA has greater haemodynamic effects.
- **Aims**: avoid hypotension and tachycardia, keep warm (vasoconstriction), manage heparin and blood loss, and protect pressure areas.

## Postop

- Protect the kidney after contrast, and treat a new pain complaint as possible graft failure until examined.

## Summary

Consider the patient as a **high cardiovascular risk** while also treating local limb threat as an urgent determinant of surgical timing.

## Apply the findings

Diabetes and medial calcification can leave the ankle–brachial index falsely elevated. Use toe pressures or waveforms when this obscures limb severity. Compare functional limitation from claudication with rest pain, tissue loss or sudden weakness. Perfusion and surveillance priorities change with each. Ask whether the skin and incision will heal, whether a planned pressure cuff or position will further compromise flow and whether a postoperative pain complaint represents graft failure. If exertional symptoms do not reflect fixed claudication, consider whether frailty, heart failure or diabetic neuropathy is also limiting exercise, and use appropriate objective measures.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization surgery (2015;15:225–230)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482); [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance: 2026 reaffirmation of 2024 recommendations](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017). · [2024 ACC/AHA multisociety lower-extremity PAD guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013)

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Atherosclerosis mechanism and risk factors
- Claudication to critical limb ischaemia
- Diabetic features: calcification and neuropathy
- Acute limb ischaemia mechanisms
- Systemic atherosclerosis and cardiac risk
- Comorbidity and polypharmacy
- Monitoring and access issues
- Anaesthetic choice and perioperative aims

items.title: 3. Vascular patient with heart failure, a cardiac device, COPD and hypertension
items.q: Describe the perioperative considerations for a patient with heart failure, atrial fibrillation with a pacemaker, COPD and treated hypertension who is listed for open aortic surgery.
items.a:
## Framework

For each condition: **identify severity and stability, optimise what can safely be changed, plan perfusion and drug management, and monitor for the characteristic postoperative complication.** Urgency decides how much optimisation is possible: elective repair deserves full assessment, whereas rupture or a threatened limb needs treatment and a rescue-ready plan in parallel.

## Preop

### Heart failure
- Define reduced EF, diastolic dysfunction/LVH, RV failure and valve disease; ask about orthopnoea, oedema, recent admissions and exercise tolerance.
- Treat decompensated failure before elective repair.

### Atrial fibrillation and the pacemaker
- Establish rhythm, ventricular rate, AF burden, thromboembolic risk, anticoagulant indication and **device dependence**. Correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺ and ask about syncope.
- Plan anticoagulant interruption and restart around bleeding, procedural heparin and regional catheters; routine bridging is inappropriate for most patients.
- Agree **device interrogation, electrosurgery arrangements and external pacing/defibrillation** before theatre.

### COPD
- Identify exacerbation, recent infection, baseline dyspnoea, sputum, bronchodilator and steroid use, hypoxaemia or CO₂ retention, sleep-disordered breathing and pulmonary hypertension.
- Optimise inhalers, treat reversible infection, support smoking cessation and arrange postoperative respiratory care. Ask whether an open transperitoneal incision (or a thoracotomy with one-lung ventilation) is tolerable; EVAR may avoid the incision but is not automatically safe.

### Hypertension
- Assess usual pressure, end-organ disease, LVH, medications and secondary causes; a single high reading does not by itself mean an unstable patient.
- Continue chronic beta-blockade; individualise ACE inhibitor or ARB by indication, HF status and procedure.

## Intraop

- **Heart failure:** a stiff LV is preload-sensitive yet vulnerable to overload; a failing systolic LV may deteriorate with the afterload of a clamp. Use arterial monitoring and targeted echo or flow assessment in higher-risk surgery; titrate fluid, vasopressor and inotrope to the mechanism, not a CVP target.
- **AF and device:** unstable perioperative tachyarrhythmia needs resuscitation and cardioversion rather than prolonged rate control; look for reversible triggers (bleeding, ischaemia, hypoxia, electrolytes). Use the agreed electrosurgery and pacing/defibrillation arrangements.
- **COPD:** allow adequate expiratory time and avoid dynamic hyperinflation.
- **Hypertension:** avoid profound induction hypotension (impaired autoregulation) and do not force BP to a population-normal value during clamping or reperfusion.

## Postop

- **Heart failure:** watch for pulmonary oedema, low output, renal and myocardial injury.
- **AF and device:** restart anticoagulation according to bleeding and catheter plans; confirm rhythm and device function as agreed.
- **COPD:** dynamic analgesia, cough, physiotherapy and an HDU/extubation strategy.
- **Hypertension:** resume usual antihypertensives as haemodynamics and renal function allow.

## Bringing it together

Document the status of each condition, the plan for monitoring, the anticoagulant and device plan, the postoperative destination and a shared decision with the patient, including whether an endovascular or less invasive option reduces the burden.

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · Set 14 notes, section 1.6

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Uses a severity, optimisation, perfusion plan and postoperative complication framework
- Heart failure: type, decompensation, preload and afterload sensitivity, monitoring
- AF and device: rhythm, anticoagulation plan, device dependence, interrogation, electrosurgery, external pacing and defibrillation
- COPD: optimisation, ventilation strategy, analgesia, extubation and HDU plan
- Hypertension: continues beta-blocker, individualises ACE inhibitor or ARB, avoids induction hypotension
- States how urgency changes the amount of optimisation
- Includes shared decision-making and destination

items.title: 4. Reperfusion injury and hypotension after unclamping
items.q: Discuss the pathophysiology of ischaemia–reperfusion injury after prolonged limb or gut ischaemia in vascular surgery, and how you would prevent and manage its consequences, including hypotension after aortic unclamping.
items.a:
## Why unclamping causes hypotension

Release removes the proximal afterload rise, exposes a large dilated distal bed, allows venous pooling and returns **acidic, hyperkalaemic blood** to the central circulation. Preload and SVR fall suddenly; acidaemia, hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia add myocardial depression. Microvascular no-reflow and endothelial injury can sustain distal malperfusion despite macrovascular restoration. This is not simply hypovolaemia, so the response must be diagnostic as well as therapeutic.

## Intraop

### Prevention before release

- Communicate the planned time and ask for **staged release**.
- Reassess volume responsiveness and blood loss; give small blood or fluid aliquots only if needed (do not fill a congested LV).
- Reduce unnecessary vasodilator, prepare noradrenaline, confirm ionised calcium, take a gas before and after release.
- Trend ECG, ETCO₂, lactate, pH, K⁺, ionised Ca²⁺, Hb and pulses afterwards. A transient fall in ETCO₂ can follow reduced pulmonary flow; persistent low ETCO₂ needs assessment of output, ventilation and embolism.

### Managing severe hypotension after release

1. Ask the surgeon about bleeding, clamp release or proximal obstruction; ensure oxygen delivery and a useful arterial trace.
2. Treat immediately threatening hypotension with a vasopressor while separating low preload, vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, arrhythmia and haemorrhage; address inotropy if there is marked failure.
3. For haemorrhage or fluid responsiveness give warmed blood in assessed aliquots; activate the major haemorrhage protocol for heavy bleeding rather than giving litres of saline.
4. Widened QRS, peaked T waves, bradyarrhythmia or VF with high K⁺: IV calcium promptly, then potassium-shifting therapy and control of ongoing release. Acidosis is treated by restoring perfusion; bicarbonate does not substitute for correcting shock.
5. Refractory deterioration: discuss temporary reclamping or staged reperfusion with the surgeon immediately.

### Organ-specific reperfusion problems

- **Muscle and limb:** ATP depletion, Na⁺/K⁺ pump failure and calcium loading; reperfusion adds free radicals, endothelial activation and capillary leak in tight fascial compartments. Potassium, acid, phosphate and myoglobin cause arrhythmias, vasoplegia and pigment-associated AKI. A returned pulse does not exclude **compartment syndrome**.
- **Gut and colon:** supracoeliac clamping interrupts splanchnic inflow; even infrarenal repair threatens colonic collaterals (inferior mesenteric, internal iliac). Mucosal failure and reperfusion cause bacterial translocation, inflammation and thrombosis. **Lactate may be normal early.**
- **Kidney and spinal cord:** reperfusion injury and atheroembolism on a CKD background; segmental artery interruption may cause immediate or delayed paraplegia.

## Postop

### Surveillance and escalation

- Record exact clamp times and compromised territories; maintain perfusing pressure and output without fluid-related bowel oedema.
- After limb revascularisation: pain disproportionate to findings, pain on stretch, tense swelling, paraesthesia; measure compartment pressure if needed and do not delay fasciotomy for a normal pulse. For rhabdomyolysis follow CK, K⁺, Ca²⁺, phosphate, bicarbonate, creatinine and urine output; control hyperkalaemia, give isotonic fluid titrated to perfusion and congestion, and use renal replacement on usual indications. Bicarbonate alkalinisation, mannitol and loop diuretics have no established benefit.
- After aortic repair: disproportionate abdominal pain, ileus, bloody diarrhoea, distension, rising lactate or unexplained shock needs immediate vascular or general surgical review with CTA, endoscopy or operation; do not just treat the acidosis.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · Set 14 notes, sections 2.4 to 2.6, 9.7

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Explains the mechanisms of hypotension after unclamping
- Prevention: communication, staged release, volume and blood assessment, vasopressor and calcium ready
- Stepwise treatment of hypotension, including hyperkalaemia
- Describes limb and muscle reperfusion injury, compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis
- Describes mesenteric and colonic ischaemia, noting that early lactate may be normal
- Names kidney and spinal cord risks
- Surveillance and escalation plan after limb and aortic repair

items.title: 5. Complications after open AAA repair and how to minimise them
items.q: List the major postoperative complications after open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair and describe how you would minimise them.
items.a:
## Complications and their prevention

| System | Complication | Prevention and management |
|---|---|---|
| **Cardiac** | Myocardial injury or infarction, arrhythmia (AF), failure | Optimise, avoid tachycardia and hypotension, troponin and ECG surveillance, continue beta-blocker and statin |
| **Renal** | **AKI** (clamping, hypovolaemia, contrast) | Maintain volume and perfusion pressure, avoid nephrotoxins, urine output, renal replacement if needed |
| **Respiratory** | Atelectasis, pneumonia, respiratory failure | Lung-protective ventilation, epidural or regional analgesia, physiotherapy, early extubation |
| **Bleeding** | Surgical or coagulopathic haemorrhage, retroperitoneal | Normothermia, targeted haemostasis, cell salvage and early surgical review/re-exploration; TXA only if indicated by the relevant protocol |
| **Gut** | **Colonic ischaemia** (low-flow state, embolisation and inadequate mesenteric/pelvic collaterals; IMA ligation alone is not the explanation), ileus, abdominal compartment syndrome | Maintain perfusion, bladder pressure, early recognition (bloody diarrhoea, acidosis, distension) |
| **Limb and spinal** | Distal embolisation or thrombosis; spinal cord ischaemia (rare in infrarenal repair) | Pulse and neurological checks, urgent exploration or imaging |
| **Neurological** | Stroke, delirium | BP control, delirium prevention, early analgesia |
| **Infection** | Wound, graft | Antibiotic prophylaxis, aseptic technique |
| **Pain** | Acute and persistent post-surgical pain | Multimodal analgesia, epidural or rectus sheath catheters, follow-up |
| **Thromboembolic** | DVT, PE | Pharmacological prophylaxis when haemostasis permits; assess arterial perfusion before compression because severe PAD can contraindicate stockings/devices on the affected limb |

## Preop

Optimise cardiac status and continue beta-blocker and statin; plan antibiotic prophylaxis, the HDU/ICU bed and epidural timing relative to anticoagulation.

## Intraop

Avoid tachycardia and hypotension, maintain volume and perfusion pressure, use lung-protective ventilation, keep normothermia, use cell salvage and targeted haemostasis, and avoid nephrotoxins.

## Postop

Return to **HDU or ICU**, correct acidosis and coagulopathy, restore perfusion without overload, provide **multimodal analgesia** (epidural with the anticoagulation timing), start early mobilisation and nutrition, and use enhanced recovery principles. Mortality after elective open repair is about 3 to 5%, and most deaths are cardiac, respiratory or renal.

## Apply the findings

New abdominal pain or bloody stool accompanied by unexplained acidosis triggers immediate review for bowel ischaemia even when urine output and proximal pressure are adequate. Postoperative oliguria can reflect ATN, emboli, branch compromise, bleeding or raised intra-abdominal pressure. Escalate a tense abdomen with organ dysfunction and measure bladder pressure where appropriate. Changes in leg warmth, Doppler signals, pain or power require vascular examination for occlusion or compartment syndrome. A pulse can persist in the latter. Ensure the handover documents clamp level, clamp time, limb signals and specific concern for bowel, kidney or limb perfusion. Trends in lactate and perfusion can guide resuscitation, but normal values early do not rule out regional ischaemia.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/); [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766). · [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [2025 ESVS mesenteric and renal guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejvs.2025.06.010)

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Cardiac complications and prevention
- Renal injury and prevention
- Respiratory complications and analgesia
- Bleeding and coagulopathy
- Colonic ischaemia and abdominal compartment syndrome
- Limb ischaemia and spinal cord ischaemia
- Stroke, delirium, infection and thromboembolism
- Analgesia and persistent post-surgical pain
- HDU or ICU, normothermia and enhanced recovery

items.title: 6. Minimising blood loss in elective open AAA repair
items.q: Outline how you would minimise blood loss and transfusion requirements in a patient having elective open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair.
items.a:
## Preop

- **Treat anaemia** (iron, erythropoietin if time); correct coagulopathy; manage **antiplatelets** (continue aspirin; plan for clopidogrel), and anticoagulants.
- **Group and crossmatch** (quantity according to predicted blood loss, baseline Hb and local maximum surgical blood-order schedule) and know the transfusion thresholds; cell salvage set up.
- Consider an **endovascular approach** where anatomy allows.

## Intraop

- **Surgical** meticulous haemostasis, clamp control, sequential clamp.
- **Cell salvage** (autologous blood recovery; infected/contaminated fields require an explicit risk–benefit decision and local protocol; washing/filters do not sterilise blood), **acute normovolaemic haemodilution** in selected patients.
- **TXA:** consider under the relevant vascular/major-haemorrhage protocol with renal-adjusted dosing and contraindication review. POISE-3 used 1 g at the start/end of noncardiac surgery and reduced bleeding, but did **not meet its prespecified cardiovascular noninferiority criterion**; this is not proof that every elective AAA or rAAA patient should receive that regimen.
- **Maintain normothermia**, calcium, acid-base and avoid dilutional coagulopathy: warm fluids, restrict crystalloid, goal-directed fluid therapy, avoid deliberate hypotension as routine blood conservation in a vasculopath; preserve critical-organ perfusion, especially during unclamping.
- **Heparin** at the appropriate dose and **protamine** reversal once the repair is complete.
- **Point-of-care testing** (TEG/ROTEM, ACT) to guide **blood products** (fibrinogen, cryoprecipitate, plasma, platelets) rather than empirical use.
- **Massive transfusion protocol** if bleeding is large.

## Postop

Continue warming, monitor for bleeding and coagulopathy, maintain Hb thresholds (restrictive, often 70–80 g/L in stable patients, individualised to active bleeding, myocardial ischaemia and physiology rather than automatically higher for any history of IHD), avoid hypertension, and return to theatre if needed.

## Apply the findings

Cell salvage can reduce donor red-cell exposure but does not replace fibrinogen or platelets. Use coagulopathy tests to guide treatment in a patient with ongoing bleeding and interpret them with temperature, pH, calcium and the surgical field. A low fibrin-based clot amplitude and weak whole-blood strength suggest different treatment targets. Reassess after each intervention and discuss further surgical haemostasis if bleeding continues despite corrected physiology and no detectable treatable deficit. For antiplatelet drugs discuss recent vascular or coronary intervention before changing treatment. Plan access, crossmatch and cell salvage before incision rather than after major bleeding has begun.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/); [POISE-3 tranexamic acid primary trial (2022)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35363452/). · [ANZCA Blue Book 2025, cardiac and vascular viscoelastic algorithm and GLP-1 chapter](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305)

## Self-marking checklist

- Preoperative anaemia, coagulation and antiplatelet plan
- Crossmatch and cell salvage
- Tranexamic acid
- Normothermia, calcium and acid-base
- Goal-directed fluids, avoids dilution
- Heparin and protamine management
- Point-of-care testing to guide products
- Massive transfusion protocol
- Restrictive transfusion thresholds

items.title: 7. Elective open infrarenal AAA repair: perioperative considerations
items.q: A 70-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease and COPD is listed for elective open infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. Outline the perioperative considerations, including how you will manage aortic clamping and unclamping.
items.a:
## Preop

### Assessment

- **Review the CT angiogram with the surgeon:** clamp level (renal arteries above or below the clamp), neck, thrombus and calcification, accessory renal arteries, inferior mesenteric and internal iliac supply, previous abdominal surgery. Ask about chronic mesenteric ischaemia, prior bowel resection and previous aortic intervention, because these predict bowel ischaemia and collateral dependence after clamping.
- **Cardiovascular risk** as for the vascular patient generally: functional capacity (limited by claudication), RCRI or a vascular-specific score, ECG, selective echo; continue aspirin, statin and beta-blocker.
- **Other organs:** creatinine/eGFR and baseline urine output, haemoglobin, coagulation and antithrombotic status, group and crossmatch, lung physiology (severe COPD makes abdominal closure and prolonged ventilation difficult).
- **Decide and document:** open versus EVAR is a shared anatomical and risk decision (ESVS 2024 considers repair of asymptomatic AAA at 5.5 cm in men and 5.0 cm in women, and advises against repair of smaller aneurysms). Plan the ICU/HDU destination and the patient's wishes about a prolonged course.

## Intraop

### Preparation and monitoring

- Preinduction **radial arterial line**, five-lead ECG with ST trend, **two large peripheral cannulae**, rapid infuser and warmer, urinary catheter, core temperature, serial gases with Hb, K⁺, ionised Ca²⁺ and lactate; blood available before induction and **cell salvage** set up.
- TEE or cardiac-output monitoring and central access are chosen for a high clamp, poor ventricular reserve or anticipated instability, not by routine.
- **Team agreements:** heparin timing, expected clamp time, who announces clamp application and release, epidural policy.

### Induction and maintenance

- Titrate induction to avoid hypotension and tachycardia in severe CAD or LVH; vasopressor ready before loss of consciousness. No particular hypnotic overcomes haemorrhage or clamp physiology.
- Titrated opioid or remifentanil blunts sympathetic peaks; avoid hypoxaemia and hypercapnia. Protect the kidney by preventing sustained hypotension, not with renal-dose dopamine, mannitol or furosemide.
- COPD: allow adequate expiratory time and avoid dynamic hyperinflation.

### Clamping

- Afterload rises: proximal pressure may rise while cardiac output falls. Follow flow and ventricular function (echo where available), not pressure alone. Avoid tachycardia and titrate vasodilator or inotrope to myocardial performance.
- Record clamp start and finish. An infrarenal clamp still allows renal and bowel injury; a suprarenal or supracoeliac clamp adds time-critical renal and splanchnic ischaemia.

### Before and after unclamping

- Announce readiness; reassess volume, blood loss, K⁺, pH, ionised calcium and lactate; prepare noradrenaline; request **staged release**; give small assessed fluid or blood aliquots.
- After release, treat hypotension diagnostically: bleeding, vasodilation, myocardial depression, hyperkalaemia and acidosis. Give calcium for hyperkalaemic ECG change; treat acidosis by restoring perfusion. Repeat gases.

### Blood conservation

Cell salvage (does not replace platelets or factors), normothermia, fibrinogen, platelets and viscoelastic testing during heavy bleeding, major haemorrhage protocol, repeated ionised calcium. Tranexamic acid is not automatic; weigh graft thrombosis, renal function and local evidence.

### Analgesia

- A thoracic epidural gives strong dynamic analgesia but complicates heparin and bleeding. Insert well before heparinisation per the neuraxial-antithrombotic policy; a bloody tap prompts reassessment of heparin timing. Alternatives: rectus sheath/TAP catheters, PCA, paracetamol, selective ketamine; avoid NSAIDs in AKI risk.

## Postop

- Extubate on haemostasis, pulmonary mechanics, temperature, acid–base and haemodynamics. HDU/ICU surveillance for bleeding, myocardial injury, AKI, bowel ischaemia, leg perfusion, pneumonia and abdominal compartment syndrome.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766) · Set 14 notes, chapters 2 and 3

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Reviews CTA: clamp level, renal arteries, mesenteric collaterals
- Cardiac, renal, respiratory and blood preparation; ICU destination
- Arterial line before induction, large-bore access, blood and cell salvage
- Induction that avoids hypotension and tachycardia in CAD
- Clamp physiology: afterload rise with falling output; follows flow not pressure
- Staged, planned unclamping with K⁺, calcium, acid–base and vasopressor plan
- Blood conservation and major haemorrhage plan
- Epidural decision linked to heparin timing, with alternatives
- Postoperative surveillance for bowel, kidney, heart, lungs and legs

items.title: 8. Anaesthetic options and management for elective EVAR with CKD
items.q: A 78-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease and a creatinine clearance of 40 mL/min is booked for elective infrarenal EVAR. Discuss the anaesthetic options and your intraoperative management.
items.a:
## Preop

### Choice of technique

EVAR can be done under **general, regional (epidural or spinal) or local anaesthesia with sedation**. Local and regional techniques are associated with shorter stay and fewer pulmonary complications, and suit patients with severe respiratory or cardiac disease, but require cooperation and a plan for conversion. **GA** gives immobility and apnoea for imaging (digital subtraction angiography) and a secure airway if it converts to an open repair. The best choice depends on patient factors, expected duration, and surgeon preference.

## Intraop

- **Monitoring:** ECG with ST analysis, SpO2, capnography, **arterial line** (left or right radial per the surgeon's access), urine output, temperature; central access in high-risk patients.
- **Heparin** (about 5000 units or 70 to 100 units/kg) with ACT according to procedure/centre protocol (often around 250 seconds); reversal is individualised to haemostasis/thrombosis risk.
- **Haemodynamic goals:** avoid hypotension and tachycardia in IHD; manage the pressor response to wire manipulation; stable BP at stent-graft deployment (the surgeon may ask for lower BP).
- **Renal protection:** minimise and dilute contrast, ensure euvolaemia, hold nephrotoxins (NSAIDs; ACE inhibitor per policy), avoid hypotension.
- **Blood:** group and screen or crossmatch because of the risk of access injury, aortic rupture or conversion; keep the surgeon aware.
- **Radiation protection:** lead apron, distance and shielding in the hybrid theatre.
- **Temperature, positioning, pressure-area care** (long procedures).

## Complications to anticipate

Access vessel injury and bleeding, **iliac or aortic rupture**, **endoleak** (I: attachment-site failure; II: retrograde branch flow; III: component/fabric failure—types I/III usually require prompt correction, whereas type II management depends on sac growth/persistence), distal embolisation, limb ischaemia, **contrast-associated AKI**, pelvic and colonic ischaemia, spinal cord ischaemia (rare), post-implantation syndrome (fever, raised CRP), and the need for conversion to open surgery.

## Postop

Groin and limb checks, urine output, creatinine at 24 to 48 hours, pain control with local infiltration, early mobilisation, and ward or HDU as required.

## Apply the findings

Have the operator identify the intended access, neck and branch anatomy and the circumstances requiring open conversion. Establish how haemorrhage, graft deployment problems and sedation-related airway compromise will be signalled under drapes. Choose GA if inability to lie still, significant anxiety, prolonged complex repair or airway concerns outweigh the physiological benefits of a lighter technique. Preserve access to the face and put vasoactive support and blood within reach.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/); [ESUR Contrast Media Safety Committee Guidelines 2026](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/). · [ANZCA professional documents, PS55 and PG09](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

## Self-marking checklist

- Compares general, regional and local techniques
- Chooses a technique with reasons
- Describes monitoring including arterial line and ST analysis
- Describes heparin and ACT
- Sets haemodynamic goals for IHD
- Describes renal protection and contrast minimisation
- Prepares blood and conversion to open repair
- Names radiation protection
- Lists complications: access injury, endoleak, rupture, embolisation, post-implantation syndrome

items.title: 9. Oliguria and rising creatinine after complex EVAR
items.q: Following a complex EVAR, a patient develops oliguria and a rising creatinine. How would you distinguish renal malperfusion from other causes and manage the patient?
items.a:
## Look for a reversible procedural cause

Assess the patient, validate urine output, check for catheter obstruction and determine timing relative to repair, hypotension and contrast. Review baseline creatinine and urine output, planned and actual graft anatomy, renal artery coverage/branch grafts, completion angiography, blood loss, duration of hypotension and perioperative nephrotoxins. Acute renal artery coverage, thrombosis, dissection, branch-stent kink or embolism can threaten a kidney before creatinine has risen substantially. Concern is especially high with bilateral compromise or one functioning kidney. Let the vascular team know immediately if urine output falls abruptly, the completion scan was equivocal, or concern remains after initial resuscitation.

## Distinguish other causes

Check vital signs and arterial pressure trend, peripheral perfusion, ECG, lactate, Hb, blood gas and potassium. Examine volume status and cardiac function, including venous congestion, and consider retroperitoneal haemorrhage, low cardiac output, sepsis or abdominal compartment syndrome when the clinical pattern fits. Urinalysis and sediment can support a renal diagnosis but do not rule out an occluded branch. Atheroembolism may evolve over days and can coexist with peripheral signs such as livedo or blue toes. Contrast-associated AKI describes timing and includes injury from hypoperfusion and emboli. It should not be assumed to be the cause after a technically complex procedure. Check the bladder and review drugs, including diuretics, NSAIDs and other potentially contributory agents.

## Investigate and treat in parallel

Review available images and obtain urgent duplex, CT angiography or direct angiography according to the anatomy, local expertise and the need for immediate intervention. A nondiagnostic duplex should not delay definitive evaluation when branch compromise is likely. Balance contrast exposure against the benefit of salvaging renal perfusion. Correct hypotension or bleeding, give assessed balanced isotonic fluid if underfilled and avoid worsening pulmonary oedema or venous congestion. Use vasopressor support where indicated and restore flow with the vascular team where an actionable obstruction is found.

Trend creatinine, urine output, acid–base status and electrolytes, adjust renally cleared medication and seek renal input. Treat hyperkalaemia promptly and plan renal replacement for refractory electrolyte, acid–base or fluid complications. For a subsequent necessary contrast procedure, use minimum diagnostic dose and route-specific risk assessment, with individualised hydration. There is no routine role for acetylcysteine or bicarbonate over saline to prevent injury.

**Sources:** [ESUR 2026 contrast guidelines](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/) · [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [BJA Education: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury (2020)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33456926/) · [PRESERVE primary randomised trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29130810/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Prioritises early recognition of renal branch or ostial compromise
- Distinguishes perfusion, embolic, urinary, contrast-associated and other causes
- Uses clinical trends and procedural imaging with appropriate urgency
- Plans timely vascular rescue rather than deferring essential imaging
- Uses targeted haemodynamic and renal supportive care
- Monitors and treats serious biochemical and volume complications

items.title: 10. Bilateral leg weakness after TEVAR
items.q: Six hours after extensive TEVAR, a patient develops new bilateral leg weakness after an episode of hypotension. Explain your assessment and immediate rescue strategy.
items.a:
## Recognise delayed spinal cord ischaemia

Activate the aortic, anaesthesia and ICU rescue pathway immediately. Establish the time of the last normal examination, relation to sedation and BP, completion angiography findings, coverage and collateral inflow. Check motor function, sensation, level, asymmetry, peripheral pulses and Doppler signals. A new deficit after a normal emergence can reflect marginal collateral perfusion becoming inadequate during hypotension, anaemia or elevated venous pressure. Bilateral weakness with preserved limb perfusion raises suspicion for cord injury. Stroke, limb malperfusion, neuraxial haematoma, residual motor block, compressive neuropathy and metabolic disturbance may mimic it. Pain, sphincter findings or a recent neuraxial procedure with anticoagulation make a compressive lesion particularly important to investigate.

## Restore oxygen delivery immediately

Check arterial monitoring, oxygenation, rhythm, Hb, blood gas and bedside cardiac function. Restore effective circulating volume where deficient, correct significant anaemia and hypoxaemia, and use titrated vasopressor or inotrope to reach the unit’s cord-rescue pressure targets. Avoid large empiric fluid loads that raise venous pressure and worsen perfusion. Spinal cord perfusion pressure can be approximated as MAP minus the higher of CSF and venous pressure. A normal MAP for routine ICU care may be insufficient following segmental and collateral artery interruption. Correct ongoing bleeding, arrhythmia or depressed output at the same time.

If a drain is present, check its level, pressure and patency with trained staff. Adjust drainage within the pressure and volume limits of the institutional rescue protocol. Do not manipulate a blocked or bloody catheter empirically. If no drain is present, urgent rescue drainage may help when safe. Coordinate anticoagulation, platelet and coagulation status before insertion and investigate suspected spinal haematoma urgently. Obtain appropriate imaging with surgical, neuroradiology and neurology input without delaying readily reversible perfusion measures.

## Identify structural causes and protect recovery

Review subclavian and internal iliac inflow, access-vessel obstruction, graft position and distal perfusion. Revascularisation or revision may be needed if anatomy is the limiting factor. Continue frequent documented neurological examinations, arterial monitoring and treatment of the precipitating hypotension. Maintain perfusion during transfers and avoid premature simultaneous withdrawal of pressure support and drain management. Explain the deficit and plan to the patient where possible and involve spinal rehabilitation early if recovery is incomplete.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic/thoracoabdominal guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/) · [BJA Education: Perioperative management of thoracic and thoracoabdominal aneurysms (2019;19:119–125)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33456880/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises delayed spinal cord ischaemia and calls the rescue team
- Establishes examination and differentiates stroke, limb ischaemia and spinal haematoma
- Restores pressure, output and oxygen content promptly
- Explains pressure equation and safe existing or rescue CSF drainage
- Assesses collateral/graft obstruction and physiological precipitants
- Plans serial examinations and stepwise de-escalation

items.title: 11. Acute type A dissection: perioperative considerations
items.q: A 58-year-old man is brought to theatre with an acute Stanford type A aortic dissection. Outline the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Principles

Type A dissection is a **surgical emergency** (rapidly progressive risk; the often-quoted 1–2%/hour is historical and not a universal contemporary prediction). The dissection involves the **ascending aorta**, with risks of **rupture, tamponade, aortic regurgitation, coronary malperfusion, cerebral, spinal, visceral and limb malperfusion**. Do not delay surgery; anaesthesia occurs in the operating theatre with the surgeon and perfusionist ready.

## Preop

- Diagnosis by CT angiography (or TOE); **anti-impulse therapy**: control pain, heart rate 60–80/min and SBP <120 or lowest preserving organ perfusion in a haemodynamically stable patient, with esmolol or labetalol first and then a vasodilator (nicardipine, GTN); avoid reflex beta-blockade/vasodilation in shock, tamponade or severe acute AR; support perfusion and expedite surgery (hypotension in tamponade needs surgery, not volume overload).
- **Blood** crossmatched (massive), assess end-organ involvement, and renal function.

## Intraop

- **Monitoring:** bilateral radial/brachial or radial and femoral arterial lines (one may be falsely low), central line, ECG, TOE, cerebral oximetry (NIRS), temperature (nasopharyngeal and bladder/rectal), urine output.
- **Induction** with the surgical team scrubbed and CPB ready (**femoral or axillary cannulation**): haemodynamically stable induction (etomidate/opioid), maintain anti-impulse control, and avoid hypertension on laryngoscopy. In tamponade, pre-induction hypotension and loss of sympathetic tone are dangerous, so induce late, keep the patient breathing spontaneously until ready, and keep the heart rate up.
- **Repair:** CPB with a cannulation/perfusion plan based on dissection anatomy. Arch work may require circulatory arrest, often with selective antegrade cerebral perfusion and individualised moderate/deep hypothermia; **not every Type A repair requires deep arrest**. For arch-arrest terminology, deep is about 14.1–20°C and moderate 20.1–28°C. Monitor brain/body temperatures and rewarm carefully without hyperthermia; adult blood-gas strategy follows the perfusion protocol.
- **Haemostasis**: massive transfusion, cell salvage, tranexamic acid and viscoelastic testing.

## Postop

ICU, with neurological checks, renal and mesenteric surveillance, bleeding, and delirium management.

## Apply the findings

At surgery separate true-lumen perfusion from arterial line numbers. With an imaging-guided cannulation strategy, follow bilateral cerebral/arterial signals and haemodynamics during cooling and antegrade perfusion when needed. A unilateral pressure fall, cerebral oximetry change or high circuit pressure can warn of malperfusion. Plan for acute AR, coronary ostial compromise and bleeding, and document neurological and visceral perfusion after repair. A root procedure and arch strategy depend on the tear and extent.

**Sources:** [ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9860464/); [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic/thoracoabdominal guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/). · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic/thoracoabdominal guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41448425/) · [ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9860464/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises type A dissection as a surgical emergency
- Describes the risks: tamponade, aortic regurgitation, malperfusion
- Anti-impulse therapy with beta-blocker first, but caution with tamponade
- Describes monitoring including bilateral arterial lines, TOE and NIRS
- Safe induction with surgical team ready
- Describes CPB, circulatory arrest and cerebral protection
- Plans for massive bleeding and coagulopathy
- ICU care and neurological monitoring

items.title: 12. Type B aortic dissection with malperfusion: TEVAR
items.q: A 60-year-old man with an acute type B aortic dissection develops new renal and leg malperfusion and is listed for urgent TEVAR. Outline the indications for intervention and the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Preop

### Indications and timing

- **Uncomplicated type B:** medical management with imaging, analgesia and impulse control; reassess for progression and plan follow-up.
- **Complicated type B:** rupture, refractory pain or hypertension, rapid expansion, **end-organ malperfusion** or threatened organ or limb; generally urgent intervention, commonly **TEVAR** where anatomy allows.
- Selected uncomplicated but high-risk patients may have delayed or subacute TEVAR after multidisciplinary review; not every type B is rushed to a stent.

### Malperfusion mechanisms

- **Static obstruction:** the flap extends into a branch and fixes a stenosis or occlusion.
- **Dynamic obstruction:** high false-lumen pressure compresses the true lumen or covers a branch origin. TEVAR sealing of the proximal entry tear can depressurise the false lumen and relieve dynamic malperfusion.
- Persistent static obstruction may need branch stenting or fenestration, so **recheck renal, bowel and leg perfusion** after a successful-looking stent.

### Anti-impulse therapy (before and during)

- Aortic wall stress depends on the speed of LV ejection (dP/dt) as well as peak pressure: **titrated IV beta-blockade first** (esmolol, or labetalol), early analgesia, then a vasodilator (nicardipine, clevidipine, carefully titrated nitroprusside) only if pressure remains high. Vasodilating before rate control can provoke reflex tachycardia.
- Targets from the 2022 ACC/AHA guideline: SBP below 120 mmHg or the lowest pressure preserving organ perfusion, HR 60 to 80. **With critical malperfusion, fixed targets must not worsen perfusion**; individualise with the aortic team.
- If the patient becomes hypotensive, look for rupture, tamponade, severe AR or malperfusion; do not follow a hypertension algorithm in shock.

## Intraop

### Anaesthesia for TEVAR

- Confirm the planned left subclavian coverage (revascularisation is recommended if coverage would obstruct antegrade flow, to reduce spinal cord ischaemia), access anatomy, rupture and malperfusion status, lumbar drain need, heparin policy and landing zone.
- Arterial access and monitoring before induction; vasopressor and vasodilator infusions ready; haemodynamically stable induction.
- Avoid uncontrolled hypertension (propagation) and prolonged hypotension (spinal, renal, cerebral malperfusion). Deployment may need transient reduced pulsatility; restore MAP promptly afterwards.
- Heparin is an individualised decision in active bleeding, brain injury or expanding haematoma, not an automatic dose.
- Check pulses, urine output and metabolic status; renal protection as for contrast.

### Complications to anticipate

Access rupture, retrograde type A dissection, new entry tear, stroke, **spinal cord injury**, left arm ischaemia or posterior-circulation stroke after subclavian coverage, renal and visceral malperfusion, contrast AKI and persistent false-lumen pressurisation.

## Postop

Serial neurovascular observations, sustained appropriate BP, renal and lactate surveillance and follow-up imaging.

**Sources:** [ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9860464/) · [ESVS 2026 descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic guideline](https://esvs.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/ESVS-2026-DTA-GL_compressed.pdf) · Set 14 notes, sections 6.3 to 6.5

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Distinguishes complicated from uncomplicated type B and gives indications for TEVAR
- Explains static versus dynamic malperfusion and why TEVAR can help
- Anti-impulse therapy: beta-blocker first, then vasodilator, with individualised targets
- Does not follow a hypertension algorithm in shock
- TEVAR anaesthesia: arterial access, stable induction, avoid hypertension and hypotension, heparin decision
- Anticipates spinal cord, stroke, retrograde type A, access and renal complications
- Plans postoperative neurovascular, renal and imaging surveillance

items.title: 13. Ruptured AAA: perioperative considerations and permissive hypotension
items.q: A 72-year-old man presents with a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, with a systolic blood pressure of 80 mmHg. Outline the perioperative considerations, including the role of endovascular repair and permissive hypotension.
items.a:
## Principles

Ruptured AAA is a time-critical haemorrhagic emergency with high mortality. Prioritise rapid haemorrhage control, oxygen delivery, warming and haemostasis. Obtain **rapid CTA for diagnosis/anatomic planning in most patients who can reach scanning without unacceptable delay**, with resuscitation during transfer; a crashing patient needs immediate control rather than a mandatory scan. Instability alone does not automatically rule out CTA or EVAR. Involve the vascular/endovascular, anaesthetic, blood-bank and critical-care teams early.

## Preop

### Resuscitation and permissive hypotension

- Two large-bore IV lines, **arterial line** (before induction if it does not delay), rapid infuser, warmed fluids, cell salvage.
- **Permissive hypotension**: accept a systolic pressure of about **70 to 90 mmHg** (a mentating patient) to avoid disrupting the clot; avoid large crystalloid volumes that cause dilution, hypertension and coagulopathy. Individualise to consciousness, coronary/cerebral perfusion and duration; avoid prolonged profound hypotension, especially in older patients.
- **Major haemorrhage protocol**, balanced component resuscitation followed by laboratory/viscoelastic-directed therapy, calcium, warming and early fibrinogen replacement when deficient. TXA is **not established routine treatment for rAAA**; use only under the relevant local protocol/individual risk–benefit decision rather than extrapolating trauma evidence automatically.

## Intraop

### Anaesthetic technique

- **Prepare, drape and have the surgeon scrubbed before induction** because induction removes sympathetic tone and may cause collapse.
- **Local anaesthesia** for femoral access and early balloon placement (associated with lower mortality in observational rEVAR data, which do not prove causation) with conversion to GA as needed; **GA** if needed for agitation or open repair, with titrated induction (ketamine or etomidate at reduced doses, rocuronium), vasopressors and **RSI**.
- **Resuscitative balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA)** or supracoeliac clamp can be used for the collapsing patient (cutting renal and visceral flow, so keep inflation short).

### Endovascular versus open repair

Endovascular repair (**REVAR**) suits suitable anatomy: lower physiological insult, less blood loss, and local anaesthesia is possible. **IMPROVE** compared an **endovascular-first strategy if anatomically feasible** with open repair, not EVAR for every patient: 30-day mortality **35.4% versus 37.4%**, OR 0.92 (95% CI 0.66–1.28), P=0.62. It did not demonstrate a significant early survival benefit. Open repair is used when anatomy or available expertise/resources preclude timely EVAR, or when it provides the fastest appropriate control; shock alone does not mandate open repair.

## Postop

Check **abdominal compartment syndrome** (bladder pressure), renal injury, colonic ischaemia, limb ischaemia, hypothermia and coagulopathy; ICU care.

## Apply the findings

At the decision point distinguish a patient who can reach immediate planning CT without an unsafe delay from one who needs urgent proximal control. Arrange a direct-to-hybrid pathway and equipment before transfer whenever possible. Avoid serial investigations that do not change management. If preserving spontaneous ventilation and sympathetic tone is useful for local EVAR, agree how pain, movement, escalating shock or loss of airway access will trigger conversion.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/); [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for endovascular repair of ruptured AAA (2022;22:208–215)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35614906/); [IMPROVE primary 30-day strategy trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24418950/). · [ANZCA Blue Book 2025, cardiac and vascular viscoelastic algorithm and GLP-1 chapter](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [ANZCA Blue Book catalogue, including 2023 radiation and aortic balloon occlusion chapters](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises ruptured AAA mortality and the need for rapid control
- Describes access, arterial line, rapid infuser and cell salvage
- Defines permissive hypotension with a target and rationale
- Uses major haemorrhage protocol, calcium/warming and targeted coagulation correction; does not assume routine TXA efficacy in rAAA
- Prepares and has the surgeon scrubbed before induction
- Compares local and general anaesthesia
- Mentions REBOA with its limits
- Compares endovascular and open repair
- Plans for abdominal compartment syndrome and ICU

items.title: 14. Carotid endarterectomy versus stenting
items.q: Compare carotid endarterectomy with carotid artery stenting, and outline the perioperative considerations for stenting.
items.a:
## Comparison

| | **CEA** | **Carotid stenting (CAS)** |
|---|---|---|
| Technique | Open surgery, neck incision | Endovascular via femoral (or radial) access with an **embolic protection device** |
| Perioperative **stroke** | Lower | Higher (particularly in older patients) |
| **MI** | Higher | Lower |
| **Cranial nerve injury, neck haematoma** | Characteristic open-neck risks | Avoids open-neck dissection risks with transfemoral CAS, but adds access/antiplatelet bleeding risks; TCAR has a neck incision |
| Suited to | Most suitable recently symptomatic patients; asymptomatic intervention requires selective assessment alongside intensive medical therapy | High-risk necks (previous radiotherapy or surgery, high bifurcation), restenosis, surgically inaccessible lesions, some younger patients |
| Late results | Durable | Similar long-term stroke risk in trials (CREST) with higher early stroke at older ages |

## Preop

### Anaesthetic considerations for stenting

- **Local anaesthesia with light sedation** is usual (allows neurological assessment), GA for agitated patients or complex anatomy.
- **Antiplatelets**: dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel) before and for at least one month after; **heparin** during the procedure (ACT 250 to 300 seconds); the patient is at risk of bleeding (access site) and of stent thrombosis if stopped.
## Intraop

- **Haemodynamic instability**: balloon inflation and stent deployment stimulate the **carotid sinus**, causing **bradycardia, asystole and hypotension** (treat with atropine or glycopyrrolate given before dilatation, and vasopressors; avoid hypertension).
- **Embolic stroke or hyperperfusion**: neuro-checks, blood pressure control after the procedure (SBP below about 140 to 160), and urgent imaging for deficits.
- **Contrast and radiation**: renal protection, allergy history, shielding.
## Postop

- Monitoring in HDU or recovery for BP, bradycardia and neurology.

## Current asymptomatic evidence: CREST-2

Two **separate parallel trials**, not a direct CAS-versus-CEA comparison, studied high-grade asymptomatic stenosis with intensive medical management (IMM). At four years, the primary composite (stroke/death through day 44, then ipsilateral ischaemic stroke) was **2.8% stenting+IMM versus 6.0% IMM** (P=0.02), and **3.7% CEA+IMM versus 5.3% IMM** (P=0.24). Thus stenting showed benefit in its trial; CEA’s difference was not statistically significant. Do not infer that CAS beat CEA directly, extrapolate to all symptomatic lesions, or automatically treat every asymptomatic stenosis. Consider anatomy, procedural risk, life expectancy, expertise and patient preference; all require intensive risk-factor therapy. Older-age stroke comparisons mainly concern **transfemoral CAS**, not automatic extrapolation to TCAR.

## Apply the findings

For symptomatic disease explain when prompt intervention matters and how anatomy, ipsilateral symptoms, recent infarct, previous neck surgery and age alter the CEA/CAS decision. During stenting the dominant tolerance issues include lying flat, embolism and carotid sinus-mediated bradycardia and hypotension. Confirm antiplatelet readiness and a plan to detect and treat a new neurological deficit before puncture.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid/vertebral disease guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374); [CREST-2 primary report: intensive medical management with/without revascularisation](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41269206/); [GALA primary randomised trial (2008)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19041130/).

## Self-marking checklist

- Compares stroke, MI, cranial nerve and haematoma risks
- Identifies patients for stenting
- Local anaesthesia with sedation, or GA
- DAPT and heparin management
- Carotid sinus reflex with atropine and vasopressor plan
- Stroke and hyperperfusion monitoring
- Contrast, radiation and postoperative care

items.title: 15. New neurological deficit during carotid endarterectomy
items.q: During an awake carotid endarterectomy the patient develops speech arrest and contralateral weakness immediately after the clamp is applied. Outline your assessment and management, and explain how your response would differ for a deficit appearing at declamping or after emergence.
items.a:
## Preop

- Document the baseline neurological state and the agreed perfusion pressure target, the monitoring plan (awake examination or EEG/SSEP/NIRS/TCD), the shunt policy and who calls clamp events.

## Intraop

### Immediate recognition and action

- **Speech arrest, altered consciousness or contralateral weakness on clamping** means inadequate collateral flow until proven otherwise.
- Tell the surgeon at once. Restore the agreed cerebral perfusion pressure (raise MAP with a vasopressor), confirm oxygenation, normocapnia and Hb, and discuss **clamp release or shunting**.
- An awake patient's examination is the monitor, so keep talking to them and repeat the neurological assessment.

### Differentiate the mechanism

- **At clamp application:** low-flow ischaemia (collateral failure); treated by perfusion pressure, release or shunt.
- **During plaque manipulation, shunt placement or declamping:** consider **embolisation, dissection or thrombosis** instead. Perfusion pressure alone will not fix an embolus; direct surgical evaluation is needed.
- **Under general anaesthesia:** an abrupt, concordant EEG/SSEP/NIRS/TCD change warrants a rapid equipment and drug check, restoration of oxygenation, CO₂, Hb and haemodynamics, then surgical evaluation. No monitor excludes all stroke.

### Systematic follow-up

- Record the time and probable mechanism and activate the local stroke/vascular pathway.
- Coordinate urgent imaging, re-exploration or endovascular options according to whether there is carotid occlusion, intracranial vessel occlusion, haemorrhage or another cause.
- **Recent surgery and anticoagulation make systemic thrombolysis hazardous; it is never an automatic response.** Selected large-vessel occlusions may still be treated with thrombectomy.
- Continue neurological monitoring after emergence even if signals recover.

## Postop

A new focal deficit may reflect carotid thrombosis, distal embolus, intracranial haemorrhage or hyperperfusion. Check last-known-normal time, glucose and oxygenation, involve vascular and stroke teams early and arrange urgent examination and imaging. Post-endarterectomy hyperperfusion and haemorrhage have their own BP strategy, set with the vascular and stroke teams rather than by a fixed number.

**Sources:** [AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke guideline 2026](https://doi.org/10.1161/STR.0000000000000513) · [CREST-2 primary report](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2508800) · Set 14 notes, sections 8.6 and 8.8

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Recognises collateral failure at clamping and alerts the surgeon at once
- Restores cerebral perfusion pressure and considers release or shunt
- Distinguishes low-flow ischaemia from embolism, dissection or thrombosis
- Describes the general-anaesthesia monitoring response (EEG, SSEP, NIRS, TCD) and its limits
- Activates the stroke pathway and arranges imaging or re-exploration
- States that thrombolysis is not automatic after recent surgery
- Plans for the deficit seen on emergence and for hyperperfusion

items.title: 16. Femoropopliteal bypass in an insulin-treated diabetic with a foot ulcer
items.q: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on insulin, an HbA1c of 78 mmol/mol and a diabetic foot ulcer presents for femoropopliteal bypass. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Risks

Diabetes is a marker of **widespread vascular disease** with silent ischaemia, **autonomic neuropathy** (labile BP, gastroparesis, silent MI), **CKD**, **infection**, poor wound healing, and **stroke**. Poor control increases infection and mortality.

## Preop

- **Assess control**: HbA1c, glucose chart, renal function, ECG, and neuropathy. HbA1c 78 mmol/mol indicates poor control and merits optimisation/specialist input; it is not an automatic cancellation threshold. Balance any elective delay against limb loss/infection and avoid delaying urgent revascularisation merely to lower HbA1c.
- **Cardiac risk** assessment as for vascular surgery (RCRI includes insulin-treated diabetes).
- **Medication plan**: omit metformin on the day (or with AKI), **stop SGLT2 inhibitors three to four days before** (euglycaemic ketoacidosis), continue basal insulin at a reduced dose (about 75 to 80%), omit meal-linked boluses while fasting but retain a prescribed correction/infusion plan, and place first on the list.
- Treat infection and revascularise urgently if limb-threatening.
- If taking **GLP-1/GIP agonists**, use the current ANZCA-led pathway: 2025 consensus generally continues treatment with a **24-hour clear-fluid diet followed by standard fasting**; if preparation is incomplete, assess gastric contents/aspiration risk or use a full-stomach strategy. Do not rely on absence of GI symptoms alone. [Consensus](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0310057X251355288).

## Intraop

- Check **glucose hourly**; target **5–10 mmol/L under ADS–ANZCA guidance**, individualised to hypoglycaemia risk; other national protocols use 6–10 (occasionally up to 12); use a variable-rate insulin infusion with dextrose if fasting more than one missed meal.
- Choose a technique that suits (regional preserves intake and reduces PONV but beware of neuropathy and anticoagulation), single-dose dexamethasone may still be appropriate for PONV with a glucose-monitoring/treatment plan.
- Treat hypotension, avoid hypoglycaemia.

## Postop

- Monitor glucose, transition insulin safely and restart each oral drug according to intake, renal function and haemodynamic stability; restart SGLT2 inhibitors only when eating/drinking adequately, clinically stable and without ketosis, and check renal function; treat PONV.
- **Analgesia** with caution (NSAIDs).
- Foot care, pressure areas, VTE prophylaxis, and referral to the diabetes team and primary care for long-term control.

## Apply the findings

If the patient has taken an SGLT2 inhibitor recently, normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis. Check blood ketones and acid–base status in a fasting, unwell or urgently operated patient, and use the local perioperative pathway for insulin/dextrose and serial monitoring. Agree the time cost of metabolic stabilisation against infection and tissue loss. Continue enough basal insulin to prevent ketosis and make an explicit postoperative restart plan.
