**Sources:** [ADS–ANZCA perioperative diabetes guideline (2022)](https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/guideline/ads-anzca-perioperative-diabetes-and-hyperglycaemia-guidelines-adults-november-2022/); [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance: 2026 reaffirmation of 2024 recommendations](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017). · [ADS/ANZCA/GESA/NACOS peri-procedural GLP-1 guidance](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12420935/) · [2024 ACC/AHA multisociety lower-extremity PAD guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2025, cardiac and vascular viscoelastic algorithm and GLP-1 chapter](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305)

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies diabetic risks: silent ischaemia, autonomic neuropathy, CKD, infection
- Assesses control with HbA1c and renal function
- Considers timing against limb-threatening ischaemia
- Gives a medication plan: metformin, SGLT2 inhibitor, insulin
- Sets glucose targets and monitoring
- Describes insulin infusion use
- Postoperative glucose, analgesia and renal care
- Cardiac risk assessment

items.title: 17. Lower limb bypass in stage 4 CKD
items.q: A 70-year-old patient with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22 mL/min) is scheduled for lower limb bypass surgery. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Preop

- **Cause and stage**: baseline creatinine and eGFR, urine output, whether dialysis is planned, and **complications**: hypertension, anaemia (Hb), electrolytes (K, Ca, phosphate, acidosis), fluid status, and **cardiovascular disease** (CKD is a strong cardiac risk factor).
- **Medications**: stop NSAIDs and nephrotoxins, review ACE inhibitors/ARBs and diuretics, adjust renally cleared drugs, and avoid contrast where possible.
- **Dialysis patients**: coordinate dialysis, often the day before, assessing volume, K and dialysis anticoagulation; stage 4 CKD alone is not an indication to start dialysis, with fistula arm protected and no BP cuff or cannulation.
- **Bloods**: potassium interpreted with trend, ECG, acidosis, urgency and local policy; no single universal safe cancellation cutoff, Hb, coagulation, platelets (uraemic platelet dysfunction), and ECG.

## Intraop

- **Technique**: regional anaesthesia is attractive but check coagulation, uraemic platelet function and heparin timing; GA with drugs not dependent on renal elimination.
- **Drug choices:** propofol, remifentanil and cisatracurium are useful. Avoid pethidine and usually morphine in advanced CKD; reduce other renally cleared analgesics. Sugammadex is **not recommended by product information in CrCl <30 mL/min**; any specialist off-label use requires explicit reasoning and quantitative neuromuscular monitoring. Avoid suxamethonium with clinically significant hyperkalaemia and avoid NSAIDs.
- **Fluids**: balanced crystalloids; avoid large volume loading; balanced crystalloids are often suitable despite their small potassium content; assess active severe hyperkalaemia individually and treat it promptly. Large saline loads may worsen hyperchloraemic acidosis.
- **Haemodynamics**: maintain renal perfusion pressure, avoid hypotension, monitor with an arterial line, and track urine output, potassium and acid-base.

## Postop

- Monitor creatinine, urine output, K and fluid balance; avoid nephrotoxins; analgesia with fentanyl, oxycodone (reduced dose), paracetamol and regional blocks.
- **Dialysis** timing, HDU care, and a plan for renal replacement if acute deterioration.

## Apply the findings

Use the operation to anticipate patient-specific renal insults: contrast in hybrid cases, brief occult hypoperfusion during bleeding, nephrotoxic exposure and venous congestion. Trend potassium and acid–base status after reperfusion. Because CKD changes drug exposure and platelet function, plan opioid selection and haemostasis rather than rely on a creatinine alone. Involve nephrology if there is refractory hyperkalaemia, acidaemia, pulmonary oedema or a need to plan perioperative dialysis. Recheck renal replacement access and avoid compressing it.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury (2020)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33456926/); [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766). · [2024 ACC/AHA multisociety lower-extremity PAD guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013)

## Self-marking checklist

- Assesses stage, cause and complications of CKD
- Reviews medications and nephrotoxins
- Manages dialysis timing and fistula protection
- Checks potassium, Hb, acid-base and platelet function
- Chooses renally safe drugs and avoids morphine and NSAIDs
- Fluid strategy and renal perfusion pressure
- Cardiac risk
- Postoperative monitoring and analgesia

items.title: 18. Acute limb ischaemia: urgency, anaesthesia and reperfusion
items.q: A patient with sudden leg pain has new foot weakness and absent arterial Doppler signals. Outline how you determine urgency, plan anaesthesia for revascularisation and manage the effects of reperfusion.
items.a:
## Preop

### Determine viability and urgency

Call vascular surgery immediately. Establish onset, prior claudication, AF, recent intervention and bleeding or dissection risk. Examine both legs for temperature, colour, refill, sensation, motor function and arterial and venous Doppler signals. A viable Rutherford I limb has no neurological deficit. A IIa limb has limited sensory change and no weakness. With new motor weakness and absent arterial but retained venous Doppler, consider Rutherford IIb and arrange immediate revascularisation. Profound anaesthesia, paralysis and loss of both signals suggest class III with irreversible injury. Reperfusion of a nonviable limb can precipitate systemic collapse. Discuss amputation instead when appropriate.

Give systemic unfractionated heparin on diagnosis unless contraindicated by bleeding, major trauma, associated aortic dissection or another overriding risk. Provide analgesia, IV access, ECG, full blood count, coagulation, renal function, potassium, gas and crossmatch as appropriate. Imaging should clarify the anatomy without delaying rescue of a threatened limb. Discuss embolic versus in-situ thrombosis, open embolectomy/bypass or endovascular treatment, time to flow restoration and possible fasciotomy.

## Intraop

### Anaesthesia and reperfusion

Choose a technique that gives rapid access, immobility and adequate analgesia while maintaining perfusion. Local anaesthesia and careful sedation may suit a short intervention in a cooperative patient. GA may be needed for extensive, urgent or painful surgery or unstable physiology. Check antithrombotics and the need for an interpretable limb examination before choosing a regional technique. With substantial ischaemia, establish invasive pressure monitoring, reliable access and immediate vasopressor, electrolyte and resuscitation capability.

Before restoring flow, tell the team when release is expected and check ECG, potassium, gas, volume status and anticipated blood loss. Reperfusion may cause vasodilation, potassium and acid washout, arrhythmia and myoglobin release. Treat severe hyperkalaemia promptly with cardiac membrane stabilisation if indicated, intracellular shift and a plan for removal. Use reassessed fluids and vasopressors to restore organ perfusion, accounting for heart failure and renal reserve.

## Postop

### Surveillance

Document signals and repeat motor/sensory examination. Escalate escalating pain, pain on passive stretch or tense swelling as possible compartment syndrome. A palpable pulse does not exclude it. Discuss urgent fasciotomy when indicated. Trend potassium, gas, CK, creatinine and urine output. Individualise fluids to renal perfusion and congestion and seek renal support for refractory biochemical or volume indications. Investigate embolic sources and agree antithrombotic, graft and wound plans.

**Sources:** [2024 ACC/AHA multisociety lower-extremity PAD guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013) · [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization surgery (2015;15:225–230)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482)

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Uses neurological findings and Doppler to classify urgency
- Escalates IIb rapidly and avoids delay for unnecessary imaging
- Uses heparin when safe and plans appropriate procedural technique
- Anticipates reperfusion hypotension, hyperkalaemia and rhabdomyolysis
- Recognises compartment syndrome and considers fasciotomy
- Plans postoperative limb, renal and embolic surveillance

items.title: 19. Urgent above-knee amputation in a diabetic with infected gangrene
items.q: A patient with diabetes and infected gangrene requires urgent above-knee amputation. Discuss how you would prepare for the operation, choose the anaesthetic and monitor for postoperative complications.
items.a:
## Preop

### Patient factors

Patients are old and frail, with **IHD, diabetes, CKD, COPD**, infection or sepsis, anaemia and poor nutrition; **perioperative mortality is high** (about 10% at 30 days). Many have severe **rest pain** and have been taking opioids. Surgery may be urgent, with sepsis or gangrene.

- **Before induction:** optimise diabetes, anaemia and renal function as time allows; antibiotics; continue aspirin and statin; assess capacity and goals.

## Intraop

### Anaesthetic plan

- **Technique:** **spinal anaesthesia** or a selected regional plan may avoid GA. **Sciatic plus femoral block alone may not cover above-knee amputation**: assess obturator, lateral/posterior femoral cutaneous and proximal incision/tourniquet supply, supplementation and conversion. A deep lumbar plexus block also carries neuraxial-like bleeding precautions in a frail patient; **GA** if neuraxial is contraindicated (anticoagulation, sepsis, patient preference). Manage hypotension with vasopressors.
- **Monitoring:** arterial line for high-risk patients, glucose monitoring, temperature.

### Pain

Pain types are **residual limb (stump) pain** and **phantom limb pain** (reported prevalence varies widely by population, timing and definition), and **phantom sensation** (not necessarily painful). Residual and phantom pain can coexist but have different differential diagnoses; chronic pain involves peripheral, spinal and cortical mechanisms.

- **Pre-emptive analgesia:** treat rest pain preoperatively with a **regional catheter** (epidural or perineural) and multimodal drugs; the evidence that a perioperative epidural reduces chronic pain is inconsistent.
- **Intraoperative:** the surgeon places a **perineural (sciatic) catheter** with local anaesthetic infusion, to support acute opioid-sparing analgesia; duration follows the service protocol. **Reliable prevention of chronic phantom pain has not been established**.
- **Multimodal:** paracetamol, selected regional techniques and titrated opioids adjusted for renal function/tolerance. Ketamine can be considered for difficult acute pain but is not proven routine chronic-pain prevention. Do not automatically start gabapentinoids prophylactically: renal accumulation, sedation, delirium and respiratory harm matter. Avoid NSAIDs when renal/cardiovascular risk outweighs benefit.
- **Phantom pain treatment:** gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants, **mirror therapy**, graded motor imagery, and referral to a pain service.

## Postop

Early mobilisation and rehabilitation, wound care, VTE prophylaxis, delirium prevention, and goals-of-care discussion.

**Current pain teaching:** investigate worsening residual-limb pain for infection/ischaemia, haematoma, neuroma, bone/prosthetic problems or referred pain before labelling it phantom pain. Explain uncertainty about preventive drugs/blocks; involve pain and rehabilitation teams early. For established neuropathic pain use individual trials of suitable neuropathic medicines plus mirror/graded motor imagery and psychological/physical rehabilitation. Specialist neuroma surgery, targeted muscle reinnervation or neuromodulation are selected options, not routine prophylaxis for every amputee.

## Apply the findings

Sepsis and critical ischaemia change timing and haemodynamics. Agree whether amputation is urgent source control and address shock, metabolic disturbance, recent dialysis if relevant and antithrombotic exposure. Choose the technique around perfusion, aspiration risk, patient cooperation and the planned incision. Record deficits and check the stump for haematoma, infection, ischaemia or surgical bleeding before interpreting new pain as phantom.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Pain after lower limb amputation (2026;26:121–129)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41727978/); [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766). · [2024 ACC/AHA multisociety lower-extremity PAD guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises frailty, comorbidity and high mortality
- Chooses spinal or nerve block versus GA with reasons
- Describes monitoring and perioperative optimisation
- Identifies stump pain, phantom pain and phantom sensation
- Perineural catheter and regional analgesia
- Multimodal analgesia with renal precautions
- Treatments for phantom pain: gabapentinoids, ketamine, mirror therapy
- Rehabilitation and follow-up
- Balances urgent infection source control, haemodynamics and postoperative wound surveillance

items.title: 20. Safe anaesthesia in the interventional radiology suite
items.q: Discuss the requirements for the safe provision of anaesthesia in the interventional radiology suite and the advantages of interventional procedures compared with open surgery.
items.a:
## Advantages of image-guided procedures

- **Less physiological stress** and tissue trauma, smaller incisions, **less blood loss**, and lower perioperative cardiac and pulmonary morbidity.
- Often possible under **local anaesthesia or sedation**, shorter admission and faster recovery.
- Suitable for **older or high-risk patients** and for some emergencies (embolisation for bleeding, REBOA, endovascular repair).
- Disadvantages: radiation and **contrast** exposure, procedure-dependent durability and reintervention/surveillance requirements (e.g. endoleak or restenosis), rather than universally inferior durability, remote location, and the possibility of conversion to open surgery.

## Preop

### Requirements for safe anaesthesia (equivalent to the main theatre)

- **Standards:** ANZCA monitoring standards, anaesthesia machine with gas supply, scavenging, suction, full resuscitation equipment (defibrillator, airway equipment, drugs), and a **recovery area** with trained staff.
- **Staff:** an anaesthetist with a **trained assistant**, and a team that understands the procedure and who calls for help.
- **Environment:** remote location with limited access, cold room, low light, **radiation protection** (lead apron, thyroid shield, glasses, distance and shielding, dosimeter badge), CT safety; MRI requires a dedicated MR-safe/conditional environment and equipment, not an ordinary anaesthetic machine in the magnet room.
- **Preparation:** preoperative assessment as for any anaesthetic, consent, fasting, **allergy and renal function check**, medication plan (antiplatelets, anticoagulants, metformin, SGLT2 inhibitor), IV access, and plan for blood.
## Intraop

- **Contrast and anticoagulation:** prepare for contrast reaction (anaphylaxis) and AKI; monitor heparin with ACT.
- **Emergency plans:** conversion to open surgery, bleeding, perforation and anaphylaxis; **surgical and blood bank support** available.
- **Communication** between radiologist, anaesthetist and nursing staff, and a clear plan for transfer to a higher level of care.

## Postop

Use a staffed recovery area with standard monitoring and an explicit handover of procedure, access-site/limb checks, neurological findings, contrast/antithrombotic doses and escalation triggers. Plan renal surveillance, analgesia and safe ward/HDU transfer according to patient and intervention.

## Apply the findings

Apply ANZCA PS55 and PG09 to the actual room before accepting the case. Confirm oxygen, suction, capnography, resuscitation and rescue airway equipment, safe access through drapes, sufficient trained staff and a monitored recovery route. Agree how to stop the procedure and move the gantry in an emergency. Separate haemorrhage, contrast reaction and oversedation contingency plans. During screening, distance and shielding protect staff only if patient monitoring and immediate access can still be maintained.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book archive (2025 latest complete edition; 2023 and 2017 relevant chapters)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29); [ANZAAG/ANZCA perioperative anaphylaxis guideline (2022)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/professional-documents/endorsed-guidelines/anaphylaxis-guideline-2022.pdf). · [ANZCA professional documents, PS55 and PG09](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents) · [ANZCA Blue Book catalogue, including 2023 radiation and aortic balloon occlusion chapters](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Lists advantages: reduced stress, less blood loss, local anaesthesia, shorter stay
- Lists disadvantages: radiation, contrast, durability, conversion
- Requires standard monitoring, machine, suction, resuscitation equipment and recovery
- Trained assistant and skilled team
- Describes radiation protection
- Preoperative assessment, allergy, renal function and medications
- Plans for contrast reaction, bleeding and conversion
- Communication and surgical back-up

items.title: 21. Contrast reaction in the interventional radiology suite
items.q: A patient develops hypotension, bronchospasm and a rash within minutes of intravenous contrast in the interventional radiology suite. Outline your immediate management and subsequent investigation.
items.a:
## Recognition

**Anaphylaxis** (IgE-mediated or non-IgE) presents with hypotension, bronchospasm, rash, angioedema, tachycardia and cardiovascular collapse. Under anaesthesia the only signs may be hypotension, high airway pressures and loss of end-tidal CO2.

## Immediate management

- **1.** **Stop the contrast**, call for help, and note the time. Maintain the airway, give **100% oxygen**, lie flat/raise legs if feasible and avoid abrupt sitting/standing; stop other potential triggers.
- **2.** **Adrenaline:** for life-threatening perioperative anaphylaxis with established IV access and experienced monitored care, **50–100 micrograms IV**, repeated/titrated every 1–2 min; moderate reactions may start at 10–20 micrograms. Use clearly labelled concentrations (e.g. **100 micrograms/mL** for bolus preparation), avoiding ratio-only labels. If IV expertise/access is unavailable, give **500 micrograms IM** into the lateral thigh (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL), repeated per protocol. Start an adrenaline infusion for persistent shock; distinguish arrest dosing.
- **3.** **Fluids**: 20 mL/kg crystalloid boluses (large volume loss).
- **4.** **Bronchospasm**: salbutamol; consider ketamine or volatile anaesthetic if ventilated.
- **5.** **Cardiac arrest**: CPR with adrenaline.
- **6.** **Refractory reaction:** reassess adrenaline delivery, fluids, diagnosis and airway; expert infusion/vasopressor escalation, glucagon for relevant beta-blockade. Antihistamines treat skin symptoms after stabilisation; corticosteroids are not routine life-saving acute treatment and do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions.
- **7.** Transfer to ICU/HDU for monitoring (**biphasic reaction**).

## Investigation

- **ANZAAG/ANZCA tryptase:** as soon as feasible after initial resuscitation, **1 hour**, **4 hours**, and a **baseline after 24 hours** (or later follow-up). Sampling must not delay treatment; a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis.
- Refer to an **anaphylaxis/allergy clinic** for skin tests and exclusion of other agents (latex, antibiotics, chlorhexidine).
- Document, report to the **ANZAAG/ADR system**, inform the patient and add an allergy alert.

## Prevention

Take an allergy history; prior contrast reaction needs alternate contrast, premedication is not reliably effective; low-osmolar or iso-osmolar non-ionic contrast has fewer reactions; have drugs ready in the radiology suite.

## Apply the findings

Airway pressure may rise before cutaneous signs appear. Under drapes, unexplained collapse temporally related to several exposures warrants anaphylaxis treatment while checking bleeding, vessel perforation, oversedation and embolic events in parallel. Document all drug, contrast and antiseptic exposures with exact times and treatment response. Referral should identify the specific contrast agent and suspected cofactors rather than permanently labelling all iodinated agents as contraindicated.

**Sources:** [ANZAAG/ANZCA perioperative anaphylaxis guideline (2022)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/professional-documents/endorsed-guidelines/anaphylaxis-guideline-2022.pdf). · [ESUR 2026 contrast guidelines](https://www.esur.org/esur-guidelines-2026/) · [ANZAAG/ANZCA perioperative anaphylaxis guideline (2022)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/professional-documents/endorsed-guidelines/anaphylaxis-guideline-2022.pdf)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises anaphylaxis, including under anaesthesia
- Stops the trigger, calls for help, oxygen
- Adrenaline with correct dose and route
- Fluids, bronchospasm treatment, and second-line drugs
- CPR if arrest
- Tryptase timing and allergy referral
- Documentation and reporting
- Prevention including allergy history and prior reactions

items.title: 22. REBOA and radiation protection
items.q: Describe resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA), its physiological effects and the anaesthetic implications, and outline how you would protect yourself from radiation during fluoroscopic procedures.
items.a:
## REBOA

A balloon catheter is placed through the **femoral artery** (Seldinger technique) and inflated in the aorta to control bleeding below the balloon and support **cardiac and cerebral perfusion**.

- **Zone I** (descending thoracic aorta between the left subclavian and the coeliac): for intra-abdominal, pelvic or junctional haemorrhage. **Zone III** (infrarenal aorta) for pelvic haemorrhage. **Zone II** (visceral segment) is avoided.
- **Physiological effects** resemble a **thoracic cross-clamp**: marked rise in proximal MAP and afterload, ischaemia below the balloon (renal, hepatic, mesenteric, spinal cord, limbs), and on deflation **reperfusion** with hypotension, acidosis, hyperkalaemia and lactate.

## Anaesthetic implications

- **Limit inflation time** (keep complete zone I occlusion **as short as possible, generally aiming under 30 minutes**; no duration is guaranteed safe and 60 minutes must not be taught as a routine acceptable target) and deflate **slowly** with resuscitation (volume, blood, vasopressors) in advance.
- **Monitoring**: right radial arterial line (for proximal pressure) and femoral line, ABG, lactate, potassium, urine output, and temperature.
- Prepare for **massive transfusion**, calcium, coagulation management, and ICU care; risks include limb ischaemia, vessel injury at access, and spinal cord and renal injury.

## Radiation protection

Follow **time, distance and shielding**:
- **Minimise exposure time**; stand as far as possible (dose falls with the **square of the distance**) and behind a **mobile lead screen**.
- Wear a **lead apron** (0.35 to 0.5 mm lead equivalent), **thyroid collar** and **lead glasses**; use a ceiling-mounted shield.
- Wear dosimetry in the location/number required by the radiation-safety programme; two badges (collar outside and trunk under apron) may be specified, but are not universal.
- Provide confidential occupational/radiation-safety advice for pregnant staff and follow jurisdictional monitoring/workplace policy; do not assume universal mandatory disclosure or exclusion from fluoroscopy.
- Communicate with the radiologist, and leave the room for non-essential exposures.

**Evidence and selection:** REBOA is a temporary bridge to immediate definitive haemorrhage control, not a replacement for it. The **UK-REBOA 2023 trauma RCT** found 90-day mortality **54% (25/46) versus 42% (18/43)**, Bayesian OR 1.58 (95% credible interval 0.72–3.52), with 86.9% probability of increased mortality. It does not support routine trauma REBOA. Trauma findings should not simply be equated with specialist proximal aortic balloon control for rAAA; indication, level, time to control and expertise differ. Do not use a distal balloon below the bleeding lesion or let balloon placement delay definitive haemostasis.

## Apply the findings

For fluoroscopy arrange the room before draping so the operator can pause screening when airway access is needed. Identify where scatter is greatest and use practical shielding and distance while preserving visibility of monitors and direct patient access. Agree the local dosimeter arrangement and check where anaesthesia staff can stand. With a balloon, track position and occlusion time and coordinate deflation with definitive haemorrhage control and resuscitation.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book archive (2025 latest complete edition; 2023 and 2017 relevant chapters)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29); [UK-REBOA primary trauma randomised trial (2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824132/). · [ANZCA professional documents, PS55 and PG09](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes REBOA placement and zones
- Physiology resembles a cross-clamp
- Inflation time limits and slow deflation
- Monitoring and resuscitation plan
- Complications of REBOA
- Time, distance and shielding principles
- Protective equipment and dosimetry
- Pregnancy and communication

items.title: 23. Sudden bilateral leg ischaemia during aorto-iliac stenting
items.q: During aorto-iliac stent placement the patient develops sudden bilateral leg ischaemia with loss of femoral Doppler signals. Discuss the likely causes, immediate assessment and management.
items.a:
## Recognise loss of distal flow

Tell the operator immediately and verify the physiological change against the last angiogram and timing of balloon inflation or deployment. Bilateral loss of femoral signals suggests loss of aorto-iliac inflow. Consider unintended balloon occlusion or prolonged inflation, graft limb obstruction or kinking, thrombosis, dissection with true-lumen compromise, distal embolisation, or a large sheath obstructing an already diseased vessel. Severe systemic hypotension can also make signals disappear. A proximal arterial line may show stable or high pressure despite distal ischaemia. Correlate waveform, ECG, oxygenation and right and left limb findings rather than treating the proximal MAP as a global perfusion measure.

## Rescue the circulation and the limb

Stop or reverse the potentially causal manoeuvre when safe, with explicit operator communication. Request immediate angiographic confirmation of inflow, branch patency and the site of obstruction. Assess sedation and airway access, call vascular and anaesthetic help, and prepare the suite for GA or conversion if needed. Maintain proximal perfusion, oxygenation, temperature and reliable IV access. Check gas, potassium, lactate, blood count and anticoagulation, and prepare blood. Assess whether hypotension represents haemorrhage, retroperitoneal access bleeding, cardiac dysfunction, contrast reaction or the reperfusion response rather than assuming a single cause.

Treat the lesion with the procedural team. Options include deflating or repositioning equipment, restoring stent patency, thrombectomy, relining, bridging or urgent open repair. Consider heparin when thrombosis is likely and bleeding/dissection risk permits, taking account of existing procedural dosing and monitoring. Record ischaemia duration and repeated examination. If a severely threatened limb cannot be restored endovascularly, transfer or convert without delay using an agreed airway, access, monitoring and communication plan.

## Anticipate reperfusion and follow-up

Warn the team before flow returns. Check ECG and serial gases, and be ready for reduced vascular tone, acidaemia, hyperkalaemia and ventricular arrhythmia. Correct haemodynamics and treat dangerous hyperkalaemia, using membrane stabilisation and intracellular shift when indicated and planning definitive elimination if necessary. After successful reperfusion document femoral and distal signals, motor and sensory function. Watch for compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, delayed bleeding, access problems and recurrent obstruction. Arrange monitored care and a plan for antithrombotics and reassessment. Persistent pain or absent flow needs further evaluation while the patient is still in a setting equipped for rescue.

**Sources:** [2024 ACC/AHA multisociety lower-extremity PAD guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013) · [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ANZCA professional documents, PS55 and PG09](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents) · [ANZCA Blue Book catalogue, including 2023 radiation and aortic balloon occlusion chapters](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises bilateral inflow loss and checks procedural timing
- Differentiates mechanical, thrombotic and systemic causes
- Coordinates airway, haemodynamic and angiographic rescue
- Selects targeted restoration of flow with a conversion plan
- Anticipates reperfusion hyperkalaemia and haemodynamic effects
- Performs serial vascular, renal and compartment checks

items.title: 24. CT-guided renal biopsy and post-biopsy haemorrhage
items.q: A patient is scheduled for CT-guided renal mass biopsy. How would you provide anaesthesia, and how would your priorities change if major post-biopsy bleeding required urgent embolisation?
items.a:
## Preop

### Plan the biopsy

Confirm the position, trajectory, anticipated pain, need for breath-holding and whether access to the airway will be restricted by prone positioning or the gantry. Review cardiorespiratory reserve, ability to lie still, aspiration risk, baseline renal function, haemoglobin and haemostatic risk. Reconcile antiplatelets and anticoagulants with the proceduralist and relevant prescriber, considering both procedural bleeding risk and the indication for treatment. Confirm a plan for post-biopsy observation and how urgent haemostasis would be obtained.

## Intraop

### Anaesthesia for the biopsy

A cooperative patient who can reproduce breath holds may tolerate local infiltration with minimal sedation. Review how less accessible positioning changes the risk of deep sedation. If immobility is essential or the patient cannot tolerate the position, consider general anaesthesia with a secured airway before positioning and agree how ventilation will be coordinated with imaging. Confirm standard monitoring and capnography appropriate to sedation depth, oxygen, suction, rescue equipment, adequate access and a rehearsed plan to stop the scan and reach the patient. Use appropriately staffed recovery and hand over site-specific risks.

## Postop

### Recognise haemorrhage and resuscitate

Flank pain, tachycardia or hypotension after renal biopsy can signal concealed bleeding. Assess airway, breathing, circulation and responsiveness, check the puncture site and notify the proceduralist. Review the BP trend, haemoglobin, gas, lactate, coagulation, fibrinogen, electrolytes and crossmatch as appropriate. Early haemoglobin may underestimate loss. Establish reliable access, warm the patient and resuscitate with blood products and targeted correction of coagulopathy if indicated. Activate the major haemorrhage pathway where warranted. Arrange rapid definitive control in parallel. Imaging or angiography should be selected with the team according to haemodynamic stability and where treatment is immediately available.

### Anaesthesia during embolisation and recovery

Superselective embolisation can stop bleeding while preserving functioning renal tissue. Anticipate pain, contrast exposure, non-target ischaemia, access complications and persistent haemorrhage. Tailor anaesthesia to shock, cooperation, airway access and expected duration. If general anaesthesia is needed, prepare vasoactive and transfusion support before induction. Protect staff with shielding and distance while keeping emergency access. Maintain communication about the expected time to control and what triggers surgical rescue. After embolisation trend perfusion, haemoglobin, urine output and renal function, check the arterial access site and watch for recurrent bleeding. Evaluate persistent severe pain, fever or worsening organ function in context. Post-embolisation inflammation may occur, but these findings can also indicate ongoing bleeding, infection or non-target ischaemia. Agree the level of postoperative care and who will reassess deterioration.

**Sources:** [CIRSE Clinical Practice Manual](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8382634/) · [CIRSE standards for emergency interventional radiology](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12868068/) · [ANZCA professional documents, PS55 and PG09](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Assesses the specific position, breath-holding and restricted airway access
- Reviews haemostatic medications, renal reserve and biopsy-site bleeding risk
- Justifies local/minimal sedation or secured-airway general anaesthesia
- Recognises concealed haemorrhage and resuscitates while obtaining control
- Plans safe anaesthesia for embolisation and a surgical rescue pathway
- Monitors for rebleeding, access problems and renal or non-target injury

items.title: 25. Thoracoscopic sympathectomy for palmar hyperhidrosis
items.q: A 24-year-old woman is scheduled for bilateral thoracoscopic sympathectomy for palmar hyperhidrosis. Outline the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Procedure

Thoracoscopic (VATS) sympathectomy divides or clips the sympathetic chain at an agreed **rib level**, commonly **R3/R4 for palmar hyperhidrosis**, with level chosen by indication/surgeon; avoid confusing rib landmarks with ganglion levels or routinely extending to T2/stellate pathways through small incisions in the axilla or chest. It is done under **GA with lung isolation** and arm abducted, usually in a beach-chair or supine position, and is day-stay.

## Preop

- Assess fitness, respiratory disease, **anxiety**, and drug use (anticholinergics, which are sometimes used for hyperhidrosis).
- Consent for complications: **compensatory sweating** (most common, up to 50 to 90%), **Horner's syndrome** (stellate ganglion injury), pneumothorax, bleeding, intercostal neuralgia, bradycardia, and rarely conversion to open surgery.

## Intraop

- **GA** with a **double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker** for one-lung ventilation (the surgeon may accept two-lung ventilation with CO2 insufflation at low pressure), or a single-lumen tube with low-pressure insufflation.
- Standard monitoring, arterial line not routinely required, careful positioning of arms (brachial plexus), and warming.
- **Haemodynamics:** sympathectomy causes **bradycardia and mild hypotension**, and the vagus nerve is stimulated; the cardiac sympathetic fibres arise from T1 to T4, so have **atropine** ready.
- **One-lung ventilation:** manage hypoxaemia (optimise dependent-lung ventilation/oxygen/PEEP and tube position; CPAP to the non-dependent operative lung if it does not obstruct surgery, or resume two-lung ventilation if needed), maintain low tidal volume and PEEP, and avoid high insufflation pressure (hypotension from reduced venous return).
- Check **bilateral hand temperature** or skin conductance to confirm the block.

## Postop

- Assess for residual/bilateral pneumothorax and respiratory compromise; imaging/drain management follows symptoms and the VATS protocol (pleural entry is intrinsic to this operation), **analgesia** with paracetamol, NSAIDs, local anaesthetic infiltration and short-acting opioid, antiemetics, and early discharge.
- Counsel regarding **compensatory sweating** and monitor for Horner's syndrome.

## Apply the findings

Discuss the surgeon’s method for exposure and whether the contralateral lung can tolerate reduced ventilation. Confirm the lung isolation device position after repositioning when used. Oxygen insufflation or one-lung ventilation may affect gas exchange, and capnothorax can lower preload and raise airway pressures. If sudden cardiovascular or respiratory compromise occurs, stop insufflation and reassess lung expansion, circuit, tension physiology and alternative causes. Afterward confirm re-expansion and assess persistent pain, breathlessness, Horner syndrome or compensatory sweating depending on symptoms and level.

**Sources:** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization surgery (2015;15:225–230)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482). · [ANZCA professional documents, PS55 and PG09](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes indication-specific rib levels (e.g. R3/R4 for palmar disease) and avoids stellate injury
- Notes consent for compensatory sweating, Horner's, pneumothorax
- Describes lung isolation or low-pressure insufflation
- Anticipates bradycardia and hypotension; atropine available
- Positioning and arm care
- One-lung ventilation management
- Postoperative chest imaging, analgesia and counselling
- Day-stay planning

items.title: 26. Acute mesenteric ischaemia: resuscitation and revascularisation
items.q: An older patient with atrial fibrillation develops severe abdominal pain and rising lactate. CT angiography shows an acute superior mesenteric artery occlusion. Outline the resuscitation and perioperative considerations for urgent revascularisation.
items.a:
## Preop

### Recognise the time-critical mechanism

Acute mesenteric ischaemia can follow embolism, acute thrombosis, low-flow vasoconstriction or venous thrombosis. In AF with a visceral arterial occlusion, embolism is plausible. Severe early pain can precede peritonism and a normal lactate does not exclude early disease. Rising lactate, acidosis, peritoneal signs, shock or organ injury suggest progression. Mobilise vascular surgery, general surgery, interventional radiology, anaesthesia and ICU. In suspected disease urgent arterial and venous phase CT angiography guides treatment, including when renal impairment is present. In this patient imaging is already diagnostic, so avoid delay to flow restoration and bowel assessment.

### Resuscitation and initial management

Provide oxygen as needed, two large-bore IVs, arterial monitoring when appropriate, ECG, gases, electrolytes, full blood count, coagulation, renal function, lactate and crossmatched blood. Give analgesia and early broad-spectrum antibiotics because barrier failure and bacterial translocation are likely. Use balanced crystalloid in assessed increments and noradrenaline if required to maintain systemic perfusion. Avoid prolonged hypotension and indiscriminate fluid loading that worsens bowel oedema. Discuss therapeutic unfractionated heparin with the team if safe, especially with an arterial occlusion requiring intervention, and adjust for active bleeding and the procedural plan.

## Intraop

### Technique

Choose endovascular, open or hybrid revascularisation based on anatomy, viability and available expertise. Peritonitis or likely necrotic bowel warrants operative assessment and source control. Many patients have ileus and a full stomach. Plan a haemodynamically supported rapid-sequence induction for laparotomy, with vasopressor connected, blood ready and adequate preoxygenation. Prepare for large losses, hypothermia and rapid metabolic change. Monitor cardiac performance when shock persists and consider the effects of sepsis, bleeding and cardiac dysfunction together.

### Reperfusion

Communicate before reperfusion. Washout of tissue metabolites and sudden vasodilation can cause hypotension, acidosis, hyperkalaemia and arrhythmia. Follow ECG and serial blood gases, give titrated vasoactive and volume support, and correct dangerous electrolyte changes promptly. With haemorrhage, obtain source control, treat hypothermia and use targeted coagulation therapy guided by clinical bleeding and available testing.

## Postop

Agree bowel viability assessment, resection or damage-control strategy and possible second-look surgery. Postoperatively monitor perfusion and lactate trends, ongoing GI ischaemia, abdominal compartment syndrome, renal function and sepsis. Plan ventilation, nutrition and antithrombotic management. Recurrent pain or lactate rise requires renewed surgical assessment rather than automatic attribution to reperfusion.

**Sources:** [2025 ESVS mesenteric and renal guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejvs.2025.06.010) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2025, cardiac and vascular viscoelastic algorithm and GLP-1 chapter](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305)

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Recognises the urgent arterial phenotype and limits avoidable delay
- Resuscitates while arranging vascular and bowel source control
- Provides antibiotic and anticoagulation decisions
- Justifies open/endovascular/hybrid choice and safe induction
- Anticipates metabolic and haemodynamic reperfusion and bleeding
- Plans ICU, bowel viability review and second look

items.title: 27. Arteriovenous fistula in a haemodialysis patient with pulmonary hypertension
items.q: A patient on haemodialysis with pulmonary hypertension and reduced LV function presents for creation of an upper-arm arteriovenous fistula. Discuss how you would prepare them, choose an anaesthetic and assess problems after surgery.
items.a:
## Preop

Clarify the dialysis access plan, site and anticipated flow. Preserve available veins and protect any functioning access from unnecessary cuffs, puncture or compression. Review the timing, adequacy and anticoagulation of the last dialysis, target weight, symptoms of fluid overload, potassium, bicarbonate, haemoglobin, bleeding history and antithrombotics. Check the ECG and evaluate LV/RV function and pulmonary pressures when clinically indicated. Discuss whether congestion, severe electrolyte abnormalities or recent dialysis hypotension need treatment first. Coordinate the schedule and plans for dialysis and postoperative monitoring with nephrology. Explain the risk that an upper-arm high-flow access can increase venous return and cardiac output demand.

## Intraop

Local infiltration with minimal sedation often suits a cooperative patient having straightforward superficial access creation. Brachial plexus block can provide anaesthesia, opioid-sparing analgesia and sympathectomy-mediated vasodilation. Choose a block that covers the operative site, consider upper medial arm intercostobrachial coverage where needed, and assess compressibility, antithrombotic exposure and bleeding risk. Diaphragmatic impairment matters in severe respiratory or RV disease, particularly with more proximal approaches. Regional techniques may improve some patency outcomes in selected settings, but the overall evidence does not justify one technique for every fistula. Explain plan for supplementary infiltration or conversion if pain, anxiety or poor exposure develops.

GA is reasonable if cooperation, immobility or surgical extent makes the other choices unsuitable. Titrate anaesthesia carefully, maintain oxygenation, normocapnia and RV perfusion, avoid abrupt afterload reduction or excessive fluid, and preserve limb flow. Use beat-to-beat monitoring according to cardiac reserve and the procedure. Check the thrill and distal perfusion with the surgeon after opening the shunt.

## Postop

Examine the hand for pain, coolness, weakness, poor capillary refill and sensory change, and check the thrill, distal signals and access site. A missing thrill suggests early access failure. A painful cool hand may indicate access-related ischaemia, especially with diabetes or arterial disease. Acute severe neuropathy can occur even with relatively preserved skin perfusion and requires urgent surgical review. Also assess bleeding and haematoma, account for expected block effects, and plan repeat examination when the block resolves. New dyspnoea, congestion or deteriorating RV function warrants evaluation of volume, ventricular function, pulmonary pressure and access flow. Reschedule dialysis and give instructions on access protection and review.

**Sources:** [KDOQI vascular access guideline, 2019 update](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32778223/) · [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization surgery (2015;15:225–230)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482)

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Reviews dialysis timing, electrolyte and fluid status and access protection
- Explains cardiac effects of a high-flow access
- Compares local, regional and GA including coverage and bleeding risk
- Provides RV and limb perfusion plan with fluid restraint
- Recognises access failure, distal ischaemia and neuropathy
- Plans dialysis and assesses new heart failure

items.title: 28. Intraoperative complications of major vascular surgery and arterial laceration
items.q: Describe the intraoperative complications of major vascular surgery and how you would manage them. Include your priorities for an actively bleeding arterial laceration with threatened distal perfusion.
items.a:
## Complications and responses

- **Major haemorrhage:** vessel injury, anastomotic leak, coagulopathy after heparin. **Large-bore access, arterial line, crossmatched blood, cell salvage, tranexamic acid**, massive transfusion protocol, calcium, warming, viscoelastic testing; surgeon pressure and clamping.
- **Haemodynamic instability:** clamp and unclamp effects (hypertension, then hypotension), embolic events, blood loss. Use invasive monitoring and cardiac output, titrate vasodilators, vasopressors and volume.
- **Myocardial ischaemia and infarction:** ST monitoring, treat tachycardia and hypotension, maintain Hb, GTN only if BP/perfusion permits, call cardiology; avoid new beta-blockade at induction.
- **Arrhythmia:** AF (rate control, cardioversion if unstable), bradycardia from carotid sinus handling (stop manipulation, atropine and vasoactive support as needed; no routine sinus blockade), electrolyte correction.
- **Venous thromboembolism and embolism:** air embolism, thrombus or atheroma embolisation to limbs, gut or brain; limb ischaemia or stroke.
- **Heparin-related issues:** inadequate or excessive anticoagulation (ACT), **heparin-induced thrombocytopenia**, protamine reaction (hypotension, pulmonary hypertension, anaphylaxis).
- **Renal ischaemia:** clamp time, hypovolaemia, contrast; maintain MAP and volume.
- **Hypothermia:** warm fluids and forced-air warming, prewarming.
- **Positioning and pressure injuries**, nerve injury, eye injury.
- **Anaphylaxis and contrast reaction** in the angiography suite.

## Principles

Anticipate through **preoperative optimisation**, **invasive monitoring**, blood availability, and **good communication** with the surgeon about clamp times and events. Treat the cause (not just the BP), and escalate early to additional help, and ICU planning.

## Apply the findings

Make rescue plans specific to the phase. Before clamping ensure arterial monitoring, adequate blood delivery and communication. When proximal pressure rises with ventricular distension, assess function and control afterload while protecting coronary perfusion. With bradycardia on carotid manipulation ask for release of the stimulus and treat poor perfusion. During endovascular collapse compare access-site bleeding, perforation, loss of distal flow, contrast reaction and cardiac causes. A proximal arterial waveform does not exclude regional ischaemia. When bleeding causes shock, coordinate prompt vascular control and targeted haemostasis with active warming and calcium assessment. Atraumatic positioning, repeat distal signals and clear ICU handover help identify delayed injury. During reperfusion confirm both proximal perfusion and the operated limb. Part of the response to unexpected hypotension is asking whether there is still an obstructed graft or another systemic cause, rather than treating every fall as a simple fluid deficit. For major arterial laceration, control external bleeding immediately, mobilise vascular surgery and resuscitate while proceeding to haemostasis. Document distal motor, sensory and Doppler findings if this can be done without delaying control. Discuss temporary shunting if definitive repair must be delayed and the limb is threatened. Coordinate vascular and skeletal management, individualise anticoagulation to bleeding risk, and reassess perfusion and compartments after repair.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/); [ESVS 2023 carotid/vertebral disease guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374). · [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [ESVS 2023 carotid/vertebral disease guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [ESVS vascular trauma guidelines 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejvs.2024.12.018)

## Self-marking checklist

- Haemorrhage with preparation and massive transfusion
- Haemodynamic instability and monitoring
- Myocardial ischaemia and arrhythmias
- Embolic events including air, thrombus and atheroma
- Heparin issues: ACT, HIT, protamine reaction
- Renal protection
- Hypothermia, positioning and pressure injury
- Anaphylaxis and contrast reaction
- Principles: anticipate, monitor, communicate, escalate
- Prioritises haemorrhage control, threatened limb perfusion and repair or temporary shunting after arterial laceration

items.title: 29. Regional anaesthesia on dual antiplatelets and heparin for limb revascularisation
items.q: Discuss the risks and benefits of regional anaesthesia and analgesia for a patient having lower limb revascularisation who will receive heparin and is taking aspirin and clopidogrel.
items.a:
## Preop

### Benefits

- Avoids airway instrumentation and the **cardiovascular and respiratory effects of GA**; the patient stays awake with spontaneous breathing, which suits those with heart or lung disease.
- Sympathetic block may improve regional blood flow and analgesia reduces stress, but **improved graft patency or survival is not an established universal causal benefit**.
- Opioid-sparing analgesia, less nausea and delirium. Epidural or spinal analgesia is the common option for bypass surgery, and **peripheral nerve blocks** (sciatic, popliteal, adductor canal) suit distal procedures.
- Evidence of outcome differences between regional and general is limited (no clear mortality difference, possible pulmonary/other benefits in some studies; observational associations are not definitive proof).

### Risks

- **Neuraxial haematoma** (epidural or spinal) is catastrophic, and the risk rises with antiplatelets and anticoagulation. Heparin (intraoperative bolus) is a particular risk if the needle placement is traumatic.
- **Hypotension** from sympathetic block, with a risk to coronary and graft perfusion; bradycardia.
- Nerve injury, infection, failure or incomplete block, and the need for conversion.
- Local anaesthetic toxicity for peripheral blocks.

### Antithrombotic management

- **Aspirin alone** generally requires no additional interval for neuraxial/deep blocks. **Clopidogrel: 5–7 days** before neuraxial or **deep plexus/deep peripheral** needle placement, favouring full recovery where bleeding risk is high. If DAPT cannot stop, avoid those blocks; consider GA, local infiltration or an appropriate superficial compressible block after site-specific assessment.
- **IV UFH:** stop for **4–6 h** and confirm normal coagulation before neuraxial/deep-block insertion or catheter removal; delay systemic heparin **≥1 h after needle placement** and re-heparinisation **≥1 h after catheter removal**. Check platelets if UFH >4 days (HIT risk). A bloody tap increases concern but **does not automatically require cancellation**: discuss surgical urgency, anticoagulation and alternatives. Use frequent neurological checks and an urgent haematoma pathway.
- Avoid epidural catheters when anticoagulation is prolonged after surgery; consider **peripheral catheters** or wound infiltration instead.

### Decision

Weigh the benefit against the haematoma risk in each patient; where DAPT is unavoidable, choose **GA with local infiltration or a carefully selected superficial compressible block**; deep plexus/deep peripheral blocks follow neuraxial anticoagulation intervals.

## Intraop

Use the chosen technique with hypotension and conversion plans, dose accounting and careful timing of systemic heparin. Protect pressure areas and assess baseline neuropathy when interpreting postoperative findings.

## Postop

Provide analgesia, ongoing neurological checks and explicit catheter-removal/restart orders. Escalate unexpected motor deficit or severe back pain urgently; do not attribute it automatically to the block.

## Apply the findings

The antiplatelet indication and whether interruption threatens a recent stent or the limb are part of the anaesthetic decision. Discuss when surgical UFH starts and how insertion, removal and restart will be handled. A superficially placed compressible block and a deep non-compressible block do not have the same bleeding consequence. Document baseline symptoms, use an appropriate concentration and preserve a plan for serial compartment and graft assessment.

**Sources:** [ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025)](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2025/09/16/rapm-2024-105766); [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization surgery (2015;15:225–230)](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/15/5/225/240482). · [2024 ACC/AHA multisociety lower-extremity PAD guideline](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013)

## Self-marking checklist

- Benefits: haemodynamic, respiratory, sympathetic block and graft flow, analgesia
- Notes limited outcome evidence
- Risks: neuraxial haematoma, hypotension, nerve injury, infection
- Aspirin acceptable; clopidogrel stop-time
- Heparin timing: block before heparin, catheter removal interval
- Alternative peripheral techniques
- Neurological monitoring after neuraxial block
- Individualised decision

items.title: 30. Perioperative stroke in vascular surgery
items.q: Discuss the risk factors for perioperative stroke in a patient having vascular surgery and describe how you would recognise and manage a suspected stroke in the recovery room.
items.a:
## Definition and burden

Perioperative stroke occurs intraoperatively or within **30 days** and substantially increases mortality/disability. Incidence varies by patient, procedure and study; it is higher after carotid/complex aortic surgery than many other noncardiac procedures. Mechanisms include embolism, hypoperfusion, thrombosis and haemorrhage; avoid extrapolating a single incidence or mortality multiplier to every vascular patient.

## Risk factors

- **Patient:** previous stroke or TIA, **carotid stenosis**, AF (doubles risk), heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, CKD, age, smoking.
- **Surgery:** vascular and cardiac surgery, aortic manipulation, long duration.
- **Anaesthetic:** **hypotension**, hypertension, withdrawal of antithrombotics or beta-blockers, anaemia, hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia.

## Prevention

- Continue **aspirin** and statin; manage **anticoagulation** and bridging carefully (clopidogrel/prasugrel interrupted per risk); consider delaying elective noncardiac surgery **at least 3 months after stroke/TIA**, individualising urgency and risk. This does not mean delaying indicated early symptomatic CEA.
- Treat suitable **symptomatic 70–99% carotid stenosis**, and selected **50–69%** disease, with CEA preferably within 14 days after appropriate neurological assessment; large disabling/haemorrhagic infarction may require deferral.
- Maintain **perfusion pressure** (MAP near baseline), avoid hypo/hypercapnia and hyperglycaemia; consider cerebral oximetry in selected cases.

## Recognition and management in recovery

- **FAST signs**, new focal deficit, speech disturbance, reduced consciousness, or failure to wake; exclude other causes (**hypoglycaemia**, residual drugs, seizure, hypoxia).
- **Call for help**, note the time of last known well, ABCs, check **glucose**, and maintain BP (avoid hypotension; individualise BP with the stroke/vascular team; routine permissive hypertension may be dangerous after CEA with hyperperfusion/haemorrhage or with acute aortic disease).
- **Urgent CT/CT angiography** with the stroke team; assess urgent **mechanical thrombectomy** eligibility for large-vessel occlusion. Recent major surgery often makes IV thrombolysis unsuitable/high-risk; eligibility is a specialist decision considering imaging, timing and operative haemostasis.
- Specific cause: carotid or graft thrombosis (re-exploration), anticoagulation-related bleed.
- ICU or stroke unit care, aspirin once haemorrhage is excluded, and rehabilitation.

## Apply the findings

After carotid surgery, first ask whether the deficit occurred during clamping, following recovery or coincident with severe hypertension. Local thrombosis or embolism may need immediate surgical or endovascular treatment, while headache, seizure and high BP raise hyperperfusion or intracranial haemorrhage. Establish last-known-well, urgently coordinate imaging and do not let nonessential tests delay a time-critical decision. Discuss recent surgery carefully before thrombolysis and look for thrombectomy eligibility when large-vessel occlusion is suspected.

For confirmed acute large-vessel occlusion, stroke teams now consider thrombectomy in selected patients with larger infarct cores or basilar occlusion. Apply the service eligibility criteria. Avoid intensive automatic reduction below SBP 140 after successful thrombectomy. Suspected haemorrhage or post-CEA hyperperfusion requires its own treatment pathway.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2023 carotid/vertebral disease guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374); [AHA/ACC perioperative guidance: 2026 reaffirmation of 2024 recommendations](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017); [ANZCA Blue Book archive (2025 latest complete edition; 2023 and 2017 relevant chapters)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29). · [ESVS 2023 carotid/vertebral disease guideline](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1078588422002374) · [AHA/ACC perioperative cardiovascular guidance, reaffirmed 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017) · [AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke guideline 2026](https://doi.org/10.1161/STR.0000000000000513)

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines perioperative stroke, burden and embolic mechanism
- Patient, surgical and anaesthetic risk factors
- Continues aspirin and statins; manages anticoagulation
- Carotid stenosis timing and surgery
- Maintains perfusion pressure and metabolic control
- Recognition: FAST signs and exclusion of mimics (glucose)
- Management: time of onset, imaging, stroke team, thrombolysis or thrombectomy
- Cause-specific management and ICU

items.title: 31. Fluid and haemodynamic management across the phases of aortic surgery
items.q: Discuss your approach to perioperative fluid and haemodynamic management across the phases of major aortic surgery. How does it change in a patient with heart failure and chronic kidney disease?
items.a:
## Principles

- **No single CVP-target policy fits every phase.** Fluid responsiveness means a bolus will raise stroke volume; it does not mean fluid is beneficial if there is pulmonary oedema or venous congestion.
- Use small challenges or valid dynamic tests, interpreted with cardiac output, BP, capillary refill, echo, blood loss and urine output. **Pulse-pressure variation is unreliable** with spontaneous breathing, arrhythmia, low tidal volumes, high intra-abdominal pressure or raised RV afterload.
- Low urine output during renal-artery clamping is not evidence that another litre of saline is the answer.

## Preop

- Identify heart failure, CKD, baseline Hb and hydration; agree the monitoring (arterial line, targeted flow assessment) and blood availability before induction.

## Intraop

### Phase by phase

| Phase or condition | Physiological problem | Reasoned initial strategy |
|---|---|---|
| Bleeding before rupture control | Blood loss; risk of losing tamponade if pressure forced too high | Controlled blood-based resuscitation, rapid source control; permissive pressure only while perfused |
| Elective pre-clamp | Enough reserve without LV overload | Replace demonstrable deficit; check flow and congestion; avoid fixed large preload |
| High aortic clamp | Rising LV impedance, possible myocardial dysfunction | Avoid tachycardia; titrate vasodilator or inotrope by cardiac output and ischaemia, not BP alone |
| Immediately before release | Expected vasodilation and venous pooling | Check responsiveness and blood loss, prepare noradrenaline, correct significant K⁺/Ca²⁺ derangements, staged release |
| After reperfusion | Vasoplegia, myocardial depression, bleeding, acid and K⁺ washout | Differentiate cause, reassess output, echo and lactate; use blood or fluid and vasopressors appropriately |
| Carotid clamping | Threatened hemispheric perfusion | Maintain baseline or higher MAP, avoid CO₂ extremes, selective shunt policy |
| Spinal protection | Maintain spinal perfusion pressure | Adequate MAP and Hb; prevent low output and high CSF pressure |
| CKD or heart failure | Both overload and organ hypoperfusion are likely | Assess individual flow, avoid nephrotoxins and large indiscriminate loads |

### Heart failure and CKD

- A stiff LV is preload-sensitive but easily overloaded; a failing systolic LV may deteriorate with the afterload of a high clamp. Use arterial monitoring and targeted echo or flow assessment; choose fluid, vasopressor or inotrope by mechanism.
- CKD: prevent sustained renal hypoperfusion without routine prophylactic boluses; avoid nephrotoxins; dose-adjust renally cleared drugs; no renal-dose dopamine or forced diuresis.

## Postop

### Reducing the need for crystalloid and postoperative prescribing

- Early haemostatic resuscitation and blood conservation reduce high-volume crystalloid and its bowel, lung and wound oedema.
- After surgery every infusion needs an indication: maintenance if genuinely unable to drink, replacement of ongoing losses, or resuscitation of a documented deficit. Record urine output, daily weight, balance, creatinine, electrolytes and clinical congestion; these are complementary, not interchangeable.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · Set 14 notes, section 13.2

## Self-marking checklist

- Organised into preop, intraop and postop
- Rejects a single universal CVP target
- Defines fluid responsiveness and its limits; names reasons dynamic indices fail
- Gives phase-specific plans: pre-clamp, clamp, before release, after reperfusion
- Does not treat low urine output at clamp as an automatic fluid indication
- Adjusts for heart failure and CKD
- Uses blood and haemostatic resuscitation to limit crystalloid
- States indications and monitoring for postoperative fluid prescribing

items.title: 32. Open, endovascular and conservative strategies and the supporting trials
items.q: Compare open, endovascular and conservative treatment for an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm, symptomatic carotid stenosis and chronic limb-threatening ischaemia. Which key trials inform each decision, and what are their limits?
items.a:
## Method

To evaluate an operation, first identify the **natural history** of the untreated disease, then compare short-term operative hazard with durability, recovery, surveillance and late-failure risk. The lowest immediate-risk operation is not necessarily the best lifelong intervention, and the most comprehensive anatomical operation may be wrong for a patient with limited reserve.

## Infrarenal AAA

- **Open repair:** durable graft; abdominal exposure, clamp-related afterload changes, major haemorrhage, pulmonary and renal injury.
- **EVAR:** less initial physiological insult but needs suitable sealing zones and access, with endoleak, migration and late rupture requiring lifelong surveillance.
- **Conservative:** small stable aneurysm or limited benefit; BP, smoking and vascular risk control with scheduled imaging.
- **EVAR-1:** early (0 to 6 months) mortality advantage of elective EVAR; over 15 years no significant difference in total or aneurysm-related mortality, but beyond 8 years aneurysm-related and total mortality were higher after EVAR (mainly late sac rupture), and reinterventions were more frequent throughout. **IMPROVE** (ruptured AAA): 30-day mortality 35.4% with an endovascular-first strategy versus 37.4% open, not significantly different, and not proof that EVAR always reduces rupture mortality.

## Symptomatic carotid stenosis

- **CEA:** removes plaque; cranial nerve, haematoma and baroreflex risks; awake neurological examination possible.
- **CAS:** avoids a neck incision but adds catheter and arch embolism, stent thrombosis and mandatory antiplatelet implications.
- **Medical therapy** is always needed and may be sole treatment for low-grade stenosis or high procedural risk.
- **GALA and the Cochrane review:** no convincing difference in stroke, MI or death between local and general anaesthesia, so technique follows cooperation, monitoring and local expertise. **CREST-2** (asymptomatic stenosis of 70% or more) was two parallel trials, not a head-to-head CEA versus CAS comparison: stenting plus intensive medical therapy reduced the composite versus its own medical arm, whereas CEA showed no significant effect against its control.

## Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia

- **Bypass:** durable vein bypass in suitable anatomy and conduit; wound and graft risks. **Endovascular:** lower initial trauma, but repeat intervention and anatomy-dependent durability. Medical therapy, infection control and foot care are mandatory; tissue loss usually still needs perfusion restoration when salvage is feasible.
- **BEST-CLI:** with a usable single-segment great saphenous vein, bypass-first had fewer major adverse limb events or deaths (42.6% versus 57.4% at a median 2.7 years); not clearly different without suitable vein.
- **BASIL-2:** in infrapopliteal disease, vein-bypass-first had more major amputation or death than best-endovascular-first (63% versus 53%). The trials differ in anatomy, strategy and patients; the lesson is multidisciplinary selection, not one method for every diabetic leg.
- **VOYAGER PAD:** low-dose rivaroxaban (2.5 mg twice daily) plus aspirin after revascularisation reduced limb and cardiovascular events at the cost of bleeding; it affects timing of later surgery and regional techniques.

## The anaesthetist's contribution

Match the strategy to the physiological reserve, anticipate the specific risks of each option (clamp and reperfusion, contrast and radiation, spinal cord, cerebral perfusion, antithrombotics), and express trial results with the population and limits.

**Sources:** [ESVS 2024 abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysm guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307694/) · [BEST-CLI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2207899) · [BASIL-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(23)00462-2) · [GALA](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(08)61699-2) · [CREST-2](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2508800) · Set 14 notes, section 14.1 and trials chapter

## Self-marking checklist

- Starts from natural history and compares risk distributions
- AAA: open versus EVAR hazards, surveillance, EVAR-1 and IMPROVE with limits
- Carotid: CEA versus CAS risks, anaesthetic technique evidence (GALA), CREST-2 design limits
- CLTI: bypass versus endovascular, BEST-CLI and BASIL-2 populations
- VOYAGER PAD and its bleeding trade-off
- Links the choice to the patient's physiological reserve and anaesthetic risks

items.title: 2026.1 Q15: Preoperative assessment and optimisation for elective EVAR
items.q: You are reviewing your patient in a high-risk anaesthesia clinic who is scheduled for elective endovascular aortic aneurysm repair (EVAR). Describe your preoperative assessment and optimisation strategies for this patient.
items.model:
## Principle

EVAR patients are older, with **heavy cardiovascular comorbidity**, but the procedure is less physiological stress than open repair. The clinic aims to **stratify risk, optimise what is modifiable, plan the anaesthetic and enable shared decision-making**.

## Preop

### Assessment

- **Cardiac:** IHD, heart failure, arrhythmia, valve disease and hypertension; DASI/functional capacity (claudication may limit it), examination and ECG. Echo for new/worsening heart failure or suspected significant valve disease; poor capacity alone does not mandate echo. Use RCRI/validated procedural risk and frailty. Select BNP/NT-proBNP and baseline troponin in elevated-risk patients; CPET/stress testing only if results change decisions, optimisation or care planning.
- **Other comorbidity:** CKD (**contrast load**, baseline eGFR), COPD and smoking, diabetes (HbA1c, **SGLT2 inhibitor** withhold for the recommended local interval before major surgery and plan perioperative ketone testing when indicated), cerebrovascular disease, anaemia, and **frailty** (Clinical Frailty Scale).
- **Medications:** continue aspirin and statin and beta-blocker; **dual antiplatelets** after stenting need a joint plan; anticoagulants managed by drug, renal function and bleeding/thrombotic risk; bridging reserved for selected very high thrombotic risk; consider omitting a renin–angiotensin system inhibitor before elevated-risk surgery in selected patients treated for hypertension. Continuation may be appropriate with HFrEF. Coordinate antiplatelet or anticoagulant interruption with the relevant team.
- **Aneurysm and procedure:** diameter, neck anatomy and **morphology** (adverse neck anatomy risks conversion), iliac access, planned **local, regional or general** technique, contrast and radiation exposure, hybrid theatre, and spinal cord protection if extensive thoracoabdominal coverage is planned. A suprarenal component alone does not mandate a CSF drain; routine infrarenal EVAR does not require one.
- **Airway and access:** airway assessment; ability to lie flat; IV access.

### Optimisation

- Medical optimisation of **hypertension, heart failure, diabetes, anaemia** (iron) and COPD; **smoking cessation**; **prehabilitation** and nutrition.
- Renal protection: avoid nephrotoxins, plan hydration, and minimise contrast.
- Plan for **haemorrhage and conversion to open repair**: group and screen or crossmatch, large-bore access, arterial line, cell salvage, and a surgical team on standby.
- **Critical care** bed if high risk, and a plan for postoperative analgesia and delirium prevention.

### Shared decision-making

Discuss **risks and benefits** (including surveillance for endoleak, reintervention and the alternative of open repair or no repair) and the patient's goals. Document consent and any limits on treatment.

## Apply the findings

Use the CT and operative plan to decide what needs optimisation: hostile access or a complex graft increases procedure length, contrast, need for GA and the consequences of rescue. Ask whether the patient can lie flat with minimal sedation and whether frailty or an unstable cardiac condition changes the balance between intervention and surveillance. Discuss expected recovery and longer-term imaging as well as perioperative mortality.

For a patient taking a GLP-1 or GLP-1/GIP drug, check the current ANZCA preparation pathway and the ability to complete a 24-hour clear-fluid diet. Identify any aspiration mitigation needed if preparation is incomplete. For metformin, consider kidney function, AKI and first-pass contrast exposure rather than using a universal eGFR 60 threshold.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/125132) · Risk stratification, cardiac comorbidity, relevant investigations and optimisation; systematic reserve assessment, complex medications, frailty and prehabilitation strengthen answers.
rubric: Stratifies cardiac risk with history, functional capacity and ECG; selects echo/CPET/biomarkers when indicated
Assesses renal function, respiratory disease, diabetes, frailty and anaemia
Reviews medications: antiplatelets continued, SGLT2 inhibitor held, anticoagulants managed
Considers aneurysm morphology, access and the anaesthetic technique
Plans for contrast and radiation, spinal drain if needed, and conversion to open repair
Optimises comorbidity, includes prehabilitation and smoking cessation
Organises blood, monitoring and critical care
Includes shared decision-making and consent

items.title: 2025.1 Q15: Awake carotid endarterectomy: regional technique and anatomy
items.q: Describe your regional anaesthesia technique, including the relevant anatomy, for a patient requiring an awake carotid endarterectomy. (50%) Justify your choice of regional technique. (50%)
items.model:
## Relevant anatomy (50% with technique)

The plexus is formed by ventral rami **C1–C4**, deep to SCM. Cutaneous branches **C2–C4** emerge near the midpoint of its posterior border: lesser occipital (C2), great auricular (C2–C3), transverse cervical (C2–C3) and supraclavicular (C3–C4). The **angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve**; chin/lower lip are V3 territory. Deep branches include muscular branches and ansa cervicalis. The phrenic nerve arises from **C3–C5**, mainly C4, on anterior scalene; C5 is not part of the cervical plexus proper.

## Preop

Choose a **unilateral ultrasound-guided intermediate cervical plexus block with planned surgeon supplementation**, explaining awake testing and possible conversion. Check cooperation, ability to lie still, airway, respiratory reserve, contralateral vocal-cord dysfunction, antithrombotics and baseline neurological function. Agree the total local anaesthetic dose and supplementation budget with the surgeon. Consent, IV access, standard monitoring, arterial BP and ready access to airway/resuscitation equipment and lipid emulsion; avoid sedation that prevents reliable testing.

## Intraop

### Technique

- **1.** Supine, head supported and gently turned away. Prepare aseptically. With a high-frequency linear probe identify **C4**, SCM, prevertebral muscles/fascia and major vessels; use Doppler and keep the needle tip visible.
- **2.** Approach from posterior in-plane, placing the tip **deep to SCM but superficial to prevertebral fascia**. Aspirate and inject incrementally at low pressure, observing spread; negative aspiration does not exclude intravascular placement.
- **3.** An example is **10–15 mL ropivacaine 0.375–0.5%** (37.5–75 mg), adjusted for the patient, spread and planned top-ups. Calculate the total mg from every injection. Use the current product/local maximum and reduce in frail patients; a nominal mg/kg ceiling does not ensure safety.
- **4.** Distinguish this from a **superficial block**, deposited subcutaneously along posterior SCM, and a **deep block**, deposited beneath prevertebral fascia near C2–C4 roots. They are not interchangeable names.
- **5.** Test the incision territory before surgery. Arrange cautious surgeon infiltration of unblocked incision/deeper carotid-sheath tissues as required, tracking cumulative dose. **Do not routinely block/infiltrate the carotid sinus** to prevent haemodynamic changes.
- **6.** Maintain verbal contact, contralateral hand grip and consciousness checks during clamping, minimal/no sedation, an agreed shunt trigger, haemodynamic support and a rehearsed conversion plan.

### Justification of chosen block (50%)

Intermediate plus surgical supplementation targets the operative field while avoiding a planned deep root injection. A superficial block alone may leave deep dissection painful; supplementation is part of the anaesthetic plan, not evidence that cutaneous analgesia alone is sufficient. Deep block adds risk of phrenic/recurrent laryngeal/vagal block, vertebral-artery injection and neuraxial spread. Superficial/intermediate techniques still risk LAST, bleeding, nerve injury, incomplete block and unintended deeper spread. Ultrasound reduces uncertainty but cannot guarantee safety.

Awake testing offers direct functional assessment of cerebral perfusion and can guide selective shunting. Cooperation and airway access remain limitations. GALA did not establish a significant difference in stroke/MI/death between local and general anaesthesia; justify **this regional technique**, rather than claiming regional anaesthesia improves survival.

## Postop

Early neurological and voice/airway assessment, neck-haematoma and BP surveillance; document block effects and any complications.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/120628) · Describe anatomy, an effective anaesthetic technique and why that block was chosen. Specify sono-anatomy and safe doses; analgesia alone is insufficient.
