items.title: 2025.1 Q8: Physiology of aortic clamping and unclamping in open AAA repair
items.q: Describe the physiological changes during aortic cross-clamping and unclamping in elective open abdominal aortic aneurysm surgery. (50%) Discuss the anaesthesia strategies used to manage these physiologic consequences. (50%)
items.model:
## Physiological changes

| | **Cross-clamping** | **Unclamping** |
|---|---|---|
| **Afterload** | **SVR rises** abruptly; MAP rises | **SVR falls** (reactive hyperaemia, vasodilator metabolites) |
| **Preload** | May rise with proximal redistribution; infrarenal response depends on venous capacitance, collaterals and ventricular function | **Relative hypovolaemia**: blood pools in reperfused legs |
| **Heart** | Increased wall tension, **ischaemia and failure** in a poor ventricle; cardiac output may fall, remain stable or rise depending on ventricular function and loading | Hypotension, reduced coronary perfusion; myocardial depressant factors |
| **Organs** | Renal, visceral and spinal ischaemia below the clamp | Reperfusion injury: **acidosis, potassium, lactate, CO2** wash out |

The effects depend on **clamp position**: higher clamps generally cause greater stress: **suprarenal** clamping interrupts renal inflow; mesenteric/coeliac ischaemia depends on the exact relationship to those vessels. **Supracoeliac** clamping additionally interrupts their inflow; **infrarenal** clamps have smaller effects. Blood pressure is not cardiac output: pressure may rise while output falls.

## Strategies

**Before clamping**
- **Arterial line**, central venous access and cardiac output monitoring (pulse contour or oesophageal Doppler or TOE in selected patients).
- Optimise volume and avoid both hypovolaemia and overload; **epidural** (thoracic) provides analgesia but causes vasodilation, so is titrated cautiously.
- **Heparin** before clamping; warm the patient, have blood and cell salvage ready.

**During clamping**
- Keep the MAP at baseline with a **vasodilator** (GTN) or deepen anaesthesia if afterload rises; use an **inotrope or vasodilator** if the ventricle struggles.
- Minimise clamp time; protect the kidney (adequate perfusion pressure and volume; low-dose dopamine is not recommended for renal protection; routine mannitol has no established benefit).

**Before and during unclamping**
- **Warn the surgeon**; replace assessed volume deficits before release, **reduce vasodilators while maintaining adequate anaesthesia**, and prepare a vasopressor (noradrenaline or phenylephrine).
- The surgeon **releases the clamp slowly**, with partial re-clamping if the BP falls.
- Check **blood gases, potassium and lactate**; treat acidosis, hyperkalaemia and calcium.

## Apply the findings

With a high proximal pressure and low stroke volume, vasodilation may reduce LV wall stress, but coronary and distal perfusion still matter. Read the pressure against LV filling, ECG and the level of the clamp. At release, hypotension from renewed vascular capacity and washout may coexist with ongoing bleeding or ventricular dysfunction. If severe and refractory, ask the surgeon to pause or temporarily reapply the clamp while evaluating those causes.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/120628) · Explain clamp/unclamp physiology and management at each stage; consider clamp position and distinguish blood pressure from output. Explain how relative preload reduction is mitigated.

items.title: 2024.1 Q12: Carotid clamping and unclamping: physiology and protection
items.q: Outline the physiological changes associated with carotid artery clamping and unclamping during carotid endarterectomy. (50%) Outline intra-operative protection strategies to minimise harm from these manoeuvres. (50%)
items.model:
## Physiological changes

**Clamping**
- **Antegrade flow through the clamped ipsilateral internal carotid stops**; cerebral perfusion depends on **collateral flow** (circle of Willis, external carotid and ophthalmic anastomoses). Collaterals are incomplete in many patients.
- In chronic stenosis, distal vessels may already be dilated with exhausted reserve; autoregulation can be impaired, increasing dependence on collateral perfusion pressure.
- Sinus manipulation can cause bradycardia/hypotension; clamping may reduce baroreceptor input and increase sympathetic tone. Responses depend on clamp location, contralateral function and anaesthesia; there is no invariant BP/HR sequence.

**Unclamping**
- Flow is restored: **embolisation** of debris or air, **reperfusion and hyperaemia** (risk of **cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome** and haemorrhage).
- Reperfusion and altered baroreceptor function may cause hypotension, bradycardia or hypertension. Assess the actual response and prevent both hypoperfusion and excessive reperfusion pressure.

## Protection strategies

**Monitor cerebral perfusion**
- **Awake patient** (regional anaesthesia) is the most sensitive: speech, consciousness and contralateral hand grip.
- Under GA: **EEG**, **somatosensory evoked potentials**, **transcranial Doppler**, **near-infrared spectroscopy** (limited sensitivity), and **stump pressure** (centres use thresholds around 40–50 mmHg, but no single value guarantees adequate cerebral perfusion).

**Maintain perfusion**
- **Arterial line before induction**; keep the **MAP at or 10 to 20% above baseline** during clamping, using phenylephrine or noradrenaline.
- **Normocapnia** (hypocapnia constricts; hypercapnia causes steal), normoglycaemia, normothermia, adequate Hb.
- **Shunt** when monitoring shows ischaemia (or routinely per surgeon), with the risk of embolism and intimal injury.

**Reduce embolic injury**
- **Heparin** (about 5000 units) before clamping; continue aspirin and statin.
- The surgeon flushes before restoring flow.

**Unclamping**
- Treat **hypertension** to avoid hyperperfusion (target within 20% of baseline or lower per surgeon) and **bradycardia** (stop sinus traction/manipulation, assess perfusion, give atropine and vasopressor as indicated; routine sinus blockade is not recommended); avoid hypotension.

## Apply the findings

A new focal deficit on clamping under awake testing warrants immediate communication, confirmation of arterial pressure and oxygenation, and an assessment of shunt need. Under GA compare a new lateralised EEG/SSEP change with the pre-clamp baseline and anaesthetic depth, or assess TCD/NIRS trends where available. Changes during shunting or after release can represent embolism even when pressure is adequate. Maintain normocapnia and correct hypoxaemia, significant anaemia or low cardiac output. Document the signal response after intervention.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/117151) · Correct haemodynamic and cerebral-flow changes, perfusion/ischaemia monitoring, BP targets and protection during and after clamping.

items.title: 2022.2 Q11: Acute descending thoracic aortic dissection: preoperative blood pressure management
items.q: A 75-year-old man presents with an acute dissection of the descending thoracic aorta. His blood pressure measures 190/110 mmHg. Justify your plan for his preoperative blood pressure management. (30%) Describe the potential complications of thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) and how you would mitigate them. (70%)
items.model:
## Preop

### Blood pressure (30%)

This is a **Type B dissection**. Propagation is driven by **aortic wall stress (dP/dt)** and the BP, so the aim is **anti-impulse therapy**: reduce **heart rate 60–80/min** and **SBP <120 mmHg or the lowest pressure maintaining organ perfusion**, while maintaining organ perfusion.

- **Arterial line** (right radial, as the left subclavian may be involved) and measure both arms.
- **Analgesia** (fentanyl or morphine) as pain drives the BP.
- **Beta-blocker first** (esmolol or labetalol IV) to lower dP/dt and prevent reflex tachycardia; add a **vasodilator** (GTN, nicardipine, or nitroprusside with cyanide caution) only after heart rate control.
- Watch for **malperfusion** (renal, mesenteric, limb, spinal): do not drop the BP so far that organs lose perfusion.

## Intraop

### TEVAR complications and mitigation (70%)

| Complication | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| **Spinal cord ischaemia** (coverage extent, compromised collaterals, hypotension) | Avoid hypotension, maintain oxygen delivery and collateral supply; assess staging/left subclavian revascularisation. Drain strategy is individualised: 2026 ESVS allows rescue rather than routine prophylactic drainage in extensive TEVAR; have immediate rescue capability |
| **Stroke** (arch manipulation, left subclavian coverage) | Gentle wire work, avoid hypotension, heparin, consider arch vessel protection |
| **Access injury and rupture** (large-bore iliofemoral access) | Imaging of access, cross-matched blood, surgical team ready |
| **Retrograde type A dissection, new tear** | Careful sizing, minimise balloon use, TOE or CT follow-up |
| **Malperfusion, endoleak, graft collapse** | Fenestration or stent, completion angiography |
| **Contrast-associated AKI** | Minimise contrast, hydrate, avoid nephrotoxins |
| **Haemodynamic instability at deployment** | Agree deployment conditions; transient BP reduction, **rapid pacing or adenosine only when required by the device/operator**, with rescue ready; arterial line for beat-to-beat monitoring |
| **Post-implantation syndrome, left arm ischaemia, radiation** | Supportive care, shielding |

**Anaesthesia:** GA is usual (immobility and apnoea), with an arterial line, central access, large-bore IV, heparin (ACT above 250 seconds), blood available, and a critical care bed.

## Postop

Critical-care neurological/limb and organ-perfusion checks, renal function and bleeding surveillance. After exclusion/repair, spinal-perfusion support may require **higher MAP** than the pre-repair anti-impulse target; agree the competing aortic and spinal goals with the team. New weakness requires immediate spinal-cord rescue. Uncomplicated acute Type B dissection starts with medical management; rupture/malperfusion or other complications warrant urgent intervention, while selected high-risk uncomplicated cases may undergo planned subacute TEVAR.

## Apply the findings

Check perfusion during initial treatment by serial limb examinations, neurological status, urine output and lactate, because branch malperfusion can evolve even when a proximal pressure looks satisfactory. Before TEVAR identify the actual proximal landing zone and likely left subclavian coverage. Anticipate left-arm or vertebrobasilar ischaemia, particularly with dependent collateral circulation or a patent left internal mammary graft. Persistent visceral or renal injury requires prompt graft/branch evaluation.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106410) · Identify descending Type B pathology, justify initial BP/rate control and address TEVAR-specific complications. Do not substitute an emergency Type A/open-rupture answer.

items.title: 2020.2 Q2: Endovascular thoraco-abdominal aneurysm repair: complications and strategies
items.q: A 75-year-old man is scheduled for elective endovascular repair of a thoraco-abdominal aortic aneurysm. List the potential complications of this procedure in this patient and discuss your strategies to mitigate these complications.
items.model:
## Complications

- **Spinal cord ischaemia** (paraplegia): loss of segmental supply with long aortic coverage.
- **Renal impairment:** contrast, atheroembolism, coverage of renal or visceral branches.
- **Haemorrhage:** access vessel injury, aortic rupture, coagulopathy after heparin.
- **Myocardial infarction** (haemodynamic stress; he is 75 with likely IHD).
- **Stroke:** arch atheroma embolisation, hypotension.
- **Visceral and limb ischaemia**, endoleak, graft migration.
- **Contrast reaction, radiation exposure, post-implantation syndrome** and respiratory complications.

## Mitigation

**Spinal cord ischaemia (specific strategies)**
- **Drain strategy:** distinguish extensive endovascular repair from open TAAA. A prophylactic drain is not automatic; the 2026 ESVS guideline permits a rescue-first strategy for extensive TEVAR (IIb C). Agree risk assessment and immediate rescue access, accounting for anticoagulation and drain-related bleeding.
- **SCPP ≈ MAP − max(CSF pressure, CVP).** Use the centre’s oxygen-delivery/MAP protocol; MAP 80 and CSF 15 give only **65 mmHg**, not 70. A new deficit requires urgent MAP augmentation (often ≥90–100 mmHg), correction of hypoxaemia/anaemia and expert CSF drainage if safe; targets balance aortic/bleeding risk.
- **Staged repair** and preservation of collateral supply (left subclavian, internal iliac arteries).
- **Motor and somatosensory evoked potentials** if available; neurological checks on waking, with prompt escalation if a deficit appears.
- Drain risks: headache, haematoma, infection, over-drainage; delay if anticoagulated.

**Renal protection:** minimise and dilute contrast, ensure hydration, stop nephrotoxins, maintain MAP, monitor urine output.

**Haemorrhage:** large-bore IV, arterial line, crossmatched blood and cell salvage, imaging of access vessels, surgeon and vascular team ready to convert.

**Cardiac and stroke:** preoperative optimisation, continue beta-blocker and antiplatelets, invasive monitoring, avoid tachycardia and hypotension, careful wire work.

**General:** GA with an arterial line (right radial if the left subclavian is covered), central access, heparin with ACT monitoring, protamine at the end, temperature control and critical care afterwards.

Acknowledge this repair is **often staged and complex** (fenestrated or branched), with higher complication rates than infrarenal EVAR.

## Apply the findings

A complex fenestrated or branched graft can obstruct renal or visceral branches through coverage, dissection or thrombosis. Check the planned targets and completion angiogram, and investigate unexpected oliguria, abdominal pain, lactate rise or loss of a pulse early. Perfusion rescue may require urgent repeat angiography or intervention despite contrast risk. Track lower limb strength once anaesthesia resolves and agree who can place a rescue drain and how anticoagulation will be managed at night.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106407) · Cover spinal cord, renal, haemorrhage, MI and stroke risks plus specific mitigation and imaging-suite context; avoid an open-repair answer.

items.title: 2018.1 Q13: Anaesthesia for lower limb angioplasty and stenting
items.q: A 75-year-old patient presents for lower limb angioplasty and stenting for peripheral vascular disease. Discuss the challenges in providing anaesthesia for this patient.
items.model:
## Preop

### Patient factors

PVD is a marker of **systemic atherosclerosis**: ischaemic heart disease (often silent), heart failure, **cerebrovascular disease**, hypertension, **diabetes**, **CKD**, **COPD and smoking**, and frailty. Functional capacity is hard to assess because claudication limits exercise. Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) are continued; statins and beta-blockers continue; diabetic drugs (SGLT2 inhibitors) and anticoagulants need a plan. Rest pain, ulcers and a painful limb may make lying flat difficult.

## Intraop

### Procedural factors

- **Radiology suite** (remote location): limited access to the patient, radiation (lead, distance, shielding), cold room, unfamiliar team and equipment.
- **Duration** is unpredictable (minutes to hours), the patient lies flat and still.
- **Access**: femoral puncture (or brachial or pedal), **heparin** (ACT), contrast load (**contrast-associated AKI**, anaphylaxis).
- **Complications**: arterial perforation or rupture, distal embolisation, haematoma or retroperitoneal bleed, acute thrombosis, and **need for conversion to open surgery**.

### Anaesthetic options

- **Local anaesthetic infiltration with minimal sedation** is often sufficient; this avoids GA in a high-risk patient and allows the patient to report pain.
- **Regional (spinal or epidural)**: effective but sympathetic blockade can cause hypotension; it needs neuraxial safety (timing with antiplatelets and anticoagulants, heparin), and the patient must lie flat.
- **General anaesthesia** if the patient cannot cooperate, the procedure is long or painful, or conversion to open is likely; airway and haemodynamic control, but greater cardiovascular effects.
- **Monitoring** to standard, plus an arterial line in high-risk patients; maintain normothermia; protect pressure areas.

## Postop

### Recovery plan

Recover with limb/access-site and bleeding checks, renal surveillance where indicated, multimodal analgesia and a clear antithrombotic/mobilisation plan. Bed rest is determined by the closure/access protocol, not a universal prolonged requirement.

## Apply the findings

Plan the transition from a quiet angioplasty to a long or painful intervention. Agree signals for oxygenation or airway difficulty under drapes, patient movement, intractable pain, access haemorrhage and conversion to GA. Deepening sedation in a poorly accessible airway can convert an otherwise stable case into a hypoventilation and aspiration emergency. Afterward, compare pulses, sensation and motor function with baseline and escalate a cold or painful limb or hypotension with a deceptively clean groin. Check total heparin exposure and the time at which sheath removal and mobilisation are planned.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106434) · Cover comorbidity, local/sedation/regional/GA choices and procedural duration, invasiveness, remote location and limited patient access.

items.title: 2017.2 Q2: Blood pressure changes in carotid endarterectomy
items.q: Discuss the significance of anticipated changes in blood pressure during anaesthesia and in the post anaesthesia care unit in a patient undergoing carotid endarterectomy. (50%) Outline strategies to manage these changes. (50%)
items.model:
## Significance

Patients have **hypertension**, impaired **cerebral autoregulation** (pressure-passive flow beyond the stenosis) and often coronary disease, so BP changes matter for the **brain and heart**.

| Time | Expected change | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| **Induction** | Hypotension (or hypertension at laryngoscopy) | Hypotension: cerebral and **myocardial ischaemia**; hypertension: ischaemia, haemorrhage |
| **Clamping** | Hypotension is dangerous; reflex rise with sinus effect | Collateral flow depends on perfusion pressure: **stroke risk** |
| **Unclamping** | Variable BP/HR response; baroreflex dysfunction and reperfusion | Hyperaemia, **hyperperfusion** |
| **PACU** | **Hypertension** common (baroreceptor dysfunction, pain, bladder, hypoxia) | **Neck haematoma and airway obstruction**, intracerebral haemorrhage and cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome, MI; hypotension gives stroke and MI |

## Preop
- Continue antihypertensives, beta-blocker, aspirin and statin; **define baseline BP** from both arms.
## Intraop

- **Arterial line before induction**; titrated induction with vasopressor ready.
- Keep MAP within **10 to 20% of baseline** (higher during clamping to support collaterals, using phenylephrine or noradrenaline).
- Stop sinus handling for bradycardia/hypotension; use atropine and vasoactive support when indicated. Routine carotid sinus local-anaesthetic blockade is not recommended. Treat hypertension with a titratable agent such as labetalol or nicardipine, accounting for heart rate and cardiac function.
- Smooth emergence without coughing; avoid hypoxia and hypercapnia.

## Postop
- Continue arterial monitoring; set **upper limits** (SBP below about 140 to 160 mmHg, per surgeon) and treat **pain, bladder, shivering and hypoxia** first, then titrate a suitable agent such as labetalol/nicardipine under the agreed protocol; avoid abrupt falls.
- **Neurological and neck checks** at regular intervals; urgent escalation for a new deficit or expanding haematoma (airway control, return to theatre).
- HDU admission for high-risk patients.

## Apply the findings

At induction and clamp application, state the patient’s reliable baseline pressure and how you would treat a deviation. Reduce an exaggerated laryngoscopy response using titrated anaesthesia while avoiding a prolonged induction-related fall. During clamping, use neurological monitoring and pressure trends to choose an individual target, then coordinate release and avoid a marked pressure surge. In PACU reassess the reliability of the arterial line, pain, hypoxia and bladder distension before repeated drug boluses. Document thresholds, neurological checks and when to call the surgeon. Severe headache or seizure with marked hypertension also raises concern for cerebral hyperperfusion or intracranial haemorrhage.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106433) · Identify risk at induction, clamping, unclamping and PACU; prevent stroke/MI and recognise hypertension-related neck haematoma.

items.title: 2016.1 Q6: Spinal cord ischaemia risk with endovascular thoraco-abdominal repair
items.q: Outline risk factors for spinal cord ischaemia in a patient undergoing endovascular repair of a thoraco-abdominal aortic aneurysm. (50%) Discuss your approach to minimising spinal cord ischaemia in this setting. (50%)
items.model:
## Risk factors (50%)

Spinal cord perfusion depends on a collateral network connecting intercostal and lumbar segmental vessels with the vertebral/subclavian and internal iliac territories. Extensive aortic coverage sacrifices segmental inflow. Risk increases with long thoracoabdominal coverage, prior infrarenal repair, interruption of multiple collateral territories, left subclavian coverage without revascularisation, bilateral hypogastric compromise and atheroembolism. Emergency or single-stage repair limits time for planning and collateral adaptation. Renal impairment, diffuse atherosclerosis and a low-output ventricle reduce reserve. Hypotension, anaemia, hypoxaemia, long iliac sheath dwell and elevated central venous or CSF pressure impair cord oxygen delivery. A normal end-of-case examination does not exclude delayed injury when pressure subsequently falls.

## Minimise risk (50%)

Preoperatively review the scan with the vascular team and map landing zones, planned segmental coverage, vertebral/subclavian anatomy, prior repair and hypogastric patency. Preserve or restore important collateral inflow when feasible. Discuss elective left subclavian revascularisation where coverage warrants it and whether an extensive elective repair should be staged. Weigh those measures against aneurysm rupture or delay. Establish a baseline leg motor and sensory examination and plan haemodynamic, neurological and postoperative rescue arrangements in advance.

Maintain effective circulation and oxygen content with arterial pressure monitoring, targeted fluids, vasoactive support, adequate oxygenation, warming and correction of clinically important anaemia. Pressure goals should reflect the anatomy, baseline BP and local cord protocol. Limit iliac access-related distal ischaemia. If neuromonitoring is used, assess bilateral signal loss or asymmetry promptly, checking haemodynamics, anaesthetic changes, limb perfusion and technical factors. Approximate cord perfusion pressure as MAP minus the higher of CSF and venous pressure. Discuss selective prophylactic or rescue lumbar drainage for extensive endovascular repair with the aortic team. The ESVS 2026 guidance supports considering a rescue-first strategy in extensive TEVAR. Bleeding risk, heparin timing, catheter complications and availability of immediate rescue affect that choice.

Plan frequent documented lower-limb motor and sensory checks in a monitored unit. For a new deficit, activate the cord-rescue pathway, raise MAP as appropriate, restore cardiac output and oxygen content and review collateral inflow. Consider rescue CSF drainage under a pressure and volume protocol if safe. Investigate competing causes in parallel, including stroke, limb malperfusion and spinal haematoma, especially in a patient with a drain or recent anticoagulation.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Identify relevant comorbidity and the haemodynamic risk, then explain how you will maintain spinal cord perfusion.

items.title: 2015.2 Q11: Complications after carotid endarterectomy in the PACU
items.q: Describe the complications that can occur post carotid endarterectomy and how these may present in the post anaesthesia care unit (PACU).
items.model:
## Specific to carotid endarterectomy

| Complication | Presentation in PACU |
|---|---|
| **Neck haematoma** | Neck pressure/swelling, dysphagia, voice change, distress or venous congestion; stridor/hypoxaemia may be late; **airway compromise is an emergency** |
| **Stroke or TIA** (embolic, thrombosis at the endarterectomy site, hypoperfusion) | New focal deficit, facial droop, weak arm, speech disturbance, reduced conscious level; often found at emergence |
| **Cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome** | Ipsilateral headache, hypertension, seizures, focal deficit (usually day 2 to 7, but may start early) |
| **Cardiovascular instability** | Hypertension or hypotension, bradycardia, **myocardial ischaemia or infarction** (about 1 to 2%), arrhythmia |
| **Cranial nerve injury** | Hypoglossal (tongue deviation), vagus or recurrent laryngeal (hoarseness, weak cough), marginal mandibular (lip), glossopharyngeal (swallowing); aspiration risk |
| **Loss of carotid body function** | Clinically important blunting of hypoxic ventilatory drive is primarily a concern with bilateral carotid-body impairment, not a usual effect of unilateral CEA |
| **Wound** | Pain, infection (later) |

## General factors

- **Patient:** IHD, heart failure, diabetes, CKD, COPD and frailty increase risk.
- **Anaesthetic:** airway obstruction, residual neuromuscular block, opioid respiratory depression, pain, nausea and vomiting, hypothermia, shivering and delirium.

## Recognition and response

Regular **neurological, airway and neck checks** with BP monitoring. Expanding haematoma with threatened airway: call surgeon/airway help, give oxygen and decompress/open the wound urgently at bedside if required; do not wait for transfer when airway compromise is evolving. Arrange definitive haemostasis and anticipate difficult intubation. A stable haematoma still needs immediate surgical review but not automatic bedside opening. New deficit: establish last-known-well, glucose and BP, activate vascular/stroke teams for urgent CTA/re-exploration decisions. Recent major surgery makes systemic thrombolysis high-risk and often unsuitable; thrombectomy may remain possible. Consider hyperperfusion/haemorrhage as well as thrombosis.

## Apply the findings

Ask immediately whether the patient can swallow, whether their voice has changed, and whether neck swelling or respiratory effort is increasing. Bleeding can produce severe laryngeal oedema and deterioration before swelling looks dramatic. Call the surgeon and airway assistance simultaneously and agree the airway and wound-decompression plan. With a new focal deficit record the last normal examination and check glucose, BP and oxygenation. Coordinate urgent surgical and stroke assessment to distinguish local thrombosis, embolic stroke, haemorrhage and hyperperfusion, as pathways differ.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106429) · Explain PACU presentation of CEA-specific bleeding/airway, stroke and cardiovascular instability, as well as general patient/anaesthetic complications.

items.title: 2010.2 Q12: General versus local anaesthesia for carotid endarterectomy
items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of general versus local anaesthesia for carotid endarterectomy?
items.model:
## General anaesthesia

**Advantages**
- **Controlled conditions**: immobile patient, secure airway, controlled ventilation and CO2.
- **Possible cerebral protection** (reduced metabolic rate with anaesthetic agents; EEG-guided).
- Patient comfort and lack of awareness; no need for cooperation.
- Avoids complications specific to local techniques (failed block, patient anxiety, panic with sudden conversion).

**Disadvantages**
- **Loss of the neurological examination**: cerebral ischaemia needs other monitoring (EEG, SSEP, TCD, stump pressure), which is less sensitive.
- More **haemodynamic instability** (induction hypotension, hypertension at intubation and emergence), requiring vasoactive drugs.
- Potential airway/pulmonary effects, PONV and recovery burden; shunt use may be higher. These are practical considerations, not proof that GA worsens major clinical outcomes.

## Local or regional anaesthesia (cervical plexus block or infiltration)

**Advantages**
- **Awake neurological monitoring**, the most sensitive test of cerebral ischaemia, so a shunt is used only when needed (fewer shunts).
- May avoid induction/intubation BP swings, but hypotension/hypertension still occur; regional anaesthesia does not restore impaired autoregulation.
- Avoids GA airway instrumentation and may facilitate recovery; GALA did not establish a hospital-stay advantage.

**Disadvantages**
- Needs a **calm, cooperative patient** who can lie flat; failure or inadequate block may need supplementation or conversion to GA with a partly draped airway.
- Block risks: phrenic nerve palsy, intravascular or intrathecal injection, local anaesthetic toxicity, anxiety and claustrophobia.
- Limited airway control if a stroke, seizure or bleed occurs.

## Evidence

**GALA (3526 patients):** stroke, MI or death within 30 days occurred in **4.8% GA versus 4.5% local**, RR **0.94 (95% CI 0.70–1.27)**. There was **no statistically significant difference**, which is not proof of equivalence. Individualise the technique to patient preference, cooperation, anatomy, team expertise and rescue capability.

## Apply the findings

Regional success depends on the patient’s ability to lie still, communicate and tolerate deep dissection with planned supplementation. Under general anaesthesia, ask how the team will detect clamp intolerance and recognise embolism, and ensure an early examination on emergence. For either technique, plan analgesia, haemodynamic control, antiplatelet management and neck/airway surveillance. Conversion from awake surgery should be rehearsed before draping and shunting decisions agreed before clamping. Balance distal neurological testing against the patient’s airway, communication and preferences.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106419) · Compare CEA-specific advantages/disadvantages, awareness/preference, airway/control, cerebral protection and neurological monitoring; interpret outcome evidence.

Lists local advantages: awake neurological monitoring, selective shunting and avoidance of GA effects
Lists local disadvantages: cooperation, failure, airway access and block complications

items.title: 2010.2 Q2: Spinal cord blood supply and protection in thoracic aortic repair
items.q: (a) Describe the arterial blood supply of the spinal cord. (50%) (b) Why is spinal cord function at risk during open repair of a thoracic aortic aneurysm and what measures are available to reduce this risk? (50%)
items.model:
## Arterial supply (50%)

The single anterior spinal artery arises from branches of the vertebral arteries and runs in the anterior median fissure. Its sulcal branches supply the anterior two-thirds, including most grey matter, anterior horns and much of the anterolateral cord. Paired posterior spinal arteries, arising variably from vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar arteries, supply the dorsal cord. Pial anastomoses connect the longitudinal vessels. Anterior and posterior radicular vessels accompany the roots through the intervertebral foramina. A subset of radiculomedullary arteries reaches and reinforces the spinal arteries. Their segmental sources include cervical arteries, posterior intercostal and lumbar vessels.

The great anterior radiculomedullary artery (Adamkiewicz) usually enters from the left in the lower thoracic or upper lumbar region, with important anatomical variation. Perfusion also depends on the paraspinal collateral network and inflow from subclavian/vertebral and pelvic territories. Anterior spinal ischaemia can produce weakness and loss of pain/temperature with relative posterior column sparing, although spinal cord injury after repair may be incomplete or multifocal.

## Why open repair threatens the cord and how to protect it (50%)

Cross-clamping interrupts distal perfusion and intercostal inflow. Exclusion or sacrifice of segmental arteries can then persist after release. Low distal pressure, emboli, anaemia, hypoxaemia and high CSF or venous pressure reduce cord oxygen delivery. Blood loss and hypotension may unmask delayed injury when the collateral circulation is marginal.

Before surgery review the extent and prior repair, collateral vessels and baseline function. During repair use sequential clamping and limit ischaemic time. Distal perfusion such as left-heart bypass reduces ischaemia when appropriate. Selective reimplantation of important patent segmental arteries and temperature management depend on operative extent and expertise. Maintain haemoglobin, oxygenation and perfusion and use motor evoked potentials when available, with an agreed response to signal loss. Options include improving distal flow and pressure, checking technical and anaesthetic causes and considering reimplantation.

Prophylactic CSF drainage is supported in open descending thoracic or thoracoabdominal repair. Coselli’s randomised trial studied extensive open TAAA, so its result should be applied in context. Use a specialist drain protocol to prevent overdrainage, haematoma and infection. After surgery maintain monitored perfusion, perform frequent leg examinations and respond urgently to a deficit with haemodynamic rescue, review of collateral or distal flow and CSF pressure, and investigation for other causes.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Describe segmental reinforcement and supply territories. Organise protection into reducing ischaemia, supporting perfusion and monitoring with a plan for abnormal signals.

items.title: 2006.2 Q3: Cardiovascular changes with supra-renal aortic clamping and unclamping
items.source: Past SAQ 2006.2 Q3 · pass rate not reported
items.q: Describe the cardiovascular changes which occur during clamping and unclamping of the supra-renal aorta during repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm in a patient with normal ventricular function and outline your strategies to maintain critical organ perfusion during these times.
items.model:
## Cardiovascular changes

**Supra-renal clamping**
- **Afterload rises sharply**: SVR and MAP increase (renal and distal arterial inflow is interrupted; greater visceral exclusion occurs only if the clamp lies above the relevant mesenteric/coeliac branches).
- **Preload** shifts to the upper body; LVEDP, wall tension and myocardial oxygen demand increase. With **normal ventricular function**, output may be maintained, rise or fall according to preload redistribution, clamp level and contractile reserve. A rise in MAP does not prove adequate flow or coronary oxygen balance.
- The kidneys and distal tissues lose direct inflow; gut ischaemia depends on the precise clamp level and collaterals, not the label “suprarenal” alone.

**Unclamping**
- **SVR falls abruptly** (vasodilator metabolites, reactive hyperaemia) and venous return falls as blood pools in the lower body: **hypotension**.
- **Acid and potassium load**, lactate and CO2 wash out; myocardial depression.
- **Reperfusion injury** of the kidneys and gut.

## Strategies to maintain critical organ perfusion

**Before clamping:** arterial and central venous monitoring (plus cardiac output); assessed volume replacement without indiscriminate loading; **epidural** for analgesia; heparin.

**During clamping (kidneys, gut, spinal cord, heart)**
- Keep MAP at baseline or just below using a vasodilator (GTN) if needed, and control heart rate; avoid ventricular distension.
- **Minimise clamp time**; the surgeon may use **distal perfusion** (shunt or partial bypass) or clamp sequentially.
- **Renal protection**: adequate volume and perfusion pressure, avoid routine renal-dose dopamine or unproven drug protection, avoid nephrotoxins; check urine output and acid-base.
- Avoid unintended hypothermia in routine open AAA repair; planned temperature reduction is reserved for specific complex-aortic protocols, balancing coagulopathy and metabolic protection.

**Before and at unclamping**
- Coordinate gradual release, replace measured/assessed volume deficits, **reduce vasodilators while maintaining adequate anaesthesia**, and prepare noradrenaline or phenylephrine.
- **Slow clamp release** with partial re-clamping if BP falls; correct acidosis, potassium and calcium.
- Maintain the perfusion pressure for the kidney, gut and spinal cord until the situation is stable.

## Apply the findings

An arterial pressure above the clamp does not demonstrate renal flow when the renal arteries are interrupted. Coordinate clamping sequence and time, discuss whether selective renal perfusion is indicated, and monitor blood loss and systemic output. At unclamping be prepared for vasodilation and washout with a titratable vasopressor and measured replacement of deficits. If profound hypotension persists, consider bleeding, myocardial dysfunction and arrhythmia and ask about staged release or temporary reclamping.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106412) · Cover both clamping AND unclamping and measures that maintain critical-organ perfusion in each; unrelated drug-protection discussion does not answer the stem.

items.title: 2006.1 Q11: General anaesthesia for carotid endarterectomy
items.source: Past SAQ 2006.1 Q11 · pass rate not reported
items.q: Discuss the principles underlying the management of a general anaesthetic for carotid endarterectomy.
items.model:
## Principles

CEA aims to **prevent stroke** while protecting the **heart**. Patients have widespread atherosclerosis, and cerebral perfusion may become increasingly pressure-dependent when reserve is exhausted. Organise the answer around **cerebral perfusion, cardiac protection, haemodynamic stability, and a rapid, assessable emergence**.

## Preop

- Assess **cerebrovascular symptoms** (recent stroke, TIA, timing: surgery within about two weeks of a symptomatic event), cardiac, renal and respiratory disease, diabetes and baseline neurology.
- **Baseline BP in both arms**; optimise hypertension.
- Continue **aspirin, statin and beta-blocker**; ECG; consider echocardiography.
- Discuss the technique, consent, and the alternative of regional anaesthesia.

## Intraop

- **Arterial line before induction**; ECG with ST analysis; capnography; temperature.
- **Haemodynamic stability**: titrated induction, short-acting agents (propofol, remifentanil), avoidance of hypotension and hypertensive responses.
- **Maintain cerebral perfusion**: keep MAP at or above baseline during clamping with a vasopressor; normocapnia; normoglycaemia; normothermia.
- **Monitor the brain** (EEG, SSEP, TCD, NIRS, stump pressure) to guide **shunting**.
- **Heparin** before clamping, protamine at the end per surgeon.
- **Carotid sinus:** stop provocative handling for bradycardia, then atropine/vasoactive support as needed. Avoid routine prophylactic local-anaesthetic sinus blockade.
- Consider avoiding nitrous oxide where air embolism is a concern; it is not a defining requirement for all CEA. Protect eyes and head position (neck extension and rotation).

## Postop

- **Smooth emergence** (avoid coughing and hypertension) with early **neurological assessment**.
- Treat **BP** within limits (neither high nor low), monitor in PACU or HDU.
- Observe for **neck haematoma and airway compromise**, stroke and cranial nerve injury.
- Analgesia, antiemetics and continued antiplatelets.

## Apply the findings

Before clamping, confirm who will request shunting and the response to a monitoring change. Avoid hypoxia, marked CO₂ deviations and a poorly tolerated pressure drop, and reassess anaesthetic or technical causes if monitors change. For a significant persistent signal change, improve perfusion and discuss shunt placement, recognising its own risk of embolism or dissection. At the end obtain an early neurological examination, then hand over comparisons with baseline, haemodynamic targets, and immediate action if voice change, stridor, severe headache or focal weakness develops. Position the head and neck to allow surgical exposure without excessive rotation, secure the airway before access is lost, and confirm an alternative plan should surgical bleeding make examination or extubation unsafe.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106411) · Organise preop/intraop/postop principles specific to CEA, rather than a generic anaesthetic recipe.
